hazard: Deploying unmanaged AI systems that lack organizational visibility and tracking.

statement: Categorize the risk level of the AI solution prior to operational deployment.
quote: organizations should categorize the AI solution’s risk prior to deployment.
hazard: Applying generic controls that are insufficient for high-risk AI implementations.

statement: Segregate pilot data environments to prevent contamination of production training pipelines.
quote: HDOs should ensure that pilot data environments are segregated to prevent pilot data from contaminating production training pipelines.
hazard: Pilot experiment data accidentally degrading production operational environments.

statement: Trigger risk or intake reassessment when detecting material changes to scope, configuration, or intended use.
quote: Any material changes to scope, configuration, or intended use identified during deployment should trigger reassessment through intake or risk categorization processes as appropriate.
hazard: Unassessed safety risks originating from undocumented post-deployment AI modifications.

statement: Incorporate human factors monitoring into ongoing AI monitoring programs.
quote: Human factors monitoring (e.g., override behavior tracking and over-reliance/automation bias detection) should be incorporated into monitoring programs.
hazard: Undetected automation bias or user over-reliance affecting healthcare quality.

statement: Define conditions triggering re-review, modification, suspension, or termination of deployed AI solutions.
quote: Organizations may also define conditions that trigger re-review, modification, temporary suspension, or termination of AI solutions.
hazard: Inability to promptly disable failing or unsafe AI systems in production.

statement: Trigger training updates based on monitoring findings that indicate problematic AI usage patterns.
quote: Training updates should be triggered by monitoring findings that reveal problematic usage patterns.
hazard: Continued staff misuse of AI tools due to uncorrected behaviors.

statement: Adopt an existing standardized model card template, such as CHAI's Applied Model Card, instead of building documentation from scratch.
quote: Start with an existing model card template rather than building from scratch. CHAI’s Applied Model Card (AMC) is recommended as it is designed specifically for healthcare delivery contexts.
hazard: Inconsistent or incomplete AI documentation that undermines informed deployment decisions

statement: Document intended use, primary end users, and out-of-scope uses in each AI system's model card.
quote: At minimum, each model card should capture: Model ID and version, Intended use and primary end users, Out-of-scope uses, Training data sources and any known biases, Performance metrics (overall and across relevant subgroups), Safety considerations and known failure modes, Monitoring and alerting information, and Vendor/developer contact information.
hazard: AI used outside its intended scope or by unintended users

statement: Document safety considerations and known failure modes in each AI system's model card.
quote: At minimum, each model card should capture: Model ID and version, Intended use and primary end users, Out-of-scope uses, Training data sources and any known biases, Performance metrics (overall and across relevant subgroups), Safety considerations and known failure modes, Monitoring and alerting information, and Vendor/developer contact information.
hazard: Users unaware of known failure modes relying on faulty outputs

statement: Record performance metrics overall and across relevant subgroups, plus known training data biases, in each model card.
quote: At minimum, each model card should capture: Model ID and version, Intended use and primary end users, Out-of-scope uses, Training data sources and any known biases, Performance metrics (overall and across relevant subgroups), Safety considerations and known failure modes, Monitoring and alerting information, and Vendor/developer contact information.
hazard: Undetected subgroup performance disparities causing inequitable care

statement: Designate staff responsible for reviewing and updating the model card for each AI system.
quote: Designate model card reviewers (staff responsible for reviewing and updating cards for each AI system).
hazard: Outdated documentation with no accountable owner

statement: Require vendors to provide model card information as part of AI procurement.
quote: For vendor-supplied AI, require model card information as part of procurement—many vendors will provide this in response to formal requests even if they do not proactively share it.
hazard: Procuring opaque vendor AI without knowledge of limitations

statement: Require model card completion as a mandatory step in the approval workflow for internally developed AI.
quote: For internally developed AI, require card completion as a mandatory step in your AI development or approval workflow.
hazard: Internal AI deployed without documented purpose, limits, or performance

statement: Make completed model cards a prerequisite for deployment approval (no model card, no deployment clearance).
quote: Consider making model card completion status a prerequisite for deployment approval (i.e., no model card = no deployment clearance).
hazard: Undocumented AI tools reaching clinical or operational use

statement: Link each model card to the AI inventory registry rather than storing it as a standalone document.
quote: Model cards are most useful when linked to your AI inventory registry (see Control 6) rather than maintained as standalone documents.
hazard: Documentation inaccessible during incident investigations or vendor reviews

statement: Maintain an AI inventory capturing minimum fields including intended use, deployment status, PHI data inputs, risk tier, approval status, and last review date.
quote: At minimum, capture: Model/system name and unique identifier, Vendor or developer name and contact, Intended use and clinical/operational domain, Deployment status, Primary end users, Data inputs (including PHI sensitivity), Risk tier, Contract/license renewal date, Link to model card or documentation, Governance approval status and date, and Last review date.
hazard: Untracked AI systems escaping governance oversight

statement: Document whether the AI inventory covers only clinical AI or also operational and administrative AI.
quote: Document whether your inventory covers only clinical AI or also operational/administrative AI—many organizations start broad and refine scope over time.
hazard: Administrative AI tools left outside governance scope

statement: Use an inventory tool that is searchable, version-controlled, linked to contract management for renewal alerts, and integrated with model cards.
quote: Document the current tool in use, its limitations, and whether it meets the key capabilities needed: searchable and accessible to governance stakeholders, version-controlled, linked to contract management for renewal alerts, and integrated with model cards.
hazard: Stale inventory and missed contract renewals

statement: Require registration through a formal intake process before any AI solution may be used.
quote: Mechanisms can include: (1) A required intake process--no AI solution may be used without being registered, (2) A regular audit cycle (at minimum annually) to verify entries are current and detect undisclosed use,
hazard: Shadow AI use of unauthorized or undisclosed tools

statement: Audit the AI inventory at least annually to verify entries are current and detect undisclosed AI use.
quote: Mechanisms can include: (1) A required intake process--no AI solution may be used without being registered, (2) A regular audit cycle (at minimum annually) to verify entries are current and detect undisclosed use,
hazard: Undetected shadow AI and outdated inventory records

statement: Provide a mechanism for staff to report AI solutions they use that may not be in the inventory.
quote: (3) A mechanism for staff to report AI solutions they are using that may not be in the inventory (tie to AI policy dissemination and shadow AI awareness efforts).
hazard: Staff use of unvetted AI tools remaining hidden

statement: Document who owns the AI intake process, how it is communicated to staff, and how compliance is monitored.
quote: Document who owns the intake process, how it is communicated to staff, and how compliance is monitored.
hazard: Intake process unenforced due to unclear ownership

statement: Include AI inventory review as a standing agenda item for the AI Governance Committee.
quote: Include inventory review as a standing agenda item for your AI Governance Committee.
hazard: Inventory neglected by governance leadership

statement: Ensure tools and resources for validation and monitoring are available, whether or not the vendor assists.
quote: Additionally, validation and monitoring can be conducted with or without vendor assistance, but the tools and resources must be available.
hazard: Inability to verify local performance or detect degradation

statement: Test AI tools beyond accuracy, including usefulness, usability, security/privacy, and clinical workflow integration.
quote: Testing should go beyond accuracy to include things like usefulness and usability, security/privacy, and clinical workflow integration.
hazard: Accurate tools that are unusable, insecure, or disrupt workflows

statement: Record which AI systems have been validated with which tools and flag unvalidated high-risk clinical AI as priority remediation items.
quote: Note which AI systems have been validated using which tools, and which have not yet been validated. Flag validation gaps—particularly for high-risk clinical AI—as priority remediation items.
hazard: High-risk AI deployed without validation

statement: Validate and monitor higher-risk AI solutions with greater rigor than lower-risk ones.
quote: Higher risk solutions should be validated and monitored with greater rigor.
hazard: Insufficient scrutiny of high-risk tools or excessive burden on low-risk ones

statement: Pilot AI in a small-scale or phased deployment after desk review, monitoring performance, errors, and satisfaction.
quote: Some organizations consider a desk review of a solution the first step of validation, following it with a small scale pilot or phased deployment where they monitor performance, errors, satisfaction, etc.
hazard: Broad deployment of tools that fail in local context

statement: Test AI performance on retrospective local data before connecting it to live data streams.
quote: Others may use retrospective data to test performance before the model ever touches live data streams.
hazard: Poor local performance discovered only after live use

statement: Evaluate whether AI tool performance differs across subgroups such as race/ethnicity, age, sex, language, and insurance status.
quote: Organizations should consider (1) Usefulness: Does the tool improve outcomes in your context? (2) Fairness: Does performance differ across subgroups (race/ethnicity, age, sex, language, insurance status)?
hazard: Inequitable performance harming specific patient groups

statement: Evaluate whether the AI tool improves outcomes in the organization's own context.
quote: Organizations should consider (1) Usefulness: Does the tool improve outcomes in your context?
hazard: Deploying tools that provide no local benefit

statement: Assess the consequences of incorrect AI outputs and confirm fail-safes are in place before deployment.
quote: (3) Safety: What are the consequences of incorrect outputs and are fail-safes in place?
hazard: Incorrect outputs causing patient harm without safeguards

statement: Evaluate whether end users can appropriately use, trust, or distrust the AI tool's outputs.
quote: (4) Transparency: Can end users appropriately use, trust, or distrust outputs?
hazard: Overreliance on or misinterpretation of AI outputs

statement: Verify during validation that the AI tool protects PHI.
quote: (5) Security/Privacy: Does the tool protect PHI?
hazard: Exposure of protected health information

statement: Assign responsibility for each validation dimension and document needed data samples or testing environments.
quote: Document who is responsible for each validation dimension and what data samples or testing environments are needed.
hazard: Validation dimensions left unassessed due to unclear ownership

statement: Produce a validation and monitoring requirements document per AI system specifying dimensions, sample sizes, subgroup requirements, approvers, and external resources.
quote: Action: Produce a validation and monitoring requirements document for each AI system specifying: required validation and monitoring dimensions, minimum sample sizes and subgroup requirements, who approves results, and any external resources needed (e.g., third-party validation, vendor data provision).
hazard: Ad hoc, inconsistent validation lacking accountable approval

statement: Require vendors to provide third-party validation reports and monitoring dashboards.
quote: (1) Require vendors to provide third-party validation reports and monitoring dashboards
hazard: Unverified vendor performance claims when internal expertise is lacking

statement: Partner with academic medical centers, health systems, or HCCNs to share validation and monitoring resources.
quote: (2) Partner with a nearby academic medical center, health systems, HCCN to share validation and monitoring resources,
hazard: Resource-limited organizations deploying AI without validation

statement: Use EHR vendor built-in performance reporting and monitoring tools as a starting point for post-pilot evaluation.
quote: (3) Use EHR vendor built-in performance reporting and monitoring tools as a starting point for post-pilot evaluation,
hazard: No post-pilot performance evaluation

statement: Contractually require vendor-managed cloud AI providers to report performance disaggregated by key subgroups.
quote: (4) For vendor-managed cloud AI, contractually require performance reporting disaggregated by key subgroups.
hazard: Hidden subgroup performance disparities in vendor-hosted AI

statement: Engage a third-party governance service to perform validation testing during the RFP process.
quote: (5) Partner with a third-party governance service that provides validation testing for health systems during their RFP process.
hazard: Selecting vendors without independent validation

statement: Conduct ongoing, not solely manual, monitoring to detect AI solutions that silently stop working after data or hardware changes.
quote: One of the issues that can arise when monitoring is not done on an ongoing basis, or when it relies purely on manual checks, is that AI solutions can silently stop working or fail to trigger due to changes in things like data access, hardware updates, etc.
hazard: Silent AI failure going unnoticed for months

statement: Conduct a mandatory annual evaluation of all deployed AI including stakeholder value check-ins, issue self-reporting, and usage and outcome review.
quote: A large academic medical center shared that their AI governance program requires a mandatory annual evaluation of all deployed AI solutions that includes: 1) Stakeholder check-in to confirm ongoing value 2) Self-reporting of issues or red-flags modeled after an IRB annual review approach 3) Review of usage statistics and outcome variables where applicable.
hazard: Deployed AI no longer used, valuable, or safe without detection

statement: When validation fails, document the failure and request vendor remediation with a defined timeline and re-validation criteria before wider deployment.
quote: Vendor/Solution remediation — Document the specific failure and formally request the vendor/developer address it before wider deployment proceeds, with a defined timeline and re-validation criteria.
hazard: Wider deployment of tools that failed local validation

statement: Document and enforce conditions, safeguards, heightened monitoring, and a re-evaluation date for any conditional deployment after failed validation.
quote: Conditional deployment with enhanced monitoring — Deploy in a limited, constrained context with explicit safeguards, heightened monitoring, and a defined re-evaluation date. Conditions must be documented and enforced.
hazard: Conditionally approved tools causing harm without safeguards

statement: Run pilots with a formal decision gate and pre-defined criteria for halting deployment.
quote: Phased pilot with a defined off-ramp — Begin with a structured pilot (single department, limited cohort, fixed time window) with a formal decision gate and pre-defined criteria for halting.
hazard: Failing pilots continuing without a stopping point

statement: Reject AI tools whose validation failures involve patient safety, systematic bias, or vendor refusal of transparency or remediation.
quote: Reject the tool — Decline deployment entirely. The right answer when failures involve patient safety, systematic bias, or when a vendor refuses transparency or remediation.
hazard: Deploying unsafe, biased, or opaque AI tools

statement: Define success and failure thresholds for each AI solution based on its risk level and use case.
quote: Organizations should define what success and failure thresholds are based on solution risk level and use-case specific considerations.
hazard: Arbitrary go/no-go decisions without predefined criteria

statement: Maintain an AI computing resource inventory including hardware, cloud dependencies, software environments, clinical data connections, and third-party API integrations.
quote: Maintain a computing resource inventory that documents: Physical hardware (servers, GPUs, AI accelerators) used for AI training or inference Cloud service dependencies (which AI systems run on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, or private cloud)
hazard: Unaudited AI infrastructure vulnerable to compromise

statement: Review who has access to AI models, training data, and inference environments as part of AI infrastructure audits.
quote: (1) Access control review—who has access to AI models, training data, and inference environments?
hazard: Unauthorized access to models or sensitive data

statement: Audit whether AI software dependencies are patched and kept up to date.
quote: (2) Patch and vulnerability management—are AI software dependencies kept up to date?
hazard: Exploitable vulnerabilities in AI software stacks

statement: Verify AI systems can be restored after ransomware or system failure and define recovery time objectives.
quote: (3) Backup and recovery—can AI systems be restored after ransomware or system failure? What is the RTO?
hazard: Prolonged AI outage disrupting clinical operations

statement: Log AI system activities to enable detection of anomalous behavior.
quote: (4) Logging and monitoring—are AI system activities logged to enable anomalous behavior detection?
hazard: Undetected manipulation or anomalous AI behavior

statement: Incorporate AI computing infrastructure into the HIPAA Security Rule compliance program, applying technical safeguards fully.
quote: Document how AI computing infrastructure is incorporated into your broader HIPAA Security Rule compliance program (HIPAA Technical Safeguard requirements apply fully to AI infrastructure).
hazard: HIPAA violations and PHI exposure via AI infrastructure

statement: Include AI systems in Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery plans so clinical AI outages are anticipated.
quote: Ensure AI systems are incorporated into Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BCDR) plans—the failure of a clinical AI system during an outage should be anticipated, not improvised.
hazard: Improvised response to AI failure during outages

statement: Document which AI systems are covered under vendor Business Associate Agreements.
quote: Document: which AI systems are covered under vendor Business Associate Agreements, what recovery procedures exist for each AI system, and what computing resources are reserved for AI system restoration.
hazard: PHI shared with AI vendors without BAA protections

statement: Produce a governance roles and responsibilities document or RACI matrix mapping each control to a responsible role.
quote: Action: Produce a Governance Roles and Responsibilities document (or RACI matrix) mapping each Domain 3 control to a responsible role.
hazard: Governance controls not implemented due to unclear ownership

statement: For each AI governance role, document who fills it by title, their responsibilities, and whether it is staffed, shared, or a gap.
quote: For each role, document: who currently fills it (by title, not name), their specific governance responsibilities, and whether that role is staffed, shared, or a gap.
hazard: Unfilled governance roles leaving oversight gaps

statement: Define explicit minimum qualifications or competencies for each AI governance role.
quote: For each AI governance role, document minimum qualifications or competencies. These need not require formal certification for most roles—but should be explicit.
hazard: Unqualified personnel making AI governance decisions

statement: Document applicable state AI training requirements and how the competency framework addresses them.
quote: For organizations subject to state AI regulations (e.g., Texas requiring AI training), document those requirements and how the competency framework addresses them.
hazard: Noncompliance with state AI training regulations

statement: Provide onboarding training for new AI governance personnel and annual refreshers on AI safety, bias mitigation, and regulatory changes.
quote: (1) Initial onboarding training for new governance personnel (2) Annual refresher training covering updates to AI safety practices, bias mitigation, and regulatory changes
hazard: Governance staff with outdated AI safety and regulatory knowledge

statement: Track AI governance training completion and tie it to governance role renewal.
quote: Track completion and tie training to governance role renewal.
hazard: Untrained staff retaining governance responsibilities

statement: Determine for each AI system whether clinical users or staff require pre-implementation training.
quote: For each AI system, determine whether pre-implementation training is required for clinical users or operational staff.
hazard: Users misinterpreting outputs or unaware of limitations

statement: Record each AI system's training requirement in the AI inventory at deployment review.
quote: Document the training requirement for each AI system in the AI inventory (see Control 6) at the time of deployment review.
hazard: Training requirements forgotten or unenforced after deployment

statement: Require greater training for AI providing direct clinical decision support, outputs prone to over-reliance, or novel interfaces and workflows.
quote: Factors that increase training necessity: direct clinical decision support, outputs that clinicians may over-rely on, novel interfaces or workflows,
hazard: Clinician over-reliance on AI outputs

statement: Determine for each AI system whether clinical users or operational staff must complete training before using it.
quote: For each AI system, determine whether pre-implementation training is required for clinical users or operational staff.
hazard: Untrained users misinterpret or over-rely on AI outputs

statement: Record each AI system's training requirement in the AI inventory at the time of deployment review.
quote: Document the training requirement for each AI system in the AI inventory (see Control 6) at the time of deployment review.
hazard: Training requirements go untracked and unenforced at deployment

statement: Include the AI tool's intended use and out-of-scope uses in user training.
quote: (1) What the AI does and does not do—intended use and out-of-scope uses,
hazard: Users apply the tool to out-of-scope tasks

statement: Train users on how to interpret the tool's outputs, including confidence scores or probability estimates.
quote: (2) How to interpret the tool's outputs, including confidence scores or probability estimates,
hazard: Misinterpretation of AI outputs

statement: Train users on the tool's known limitations and failure modes, including when to distrust its output.
quote: (3) Known limitations and failure modes—when to distrust the tool's output,
hazard: Automation bias; acting on erroneous outputs

statement: Train clinicians on what action to take when AI output appears incorrect or unusual.
quote: (4) What action clinicians should take if the output appears incorrect or unusual,
hazard: Incorrect outputs acted upon without correction

statement: Train users on how to report performance concerns or adverse events related to the AI tool.
quote: (5) How to report performance concerns or adverse events related to the AI tool,
hazard: AI failures and adverse events go unreported

statement: Train users on applicable regulatory requirements, such as documentation requirements for AI-assisted decisions.
quote: (6) Applicable regulatory requirements (e.g., documentation requirements for AI-assisted decisions).
hazard: Noncompliant documentation of AI-assisted decisions

statement: Evaluate vendor training materials against the organization's training content criteria and supplement them where gaps exist.
quote: Where vendor training materials are available, evaluate them against these criteria and supplement where needed.
hazard: Vendor training omits local context or key limitations

statement: Retrain or reassess user competency when the AI model is updated or its clinical context of use shifts.
quote: Some AI solutions warrant periodic retraining or competency assessment—particularly when the AI model is updated, when clinical evidence about the tool's performance changes, or when the clinical context of use shifts.
hazard: Users unaware of changed model behavior after updates

statement: Document for each AI solution the ongoing training cadence, whether competency assessment is required, and who owns training completion.
quote: Document for each AI solution: whether ongoing training is required, at what cadence (annual, following model updates, following significant clinical events), whether formal competency assessment is warranted, and who is responsible for managing training completion.
hazard: Ongoing training lapses without accountable owner

statement: Conduct annual check-ins for high-risk clinical AI reviewing ongoing clinical value, user feedback, and usage statistics.
quote: For high-risk clinical AI, consider mirroring the annual check-in model (similar to IRB continuing review) in which ongoing clinical value, user feedback, and usage statistics are reviewed at defined intervals.
hazard: High-risk AI continues without periodic value and safety review

statement: Trigger training updates when monitoring reveals problematic usage patterns such as misuse or non-use.
quote: Training updates should be triggered by monitoring findings that reveal problematic usage patterns.
hazard: Persistent misuse of AI tools

statement: Require completion of a training module before granting user access to a new AI tool, tracking completion in the LMS.
quote: For a new sepsis alert AI, a 30-minute online module is required before access is granted; completion is tracked in the LMS.
hazard: Untrained users access clinical AI tools

statement: Require synchronous training with demonstrated competency before use of high-risk AI tools.
quote: High-risk diagnostic AI (e.g., radiology AI) requires in-person or synchronous training with demonstration of competency before use.
hazard: Incompetent use of high-risk AI

statement: Apply output filtering to generative AI tools to catch unexpected content containing PHI.
quote: Require vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports; apply output filtering for generative AI.
hazard: Generative AI outputs expose PHI

statement: Require AI vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports.
quote: Require vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports; apply output filtering for generative AI.
hazard: Undetected vendor security weaknesses

statement: Include penetration testing and vulnerability scanning rights in AI vendor contracts at the procurement stage.
quote: Include testing rights in contract language at procurement stage—retrofitting contracts is significantly harder.
hazard: Vendors block security testing of deployed AI

statement: Use existing security frameworks to structure AI-specific security evaluations where dedicated testing tools are lacking.
quote: Use existing frameworks to structure evaluations even where dedicated tools don’t yet exist.
hazard: AI-specific vulnerabilities go unevaluated

statement: Create a simple, low-friction, visible intake pathway so staff use the official process instead of unauthorized AI tools.
quote: Focus AI policy dissemination on making the governance process easy and visible; create a simple, low-friction intake pathway so staff want to use the official process.
hazard: Widespread shadow use of public generative AI

statement: Leverage shared services, regional consortia, or health center controlled networks to fill AI governance expertise gaps.
quote: Leverage shared services models, regional health system consortia, and primary care/health center controlled networks.
hazard: Insufficient expertise for AI security and bias evaluation

statement: Include a notification SLA in AI vendor contracts and BAAs requiring notice within a set timeframe of material changes or new versions.
quote: Specifically, AI vendor contracts and BAAs should include a defined notification SLA, requiring the vendor to notify the organization within a specified timeframe whenever a material change occurs to the AI system or whenever a new version is deployed.
hazard: Undisclosed vendor model changes make documentation outdated

statement: Explicitly define material changes in vendor contracts, including intended use, added features, performance degradations, and infrastructure or subprocessor changes.
quote: Material changes should be explicitly defined in the contract to include changes, for example, to intended use, scope of use, or out-of-scope uses, added features, known performance changes or degradations, and changes to underlying infrastructure or subprocessors.
hazard: Ambiguity lets vendors skip notifying significant changes

statement: Prioritize state and federal regulatory requirements, especially for AI solutions meeting the FDA SaMD definition.
quote: Organizations should prioritize state and federal regulatory requirements, especially for AI solutions that meet the definition of a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), as defined by the FDA.
hazard: Regulatory noncompliance for medical device AI

statement: Define an explicit pathway for transitioning successful research AI models into operational use.
quote: HDOs should also define an explicit onramp path for transitioning a successful research model/solution into operational use.
hazard: Research models enter operations without governance review

statement: Explicitly define academic partners' roles and responsibilities in AI codevelopment agreements.
quote: the role and responsibilities of academic partners should be explicitly defined in codevelopment agreements.
hazard: Ambiguous accountability in co-developed AI

statement: Conduct periodic feature-inventory audits of health IT systems when vendors won't commit to advance notice of AI feature changes.
quote: Lastly, some vendors will not voluntarily commit to advance notification of model/solution updates or feature changes: in those cases, HDOs should consider adding periodic feature-inventory audits and/or contractual notification requirements as compensating controls.
hazard: Embedded AI features activated without organizational review

statement: Seek vendor advance notification of new AI functionality or upgrades so they can be reassessed through intake and governance.
quote: HDOs should strive for vendors to provide advance notification of new AI functionality or upgrades. This allows new models/solutions to be re-assessed through the organizational intake and governance process.
hazard: New AI features bypass governance review

statement: Map vendor product architecture, including API calls to third-party models, to applicable contract terms.
quote: Vendors may also expose new functionality within existing terms and conditions, or rely on API calls to third-party models whose terms differ from the platform contract; understanding how product architecture maps to applicable contract terms is critical.
hazard: Third-party model terms conflict with platform contract protections

statement: Publish an explicit list of AI solutions, including LLM tools, that staff are permitted to use.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: Staff use unapproved consumer LLMs

statement: Specify conditions of use for permitted AI tools, including rules for handling PHI.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: PHI entered into unsecured consumer AI tools

statement: Establish and communicate channels for staff to request new AI solutions.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: Unmet needs drive shadow AI use

statement: Address mobile and shadow AI use in staff training.
quote: Mobile and shadow AI should be addressed in policy, training, and ongoing monitoring.
hazard: Staff unaware of risks of unauthorized AI

statement: Monitor on an ongoing basis for mobile and shadow AI use by staff.
quote: Mobile and shadow AI should be addressed in policy, training, and ongoing monitoring.
hazard: Undetected unauthorized AI use

statement: Designate accountable owners, such as an executive sponsor and operational owner, for each AI ingestion modality.
quote: It is recommended that each ingestion modality be paired with a formally designated accountable owner(s) (e.g., an executive sponsor and an operational owner) responsible for lifecycle compliance.
hazard: Ambiguous accountability for vendor and embedded AI

statement: Apply a risk-proportionate approach at each lifecycle step, with a lightweight path for low-risk use cases.
quote: Ensure a risk-proportionate approach across each lifecycle step (e.g., lightweight path for low-risk use cases).
hazard: Governance burden misallocated relative to risk

statement: Define each AI use case by a clear problem, setting, and stakeholders before selecting a solution.
quote: HDOs should identify a clear problem, its setting, and stakeholders involved (which together comprise a use case), thereby quantifying potential return on investment, return on health outcomes, and improvement of healthcare operations.
hazard: AI deployed without clear purpose or value

statement: Capture intended users as well as intended use during AI intake.
quote: Intake should explicitly capture intended users in addition to the intended use.
hazard: AI used by unintended user groups

statement: Collect intake information through a model card or comparable documentation plus a standardized intake questionnaire.
quote: CHAI recommends collecting this information through a model card (see CHAI’s Applied Model Card, hereafter “Applied Model Card AMC)”) or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire
hazard: Incomplete understanding of AI risks and limitations

statement: Use a light-touch initial intake questionnaire to triage AI solutions into low, medium, or high risk.
quote: Part 1 - initial, light-touch set of intake questions to categorize risk (low risk, medium risk, high risk) for triage purposes.
hazard: Inefficient or inconsistent risk triage

statement: Define minimum vendor governance requirements and add them to the AI intake questionnaire.
quote: Minimum vendor governance requirements should be defined by the organization and added to the AI Intake questionnaire.
hazard: Vendors onboarded without baseline governance

statement: Log all AI systems in a centralized inventory capturing intended use, risk tier, monitoring owner, and version.
quote: It is recommended that all AI systems, regardless of ingestion modality, be logged in a centralized AI inventory that captures: intended use, risk tier, monitoring owner, version tracking, and other relevant components.
hazard: Untracked AI systems escape oversight

statement: Categorize each AI solution's risk before deployment.
quote: Once intake information has been gathered, organizations should categorize the AI solution’s risk prior to deployment.
hazard: Inadequate controls for high-risk AI

statement: Update clinical, population, and organizational risk assessments using insights from validation and silent evaluation.
quote: Updates to clinical, population, and organizational risk should be incorporated based on insights from development, validation, and silent evaluation.
hazard: Risk assessment ignores pre-deployment evidence

statement: Define what constitutes sufficient validation evidence at each risk tier.
quote: Evidence standards for validation should be risk-tiered, including: (1) what constitutes sufficient validation evidence at each tier; (2) when local validation is mandatory versus accepted by vendor attestation; and (3) the role of the governance body in defining acceptable and unacceptable uses.
hazard: Insufficient validation for high-risk AI

statement: Specify when local validation is mandatory versus when vendor attestation is acceptable.
quote: Evidence standards for validation should be risk-tiered, including: (1) what constitutes sufficient validation evidence at each tier; (2) when local validation is mandatory versus accepted by vendor attestation; and (3) the role of the governance body in defining acceptable and unacceptable uses.
hazard: Vendor claims accepted without local performance check

statement: Have the governance body define acceptable and unacceptable uses of each AI solution.
quote: Evidence standards for validation should be risk-tiered, including: (1) what constitutes sufficient validation evidence at each tier; (2) when local validation is mandatory versus accepted by vendor attestation; and (3) the role of the governance body in defining acceptable and unacceptable uses.
hazard: AI used for inappropriate purposes

statement: Include a conditional right-to-terminate clause without penalty when contracts are signed before pre-deployment assessment is complete.

statement: Leverage a rigorous risk assessment to evaluate AI solutions categorized as higher risk.

statement: Map vendor product architecture, including API calls to third-party models, to applicable contract terms.

statement: Explicitly state which AI solutions, including consumer LLMs, staff are permitted to use.

statement: Anchor AI definitions to an established external standard or recognized literature.

hazard: Arbitrary or inconsistent definitions creating governance scope disputes.

statement: State that AI policy definitions are subject to revision.
quote: Anchor definitions to an established external standard (e.g., NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 22989:2022, FDA definitions, academic/industry literature) and acknowledge that definitions are subject to revision.
hazard: Static definitions excluding emerging AI technologies from governance.

statement: Translate formal AI definitions into practical yes/no decision trees staff can apply to specific tools.
quote: Supplement formal definitions with a practical decision tree translating the definition into yes/no questions staff can apply to a specific tool.
hazard: Staff failing to recognize tools that meet the organization's AI definition.

statement: Include examples of tools and uses that are inside and outside AI governance scope.
quote: Include illustrative examples of what is and is not in scope to reduce interpretive variance.
hazard: Inconsistent interpretation of AI governance applicability.

statement: Document a review calendar for the AI policy.
quote: Assign named policy ownership with a documented review calendar.
hazard: Policy reviews being missed because their timing is undocumented.

statement: Use a tiered policy review schedule that distinguishes lightweight annual checks from comprehensive biennial reviews.
quote: Use a tiered review schedule (lightweight annual check vs. comprehensive biennial review).
hazard: Unsustainable review burden or inadequate depth of policy reassessment.

statement: Maintain a standardized change log within the AI policy document.
quote: Maintain a standardized change log within the document.
hazard: Fragmented or inconsistent records of policy revisions.

statement: Use policy language that requires review rather than automatic expiration.
quote: Use language that triggers a required review — not automatic expiration — to prevent the policy from becoming outdated without deliberate action.
hazard: AI governance lapsing through automatic policy expiration or unattended obsolescence.

statement: Implement risk mitigation controls to reduce identified AI hazards and re-evaluate the risk level.
quote: Organizations should implement risk mitigation controls (i.e., specific actions taken to reduce identified hazards) and then re-evaluate the risk level to determine if the residual risk is acceptable.
hazard: Unacceptable residual risks persisting in deployed AI systems.

statement: Integrate the analysis of applicable regulatory frameworks into formal AI risk assessments.
quote: HDOs should familiarize themselves with applicable regulatory frameworks and integrate this analysis into the formal risk assessment.
hazard: Deployment of non-compliant AI systems violating medical device or privacy regulations.

statement: Trigger formal committee review and enhanced monitoring for high-risk AI categorizations.
quote: Higher risk categorization should trigger defined governance actions, including: formal committee review, enhanced post-deployment monitoring, documented residual risk acceptance by designated governance authority, and defined re-review triggers
hazard: Inadequate oversight and monitoring of high-risk AI models.

statement: Define explicit conditions under which an AI solution will not proceed to deployment.
quote: Additionally, HDOs should define explicit conditions under which an AI solution will not proceed to deployment, including: Unmitigated high-severity harm potential that cannot be reduced through available controls
hazard: Deployment of AI solutions presenting unmitigated high-severity harm potential.

statement: Require a designated AI governance authority to make decisions on halting AI deployment under predefined conditions.
quote: Decisions to halt deployment under these conditions should be made by the designated AI governance authority (e.g., AI governance committee), and organizations should define a documented appeal or reconsideration pathway
hazard: Inconsistent or unauthorized decisions regarding the deployment of dangerous AI solutions.

statement: Define a documented appeal or reconsideration pathway for decisions that halt AI deployment.
quote: organizations should define a documented appeal or reconsideration pathway (e.g., who may submit an appeal, what new evidence or mitigations would warrant re-review, and the body responsible for the final determination).
hazard: Lack of recourse for halted AI solutions that could safely provide value.

statement: Define quantitative subgroup performance disparity thresholds that trigger escalation or deployment pause.
quote: Organizations should define quantitative subgroup performance disparity thresholds that trigger escalation or deployment pause when thresholds aren’t met.
hazard: Exacerbation of healthcare disparities due to biased AI performance across subgroups.

statement: Document testing results, identified data gaps, and the effectiveness of implemented risk mitigation controls.
quote: Documentation should include the results of testing against predefined metrics, identified data gaps, and the effectiveness of implemented risk mitigation controls.
hazard: Loss of critical context regarding AI system risks and mitigations over time.

statement: Update risk assessment documentation whenever the AI system undergoes significant changes like retraining.
quote: This documentation should be updated whenever the system undergoes significant changes, such as retraining or a shift in use case setting.
hazard: Outdated risk profiles failing to reflect new hazards introduced by system updates.

statement: Require documented sign-off by a designated governance authority for accepting residual risk of higher-risk AI.
quote: Residual risk acceptance for higher risk AI systems should require documented sign-off by the designated governance authority, consistent with organizational risk governance policies.
hazard: Acceptance of severe AI risks without appropriate leadership visibility and accountability.

statement: Make risk acceptance decisions time-bound and subject to re-evaluation at defined intervals.
quote: Acceptance decisions should be time-bound and subject to re-evaluation at defined intervals or when material changes occur.
hazard: Prolonged exposure to AI risks whose profiles have degraded over time.

statement: Define methods for measuring whether implemented risk and mitigation controls achieve their intended effect.
quote: Organizations should define how they will measure whether implemented risk and mitigation controls are achieving their intended effect.
hazard: Ineffective mitigation controls allowing predicted AI harms to materialize unnoticed.

statement: Define clear internal thresholds that trigger a formal AI System Impact Assessment.
quote: organizations should define clear internal thresholds (e.g., risk level, scale of deployment, patient-facing functionality) that trigger one.
hazard: Failure to evaluate the broader systemic impacts of high-stakes AI tools.

statement: Document criteria distinguishing when a full impact assessment is required versus a lighter-weight review.
quote: Specifically, organizations should articulate when a full impact assessment is required (typically for higher-risk, patient-facing, or broadly deployed solutions) versus when a lighter-weight review is sufficient, and document the criteria that distinguish the two paths.
hazard: Inconsistent application of rigorous impact assessments across different AI models.

statement: Periodically evaluate cumulative AI risk across all deployed systems influencing the same workflow or patient population.
quote: HDOs should periodically evaluate cumulative AI risk across all deployed systems, particularly where multiple AI solutions influence the same workflow, patient population, or workforce staff (e.g., clinicians, nurses, or other employees who participate in multiple AI-supported workflows simultaneously).
hazard: Compounding errors or automation bias caused by overlapping AI systems.

statement: Review portfolio-level risk at defined governance intervals and report to the designated governance authority.
quote: Portfolio-level risk should be reviewed at defined governance intervals (e.g., semi-annually or annually) and reported to the designated governance authority.
hazard: Lack of leadership awareness of cumulative, organization-wide AI risks.

statement: Establish and maintain a structured data acquisition register for data used in AI systems.
quote: Establish and maintain a structured data acquisition register for data used in AI systems.
hazard: Untracked data sources leading to undocumented bias or privacy violations.

statement: Establish comprehensive agreements defining terms for AI vendor data use, security, and return or destruction.
quote: Establish comprehensive agreements defining terms for permissible/nonpermissible uses, re-identification and redistribution preferences, requirements for vendor security compliance, audit rights, and data return/destruction terms.
hazard: Vendor misuse of sensitive health data due to inadequate contractual terms.

statement: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies and validate de-identification before AI training use.
quote: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies; evaluate PHI datasets to select the appropriate method; validate de-identification before AI training use; maintain oversight of linked datasets.
hazard: Exposure of protected health information in AI training datasets.

statement: Establish a process and owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation.
quote: Establish a process and owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation to help identify quality gaps and known sources of bias.
hazard: Undetected degradation of data quality resulting in biased or unsafe AI outputs.

statement: Establish a standard operating procedure for AI data preparation including rules for data cleaning and encoding.
quote: Establish a standard operating procedure (SOP) for AI data preparation including rules for data cleaning, encoding practices, normalization/standardization methods, and partitioning procedures
hazard: Inconsistent data preparation leading to unreliable AI model performance.

statement: Explicitly list AI-specific permitted uses and disclosures in vendor Business Associate Agreements.
quote: AIspecific uses should be explicitly listed.
hazard: Unauthorized use of protected health information by vendors for unapproved AI purposes.

statement: Require vendors to flow-down all Business Associate Agreement obligations to subcontractors accessing protected health information.
quote: Subcontractors: Flow-down of all BAA obligations to any subcontractors who access PHI.
hazard: Unauthorized data access by third-party subcontractors lacking appropriate safeguards.

statement: Require vendor destruction of protected health information, including AI model weights, upon contract termination.
quote: Return or Destruction of PHI: Required upon contract termination, including AI model weights or embeddings trained on PHI.
hazard: Continued retention or use of patient data by vendors after contract expiration.

statement: Explicitly identify AI-specific use cases as permitted uses in Data Use Agreements.
quote: AI-specific use cases must be explicitly identified.
hazard: Unauthorized use of limited data sets for unspecified AI applications.

statement: Require data recipients to notify the covered entity of any misuse or unauthorized disclosure.
quote: Reporting Obligations: Recipient must notify the covered entity of any misuse or unauthorized disclosure.
hazard: Delayed response to data breaches due to lack of vendor reporting obligations.

statement: Maintain a centralized documentation hub containing each AI system’s model card, vendor contract, security assessment summary, and data source description.
quote: A small hospital or FQHC uses a single SharePoint site as its AI documentation hub, with folders for each AI system containing: the model card, the vendor contract, the security assessment summary, and a brief data source description.
hazard: Fragmented documentation prevents effective governance review.

statement: Assign ownership of AI documentation to a clinical informatics or IT lead.
quote: The documentation owner is the clinical informatics or IT lead.
hazard: Unowned documentation becomes incomplete or outdated.

statement: Have the compliance officer confirm that existing document retention policies apply appropriately to AI records.
quote: The organization uses its existing document retention policy as a starting point, with compliance officer review to confirm AI records applicability.
hazard: AI governance records are retained or discarded inappropriately.

statement: Use a structured AI asset documentation template covering datasets, tools, and versions.
quote: A regional health system implements a structured documentation template for each AI system's asset record, covering datasets, tools, and versions.
hazard: Inconsistent asset records obscure dependencies and system versions.

statement: Conduct semiannual audits of AI documentation.
quote: A semi-annual documentation audit is conducted by the clinical informatics team, with gaps reported to the AI Governance Committee.
hazard: Documentation gaps remain undetected.

statement: Report AI documentation audit gaps to the AI Governance Committee.
quote: A semi-annual documentation audit is conducted by the clinical informatics team, with gaps reported to the AI Governance Committee.
hazard: Governance leaders remain unaware of documentation deficiencies.

statement: Integrate model cards, dataset documentation, version histories, and audit logs into an AI asset management system.
quote: An academic medical center implements a formal AI Asset Management System integrating model cards, dataset documentation, version histories, and audit logs.
hazard: Disconnected records prevent tracing AI assets and changes.

statement: Use automated version control to capture changes to AI model artifacts and configurations.
quote: Automated version control captures changes to model artifacts and configurations.
hazard: Untracked system changes undermine auditability and incident investigation.

statement: Document available and needed tools for standardized AI documentation and integration with the AI inventory.
quote: Control 3.5: Identify and document tools and resources available and needed for standard documentation of all AI systems and for integrating them into an AI inventory, such as adopting a Model Card.
hazard: Insufficient documentation resources leave AI systems ungoverned.

statement: Start with an existing model card template rather than creating one from scratch.
quote: Start with an existing model card template rather than building from scratch.
hazard: Ad hoc templates omit important governance information.

statement: Adopt CHAI’s Applied Model Card as a healthcare-specific model card template.
quote: CHAI’s Applied Model Card (AMC) is recommended as it is designed specifically for healthcare delivery contexts.
hazard: Generic documentation misses healthcare governance requirements.

statement: Include identity, version, uses, users, exclusions, training sources, biases, subgroup performance, safety, failure modes, monitoring, alerting, and vendor contacts in each model card.
quote: At minimum, each model card should capture: Model ID and version, Intended use and primary end users, Out-of-scope uses, Training data sources and any known biases, Performance metrics (overall and across relevant subgroups), Safety considerations and known failure modes, Monitoring and alerting information, and Vendor/developer contact information.
hazard: Incomplete information prevents informed judgments about AI suitability and limitations.

statement: Designate staff responsible for reviewing and updating each AI system’s model card.
quote: Designate model card reviewers (staff responsible for reviewing and updating cards for each AI system).
hazard: Model cards become outdated without assigned reviewers.

statement: Obtain initial model cards from the AI developer or vendor.
quote: Initial model cards should be submitted by the developer or vendor, while intial review may be the responsibility of the AI governance lead or equivalent, and updates may be the responsibility of a health informatics analyst or whoever is closest to the monitoring of the AI solution.
hazard: Deployment decisions lack authoritative system documentation.

statement: Assign initial model card review to the AI governance lead or an equivalent role.
quote: Initial model cards should be submitted by the developer or vendor, while intial review may be the responsibility of the AI governance lead or equivalent, and updates may be the responsibility of a health informatics analyst or whoever is closest to the monitoring of the AI solution.
hazard: Initial model cards lack governance scrutiny.

statement: Assign model card updates to a health informatics analyst or staff closest to monitoring the AI system.
quote: Initial model cards should be submitted by the developer or vendor, while intial review may be the responsibility of the AI governance lead or equivalent, and updates may be the responsibility of a health informatics analyst or whoever is closest to the monitoring of the AI solution.
hazard: Documentation fails to reflect observed system behavior.

statement: Require model card information during procurement of vendor-supplied AI.
quote: For vendor-supplied AI, require model card information as part of procurement—many vendors will provide this in response to formal requests even if they do not proactively share it.
hazard: AI is purchased without information needed for governance review.

statement: Require model card completion in the approval workflow for internally developed AI.
quote: For internally developed AI, require card completion as a mandatory step in your AI development or approval workflow.
hazard: Internally developed AI bypasses documentation requirements.

statement: Make model card completion a prerequisite for deployment approval.
quote: Consider making model card completion status a prerequisite for deployment approval (i.e., no model card = no deployment clearance).
hazard: Undocumented AI reaches clinical or operational use.

statement: Submit model cards to the CHAI registry, directly or through vendors.
quote: You can also submit model cards or request that vendors submit model cards to the registry here.
hazard: Limited documentation visibility weakens external accountability.

statement: Link model cards to the AI inventory rather than maintaining them as standalone documents.
quote: Model cards are most useful when linked to your AI inventory registry (see Control 6) rather than maintained as standalone documents.
hazard: Governance reviewers cannot readily find relevant system documentation.

statement: Require vendors to complete model card fields during contract renewal.
quote: A small hospital starts with a Model Card template and requires its two AI vendors to complete key fields as part of contract renewal.
hazard: Renewed contracts perpetuate missing AI documentation.

statement: Make model cards accessible to IT, clinical leadership, and compliance officers.
quote: Cards are stored in a shared SharePoint folder accessible to the IT director, CMO, and compliance officer.
hazard: Key oversight roles cannot access AI documentation.

statement: Use a checklist to verify model card completion before approving a new AI tool.
quote: The hospital uses a simple checklist to verify completion before approving any new AI tool.
hazard: Incomplete model cards pass deployment review unnoticed.

statement: Use standardized AI intake forms that populate the inventory and link model cards.
quote: It uses a standardized Microsoft Formsbased intake that populates a SharePoint list (serving as a lightweight AI inventory), with model cards stored as linked PDFs.
hazard: Inconsistent intake produces incomplete or disconnected inventory records.

statement: Send automated reminders to requesting departments when model cards are incomplete.
quote: Incomplete cards trigger an automated reminder to the requesting department.
hazard: Documentation deficiencies persist without follow-up.

statement: Integrate model card fields into the MLOps platform to populate selected fields automatically from model metadata.
quote: An academic medical center integrates a standard model card’s fields into its MLOps platform (e.g., Azure ML, AWS SageMaker, or Domino Data Lab), enabling automated population of select fields from model training metadata.
hazard: Manual documentation introduces missing or inconsistent model metadata.

statement: Have departmental model card reviewers review and attest to cards before deployment.
quote: Designated model card reviewers in each clinical department review and attest to cards before deployment.
hazard: Deployment proceeds without accountable departmental review.

statement: Maintain an internal model card library documenting AI systems approved for use.
quote: Michigan Medicine’s Clinical Integration Center (CIC) has published a Model Card Library documenting AI models approved for use across the health system.
hazard: Staff lack a reliable reference for approved AI systems.

statement: Document resources needed to maintain an AI inventory covering internal and third-party solutions.
quote: Control 3.6: Identify and document the tools and resources available and needed to implement and maintain an AI inventory registry to track internal and third party solutions.
hazard: Inventory infrastructure fails to cover all deployed AI.

statement: Assess current inventory capabilities, gaps, and resources needed for a sustainable, current, comprehensive registry.
quote: This control requires documenting current inventory capabilities, identifying gaps, and defining what resources would be needed to achieve a sustainable, current, and comprehensive registry.
hazard: Resource gaps make the AI inventory incomplete or unsustainable.

statement: Record each AI system’s identifier, supplier contacts, purpose, domain, status, users, input sensitivity, risk tier, renewal date, documentation link, approval status and date, and last review.
quote: At minimum, capture: Model/system name and unique identifier, Vendor or developer name and contact, Intended use and clinical/operational domain, Deployment status, Primary end users, Data inputs (including PHI sensitivity), Risk tier, Contract/license renewal date, Link to model card or documentation, Governance approval status and date, and Last review date.
hazard: Missing inventory fields prevent risk-based oversight and lifecycle management.

statement: Document whether the AI inventory covers clinical systems, operational systems, or both.
quote: Document whether your inventory covers only clinical AI or also operational/administrative AI—many organizations start broad and refine scope over time.
hazard: Unclear inventory scope leaves categories of AI outside oversight.

statement: Document available inventory tools, including spreadsheets, shared lists, governance platforms, and existing asset or vendor management systems.
quote: Document what tools are available to support your inventory: a shared spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets), SharePoint-based list, purpose-built AI governance platform (see Platforms in CHAI’s Partnership Ecosystem), or integration with an existing CMDB or vendor management system.
hazard: Inventory planning overlooks available infrastructure.

statement: Assess whether the inventory tool supports stakeholder access, search, version control, renewal alerts, and model card integration.
quote: Document the current tool in use, its limitations, and whether it meets the key capabilities needed: searchable and accessible to governance stakeholders, version-controlled, linked to contract management for renewal alerts, and integrated with model cards.
hazard: Inventory tool limitations prevent timely and traceable governance.

statement: Document a process for identifying and auditing unauthorized or undisclosed AI use.
quote: An AI inventory should include a documented process for identifying and auditing shadow AI use.
hazard: Shadow AI bypasses safety, privacy, and governance review.

statement: Require AI registration before any solution is used.
quote: Mechanisms can include: (1) A required intake process--no AI solution may be used without being registered,
hazard: Unregistered AI operates outside organizational oversight.

statement: Audit the AI inventory at least annually to verify entries and detect undisclosed use.
quote: (2) A regular audit cycle (at minimum annually) to verify entries are current and detect undisclosed use,
hazard: Stale inventory entries and shadow AI remain undetected.

statement: Provide staff a mechanism to report AI tools missing from the inventory, linked to policy dissemination and shadow AI awareness.
quote: (3) A mechanism for staff to report AI solutions they are using that may not be in the inventory (tie to AI policy dissemination and shadow AI awareness efforts).
hazard: Staff use unregistered AI without notifying governance teams.

statement: Document ownership of the AI intake process.
quote: Document who owns the intake process, how it is communicated to staff, and how compliance is monitored.
hazard: Unclear intake accountability allows requests to bypass review.

statement: Document how the AI intake process is communicated to staff.
quote: Document who owns the intake process, how it is communicated to staff, and how compliance is monitored.
hazard: Staff do not know how to register proposed AI use.

statement: Document how compliance with the AI intake process is monitored.
quote: Document who owns the intake process, how it is communicated to staff, and how compliance is monitored.
hazard: Intake policy violations persist without detection.

statement: Make inventory review a standing AI Governance Committee agenda item.
quote: Include inventory review as a standing agenda item for your AI Governance Committee.
hazard: Inventory changes receive insufficient governance attention.

statement: Establish a center of excellence to oversee AI governance, inventory currency, and consistent ethical standards.
quote: The organization established a Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Center of Excellence to oversee AI governance, maintain inventory currency, and ensure ethical standards are applied consistently across deployments.
hazard: Distributed deployments receive inconsistent oversight.

statement: Assign clinical informatics leadership to oversee vetting and approval of new AI solutions.
quote: The initiative is led by AltaMed’s Medical Director of Clinical Informatics, who oversees the process for vetting and approving new AI solutions, a role analogous to an AI inventory governance function.
hazard: New AI solutions lack accountable clinical review.

statement: Have the IT lead review the AI inventory quarterly.
quote: The IT lead reviews it quarterly and updates it during the annual HIPAA security review.
hazard: Inventory records become outdated between annual reviews.

statement: Update the AI inventory during the annual HIPAA security review.
quote: The IT lead reviews it quarterly and updates it during the annual HIPAA security review.
hazard: Security reviews overlook changes in deployed AI.

statement: Require staff to submit an AI tool request form before using a new tool.
quote: Staff submit an AI Tool Request Form before using any new AI tool.
hazard: New AI use begins without formal intake.

statement: Connect the AI registry to vendor management and automated contract renewal alerts.
quote: A regional health system documents a SharePoint-based AI registry with automated contract renewal alerts, linked to its vendor management system.
hazard: Contract renewals occur without timely AI governance review.

statement: Cross-reference the inventory against purchasing records and EHR change logs during semiannual audits.
quote: Clinical informatics staff audit the inventory semi-annually and cross-reference against IT purchasing records and EHR change logs to identify potential shadow AI.
hazard: Departmental AI purchases and EHR changes escape inventory detection.

statement: Document an escalation procedure for AI procurement that bypasses the formal registry.
quote: A gap assessment identifies that departmental procurement of AI solutions sometimes bypasses the formal registry process—an escalation procedure is documented.
hazard: Registry bypasses lack a defined corrective response.

statement: Integrate the AI governance platform with configuration management and procurement systems.
quote: A large academic medical center documents a purpose-built AI governance platform integrated with its CMDB and procurement systems.
hazard: Disconnected procurement and asset records conceal AI deployments.

statement: Use automated vendor API queries to flag potential new AI deployments.
quote: Automated scripts query vendor APIs to flag potential new AI system deployments.
hazard: New vendor AI features are deployed without detection.

statement: Provide governance stakeholders a real-time AI inventory dashboard.
quote: The inventory is visible to all governance stakeholders via a real-time dashboard.
hazard: Oversight decisions rely on inaccessible or outdated inventory information.

statement: Document a reconciliation process between separate research and clinical AI registries.
quote: A gap assessment identifies that AI solutions used in research contexts are tracked in a separate research registry with no integration to the clinical registry—a reconciliation process is documented.
hazard: Research AI moving into clinical use escapes governance tracking.

statement: Independently verify AI performance and potential harm in the organization’s own context.
quote: Validation testing is the process of independently verifying that an AI system performs as expected—and does not cause harm—in the context of your organization.
hazard: Benchmark performance fails to translate to local patients and workflows.

statement: Use ongoing monitoring to track AI performance, use, key performance indicators, and outcomes over time.
quote: Monitoring AI solutions can therefore help prevent undesirable shifts in performance and use (which can impact safety or operational integrity), and can help track KPIs and outcomes over time.
hazard: Performance deterioration, misuse, or lack of benefit goes unnoticed.

statement: Apply greater validation and monitoring rigor to higher-risk AI systems.
quote: Higher risk solutions should be validated and monitored with greater rigor.
hazard: High-risk deployments receive insufficient assurance.

statement: Ensure tools and resources are available for AI validation and monitoring, whether or not vendors assist.
quote: Additionally, validation and monitoring can be conducted with or without vendor assistance, but the tools and resources must be available.
hazard: Deployments lack capacity to establish and maintain safety.

statement: Test AI usability in addition to accuracy.
quote: Testing should go beyond accuracy to include things like usefulness and usability, security/privacy, and clinical workflow integration.
hazard: Difficult interfaces cause errors or ineffective use.

statement: Test AI integration with clinical workflows.
quote: Testing should go beyond accuracy to include things like usefulness and usability, security/privacy, and clinical workflow integration.
hazard: Workflow incompatibilities undermine safe clinical use.

statement: Evaluate AI security and privacy beyond performance accuracy.
quote: Testing should go beyond accuracy to include things like usefulness and usability, security/privacy, and clinical workflow integration.
hazard: Accurate systems still expose sensitive data or security vulnerabilities.

statement: Document internal expertise, analysis tools, testing frameworks, EHR reporting, and external partners available for validation and monitoring.
quote: Document what validation and monitoring capabilities your organization has: internal data science or clinical informatics expertise, access to statistical analysis tools, structured testing frameworks (CHAI T&E Frameworks, AHRQ evaluation toolkits), EHR-based performance reporting, and any external validation partners (academic medical center, regional consortium).
hazard: Validation planning assumes capabilities the organization does not possess.

statement: Record which AI systems have been validated, the tools used, and systems still awaiting validation.
quote: Note which AI systems have been validated using which tools, and which have not yet been validated.
hazard: Unvalidated systems are mistaken for adequately tested deployments.

statement: Prioritize remediation of validation gaps, especially for high-risk clinical AI.
quote: Flag validation gaps—particularly for high-risk clinical AI—as priority remediation items.
hazard: Critical validation deficiencies remain unresolved.

statement: Use a desk review as an initial AI validation step.
quote: Some organizations consider a desk review of a solution the first step of validation, following it with a small scale pilot or phased deployment where they monitor performance, errors, satisfaction, etc.
hazard: Obvious suitability or evidence gaps are missed before live testing.

statement: Follow initial review with a small pilot or phased deployment that monitors performance, errors, and satisfaction.
quote: Some organizations consider a desk review of a solution the first step of validation, following it with a small scale pilot or phased deployment where they monitor performance, errors, satisfaction, etc.
hazard: Broad deployment exposes users before local problems are identified.

statement: Test AI performance on retrospective data before connecting the system to live data streams.
quote: Others may use retrospective data to test performance before the model ever touches live data streams.
hazard: Initial testing exposes live workflows to unverified performance.

statement: Document each AI system’s validation and monitoring scope according to its risk.
quote: For each AI system, and depending on risk, document what validation and monitoring should cover.
hazard: Validation and monitoring omit risks relevant to the deployment.

statement: Evaluate whether the AI tool improves outcomes in the local context.
quote: Organizations should consider (1) Usefulness: Does the tool improve outcomes in your context?
hazard: Technically capable AI provides no meaningful local benefit.

statement: Evaluate performance differences by race or ethnicity, age, sex, language, and insurance status.
quote: (2) Fairness: Does performance differ across subgroups (race/ethnicity, age, sex, language, insurance status)?
hazard: Aggregate performance conceals unequal harms across patient groups.

statement: Assess the consequences of incorrect AI outputs.
quote: (3) Safety: What are the consequences of incorrect outputs and are fail-safes in place?
hazard: Deployment decisions underestimate the harm of erroneous outputs.

statement: Verify that fail-safes are in place for incorrect AI outputs.
quote: (3) Safety: What are the consequences of incorrect outputs and are fail-safes in place?
hazard: Incorrect outputs reach users without protective safeguards.

statement: Evaluate whether end users can appropriately use, trust, or distrust AI outputs.
quote: (4) Transparency: Can end users appropriately use, trust, or distrust outputs?
hazard: Users overtrust or misinterpret AI outputs.

statement: Verify that the AI tool protects protected health information.
quote: (5) Security/Privacy: Does the tool protect PHI?
hazard: AI use exposes protected health information.

statement: Assign responsibility for each validation dimension.
quote: Document who is responsible for each validation dimension and what data samples or testing environments are needed.
hazard: Validation dimensions are omitted because ownership is unclear.

statement: Document the data samples and testing environments needed for validation.
quote: Document who is responsible for each validation dimension and what data samples or testing environments are needed.
hazard: Testing uses inadequate data or unsuitable environments.

statement: Create system-specific validation and monitoring requirements specifying dimensions, minimum samples, subgroups, result approvers, and external resources.
quote: Action: Produce a validation and monitoring requirements document for each AI system specifying: required validation and monitoring dimensions, minimum sample sizes and subgroup requirements, who approves results, and any external resources needed (e.g., third-party validation, vendor data provision).
hazard: Unspecified assurance requirements allow inconsistent or insufficient testing.

statement: Require vendors to provide third-party validation reports when addressing internal validation capability gaps.
quote: Document available options to bridge this gap: (1) Require vendors to provide third-party validation reports and monitoring dashboards
hazard: Limited internal expertise leaves vendor performance claims unverified.

statement: Require vendor monitoring dashboards when addressing internal monitoring capability gaps.
quote: Document available options to bridge this gap: (1) Require vendors to provide third-party validation reports and monitoring dashboards
hazard: Organizations cannot observe vendor-managed system performance.

statement: Partner with academic centers, health systems, or health center controlled networks to share validation and monitoring resources.
quote: (2) Partner with a nearby academic medical center, health systems, HCCN to share validation and monitoring resources,
hazard: Resource shortages prevent adequate validation and monitoring.

statement: Use built-in EHR performance reporting and monitoring as a starting point for post-pilot evaluation.
quote: (3) Use EHR vendor built-in performance reporting and monitoring tools as a starting point for post-pilot evaluation,
hazard: Post-pilot performance is not evaluated because specialized tools are unavailable.

statement: Contractually require subgroup-disaggregated performance reporting for vendor-managed cloud AI.
quote: (4) For vendor-managed cloud AI, contractually require performance reporting disaggregated by key subgroups.
hazard: Vendor reporting conceals subgroup performance disparities.

statement: Use third-party governance services to perform validation during the request-for-proposals process.
quote: (5) Partner with a third-party governance service that provides validation testing for health systems during their RFP process.
hazard: Procurement decisions lack independent validation evidence.

statement: Partner with vendors to share validation and monitoring resources.
quote: 6) Partner with vendor to share resources for validation and monitoring
hazard: Available vendor resources are not used to address assurance gaps.

statement: Document each AI system’s chosen approach to validation capability gaps and any unresolved gaps.
quote: Document which approach is used for each AI system and any gaps that remain.
hazard: Residual assurance gaps disappear from governance visibility.

statement: Conduct annual evaluations of all deployed AI, checking stakeholder value, reported issues, usage statistics, and applicable outcomes.
quote: A large academic medical center shared that their AI governance program requires a mandatory annual evaluation of all deployed AI solutions that includes: 1) Stakeholder check-in to confirm ongoing value 2) Self-reporting of issues or red-flags modeled after an IRB annual review approach 3) Review of usage statistics and outcome variables where applicable.
hazard: Inactive, problematic, or ineffective AI remains deployed indefinitely.
