hazard: Some acquisition pathways escape responsible AI assessment.

statement: Have a core team review and score responsible AI survey responses using a defined evaluation rubric.
quote: A core team then reviews and scores these responses using a Responsible AI Evaluation Rubric.
hazard: AI assessments are inconsistent or unsupported by explicit criteria.

statement: Ensure AI models are representative of the health system's patient population.
quote: a. Fairness: Ensuring models are representative of the system's patient population and include processes for recalibration if the population changes.
hazard: Underrepresented local patients receive less reliable AI-supported care.

statement: Document the intended users of each AI solution.
quote: b. Transparency: Documenting intended users, out-of-scope use cases, and the model or solution’s building/maintenance process.
hazard: AI is used by people for whom it was not designed.

statement: Document out-of-scope uses for each AI solution.
quote: b. Transparency: Documenting intended users, out-of-scope use cases, and the model or solution’s building/maintenance process.
hazard: AI is applied to unvalidated or inappropriate tasks.

statement: Document each AI solution's development process.
quote: b. Transparency: Documenting intended users, out-of-scope use cases, and the model or solution’s building/maintenance process.
hazard: Reviewers cannot trace how an AI solution was built.

statement: Document each AI solution's maintenance process.
quote: b. Transparency: Documenting intended users, out-of-scope use cases, and the model or solution’s building/maintenance process.
hazard: AI updates and maintenance occur without transparent procedures.

statement: Define clear AI governance roles for developers and subject matter experts.
quote: c. Accountability: Defining clear roles for developers and subject matter experts (SMEs), and establishing processes to track performance over time.
hazard: Responsibility for AI decisions and problems is ambiguous.

statement: Educate clinicians and operational users about how deployed AI models work.
quote: d. Trustworthiness: Educating clinicians and operational users about how the model works and providing independent validation of findings.
hazard: Users rely on AI without understanding its operation.

statement: Provide independent validation of AI findings.
quote: d. Trustworthiness: Educating clinicians and operational users about how the model works and providing independent validation of findings.
hazard: Incorrect AI findings are accepted without independent validation.

statement: Submit a rubric-based responsible AI recommendation to the oversight group before enterprise architecture review.
quote: Based on the rubric scores, the core team makes an RAI recommendation to the AAA group, which then votes on whether the solution is approved to proceed into the Enterprise Architecture process.
hazard: Technical integration proceeds without an evidence-based governance recommendation.

statement: Ensure deployed AI avoids prejudice toward specific groups.
quote: Fair: Avoiding prejudice toward specific groups.
hazard: AI disadvantages particular patient or user groups.

statement: Match AI tools to their specific deployment contexts and populations.
quote: Appropriate: Matched to specific contexts and populations.
hazard: AI is deployed in contexts or populations for which it is unsuitable.

statement: Demonstrate real-world benefit from deployed AI tools.
quote: Effective: Demonstrating real-world benefit.
hazard: AI deployment consumes resources or changes care without meaningful benefit.

statement: Ensure probable AI benefits outweigh known risks.
quote: Safe: Ensuring probable benefits outweigh known risks.
hazard: AI deployment creates more harm than expected benefit.

statement: Collaborate with trusted partners for AI governance, testing, data management, or advisory support.
quote: Collaborate with trusted partners delivering excellence in AI governance, testing, data management, and advisory services - all aligned with the CHAI AI Governance Framework.
hazard: Organizational capability gaps undermine responsible AI deployment.

statement: Consider responsible AI principles when developing lifecycle management processes.
quote: Note: CHAI’s RAIG highlights core, industry-aligned responsible AI (RAI) principles (usefulness/usability/efficacy, fairness/bias management, safety/reliability, transparency, privacy, and security) that should be considered as HDOs develop their AI lifecycle management processes.
hazard: Lifecycle governance omits essential quality, safety, fairness, or data-protection principles.

statement: Prioritize state and federal regulatory requirements, particularly for AI qualifying as Software as a Medical Device.
quote: Organizations should prioritize state and federal regulatory requirements, especially for AI solutions that meet the definition of a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), as defined by the FDA.
hazard: Voluntary governance guidance displaces applicable legal obligations.

statement: Consult qualified legal, clinical, and other relevant professional advisors before acting on the playbook's deployment guidance.
quote: Readers should consult with qualified legal counsel, clinical experts, and other appropriate professional advisors before taking, or refraining from taking, any action based on the information in this playbook.
hazard: General guidance is applied without context-specific professional judgment.

statement: Conduct pre-deployment risk categorization within the organization's defined AI use-case scope.
quote: Conduct a Risk Categorization assessment (pre-deployment) to categorize risk in the context of the organization's AI use case scope.
hazard: AI enters deployment before its use-case-specific risk is categorized.

statement: Document actions taken to mitigate identified AI risks.
quote: 3. Risk Mitigation: Implement and document actions (risk mitigation controls) to reduce identified risks.
hazard: Risk-control decisions lack an auditable record.

statement: Continuously monitor AI performance over time.
quote: 4. Risk Monitoring: Continuously monitor the AI solution’s performance and safety over time.
hazard: Performance deterioration goes undetected after deployment.

statement: Continuously monitor AI safety over time.
quote: 4. Risk Monitoring: Continuously monitor the AI solution’s performance and safety over time.
hazard: Emerging AI harms remain undetected.

statement: Integrate AI risk categorization and assessment into enterprise risk management.
quote: AI risk categorization and assessment processes should integrate into the organization's broader Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.
hazard: AI risks are managed separately from enterprise-wide risk accountability.

statement: Include high-risk AI solutions in existing organizational risk registers.
quote: High-risk AI solutions should be visible within existing risk registers and, where appropriate, escalated to executive or board-level oversight consistent with the organization's risk governance model.
hazard: Enterprise leaders lack visibility into high-risk AI deployments.

statement: Escalate high-risk AI solutions to executive or board-level oversight when appropriate under organizational risk governance.
quote: High-risk AI solutions should be visible within existing risk registers and, where appropriate, escalated to executive or board-level oversight consistent with the organization's risk governance model.
hazard: Consequential AI risks exceed the authority of their current reviewers.

statement: Categorize and assess risk at the specific AI solution and defined use-case level, not the underlying foundation-model level.
quote: Risk categorization and assessment should be conducted at the level of the specific AI solution and its defined use case (e.g., ambient technology, AI-supported patient scheduling, AI-supported revenue cycle management), not at the level of the underlying foundation model.
hazard: Model-level assessments miss workflow, input-data, and use-context risks.

statement: Document procedures for evaluating, recording, retaining, and reviewing AI risk categorization.
quote: Document how Risk Categorization is evaluated, recorded, retained, and reviewed.
hazard: Risk categories cannot be consistently assigned or audited.

statement: Conduct rigorous risk assessments for AI solutions categorized as higher risk by the organization.
quote: Leverage a rigorous Risk Assessment to evaluate AI solutions that are categorized as higher risk (as defined by the organization).
hazard: Higher-risk AI receives only superficial assessment.

statement: Document procedures for evaluating, recording, retaining, and reviewing AI risk assessments.
quote: Document how Risk Assessment is evaluated, recorded, retained, and reviewed.
hazard: Risk assessment evidence and decisions are inconsistent or unauditable.

statement: Conduct and document an AI system impact assessment evaluating risks and benefits.
quote: Conduct and document an AI System Impact Assessment that includes evaluation of risks and benefits for AI solutions.
hazard: AI deployment proceeds without a recorded assessment of overall impacts.

statement: Evaluate AI risks across patient safety, technology, data, financial, legal, operational, and reputational domains.
quote: HDOs should evaluate AI solutions across specific risk domains. High-priority risk domains include components of risk that contribute to Life & Patient Safety and Technology & Data. Additional risk domains to consider include Financial, Legal, Operational, and Reputational risk.
hazard: Risk review overlooks clinically or organizationally consequential harms.

statement: Select organization-specific AI risk domains according to overall organizational risk tolerance.
quote: Organizations should consider their own risk domains depending on overall organizational risk tolerance.
hazard: Generic risk domains omit locally important exposures.

statement: Categorize AI use cases as low, medium, or high risk based on intended-use context.
quote: Use cases should be categorized as Low, Medium, or High risk based on the context of their intended use.
hazard: Risk levels do not reflect the consequences of actual intended use.

statement: Account for staffing levels, shift coverage, and other operational context when categorizing AI risk.
quote: Categorization should also account for how risk may stack, multiply, or attenuate based on operational context (e.g., staffing levels, shift coverage) and aggregate use (e.g., multiple AI solutions influencing the same workflow or patient population).
hazard: Risk is underestimated when operational capacity weakens safeguards.

statement: Account for cumulative risks from multiple AI solutions affecting the same workflow or patient population.
quote: Categorization should also account for how risk may stack, multiply, or attenuate based on operational context (e.g., staffing levels, shift coverage) and aggregate use (e.g., multiple AI solutions influencing the same workflow or patient population).
hazard: Individually acceptable tools combine to create unrecognized cumulative harm.

statement: Adjust risk categorization when contextual or cumulative factors materially change risk exposure.
quote: Where contextual or cumulative factors materially change risk exposure, the categorization should be adjusted accordingly.
hazard: Outdated categories provide insufficient oversight for changed conditions.

statement: Track additional risk domains as agentic AI capabilities expand.
quote: As agentic AI capabilities expand, HDOs should begin tracking additional risk domains beyond those listed above.
hazard: Traditional risk frameworks overlook risks introduced by autonomous AI actions.

statement: Assess the independent decision-making authority granted to AI agents.
quote: Within these domains, organizations should also consider risk modifiers such as level of agent decision-making authority, scope creep potential, and the presence/quality of defined stop conditions.
hazard: Agents receive more decision-making authority than their safeguards support.

statement: Assess how difficult or impossible it would be to reverse an AI agent's actions.
quote: These may include: Autonomy: The level of independent decision-making authority granted to the agent. Irreversibility: The difficulty or impossibility of reversing actions an agent has taken.
hazard: Irreversible agent actions create harms that cannot be corrected.

statement: Assess risks from interactions or handoffs between multiple AI agents.
quote: These may include: Autonomy: The level of independent decision-making authority granted to the agent. Irreversibility: The difficulty or impossibility of reversing actions an agent has taken. Agent-to-Agent: Risks arising from interactions or hand-offs between multiple AI agents.
hazard: Agent interactions propagate errors or lose responsibility during handoffs.

statement: Assess the potential for AI agent scope creep.
quote: Within these domains, organizations should also consider risk modifiers such as level of agent decision-making authority, scope creep potential, and the presence/quality of defined stop conditions.
hazard: Agent activity expands beyond its assessed or authorized scope.

statement: Assess the presence and quality of defined AI agent stop conditions.
quote: Within these domains, organizations should also consider risk modifiers such as level of agent decision-making authority, scope creep potential, and the presence/quality of defined stop conditions.
hazard: Agents continue operating when safety conditions require stopping.

statement: Formally define AI risk appetite and tolerance thresholds across risk domains.
quote: HDOs should formally define AI-related risk appetite and tolerance thresholds across risk domains.
hazard: AI risk acceptance is inconsistent or arbitrary.

statement: Have the designated AI governance authority set risk thresholds in coordination with enterprise risk management.
quote: These thresholds should be set by the designated AI governance authority (e.g., AI governance committee or equivalent body) in coordination with Enterprise Risk Management, and documented in the organization’s AI policy or equivalent reference document so they can be cited consistently in decisions.
hazard: AI risk thresholds conflict with enterprise risk governance.

statement: Document AI risk thresholds in organizational AI policy or an equivalent reference document.
quote: These thresholds should be set by the designated AI governance authority (e.g., AI governance committee or equivalent body) in coordination with Enterprise Risk Management, and documented in the organization’s AI policy or equivalent reference document so they can be cited consistently in decisions.
hazard: Reviewers cannot consistently reference approved risk thresholds.

statement: Reference predefined tolerance levels in AI risk categorization decisions.
quote: Risk categorization decisions should reference these predefined tolerance levels.
hazard: Risk categories are assigned without reference to approved tolerance.

statement: Use CHAI's Risk Categorization Tool v2 to operationalize pre-deployment risk categorization.
quote: Use the Risk Categorization Tool (v2) as a multi-stakeholder, consensus-defined tool to help operationalize the organization’s pre-deployment categorization of risk.
hazard: Pre-deployment risk categorization lacks a structured method.

statement: Assess how operationally or physically close AI outputs are to patients during risk categorization.
quote: How operationally or physically close is the AI output to the patient (e.g., back-office administration vs. clinical diagnosis support)?
hazard: Risk review overlooks how directly outputs can affect patients.

statement: Assess human involvement in reviewing, verifying, or overriding AI outputs before they affect care.
quote: To what extent is a human involved in reviewing, verifying, or overriding AI outputs before they affect care?
hazard: AI errors reach patient care without meaningful human interception.

statement: Assess the potential severity of patient harm if AI provides incorrect information.
quote: What is the potential severity of negative outcomes, such as morbidity or mortality, if the AI provides incorrect information?
hazard: Risk categorization underestimates severe consequences of incorrect AI information.

statement: Identify use involving pediatric, older, or training-data-underrepresented patient groups during risk categorization.
quote: Is the solution used for patients in sensitive groups, such as pediatrics, older adults (aged 65 and older), or populations underrepresented in training data?
hazard: Risk review overlooks heightened vulnerability or underrepresentation.

statement: Determine whether the proposed workflow uses PHI or de-identified data with residual reidentification risk.
quote: Does the system rely on identified protected health information (PHI) or de-identified data with residual reidentification potential?
hazard: Sensitive patient information is exposed or reidentified unexpectedly.

statement: Identify the types of AI used by each solution during risk categorization.
quote: What type(s) of AI is the solution using (large language model, regression model)?
hazard: Assessments overlook risks associated with the solution's AI technology.

statement: Assess how likely AI outputs are to directly affect patient care or care decisions.
quote: How likely is the AI output to directly impact patient care or patient care decisions?
hazard: Clinically consequential outputs receive insufficient scrutiny.

statement: Assess how and where AI data is stored for the intended use case.
quote: How and where is the data stored for the purpose of the intended use case?
hazard: Data storage arrangements introduce unrecognized privacy or security risks.

statement: Assess data storage and deletion arrangements after the intended AI use.
quote: How is the data stored or deleted after its intended use?
hazard: Patient data remains available beyond its intended use.

statement: Account for backups, replication, and other data retention measures in AI risk categorization.
quote: Is the data subject to backups, replication, or other retention measures that should be accounted for in the risk categorization?
hazard: Unrecognized copies undermine data deletion or retention controls.

statement: Assess the difficulty of detecting unintended AI results, negative effects, or model drift.
quote: What is the level of difficulty in detecting unintended results, negative effects, or model drift?
hazard: Hard-to-detect AI failures persist without appropriate monitoring.

statement: Assess organizational control over AI inputs and outputs, including connections to external actors.
quote: To what extent does the organization fully control the AI and its outputs (e.g., does it rely on inputs from outside the organization or send outputs to outside actors)?
hazard: External dependencies or output recipients create unmanaged exposure.

statement: Assess AI deployment's technical load, integration dependencies, downstream impacts, and ongoing maintenance burden.
quote: What is the technical load and integration burden of deploying this AI solution (e.g., interface dependencies, data pipeline changes, downstream system impacts, and ongoing maintenance overhead)?
hazard: Integration complexity or maintenance demands compromise safe operation.

statement: Assess the sensitivity and downstream consequences of information generated or inferred by AI.
quote: How sensitive is the information being generated or inferred by the AI (e.g., predictions of risk for developing a chronic condition or other inferences that could carry downstream consequences for the patient)?
hazard: Sensitive AI inferences cause privacy harms or adverse downstream decisions.

statement: Assess whether errors in embedded AI could cascade into other health IT systems or workflows.
quote: Important: How deeply is the AI embedded in the health IT environment, and could an error in this solution cascade or propagate to other systems and workflows?
hazard: A local AI error propagates across interconnected systems.

statement: Standardize the risk categorization of AI use cases.
quote: Standardizing the categorization of use cases is essential for consistency.
hazard: Comparable AI use cases receive inconsistent risk classifications.

statement: Retain all documentation supporting AI risk categorization decisions.
quote: All documentation regarding these decisions should be retained and reviewed periodically to account for changes in the AI's performance or its environment.
hazard: Risk classification decisions cannot be audited or reconstructed.

statement: Periodically review risk categorization documentation for changes in AI performance or deployment environment.
quote: All documentation regarding these decisions should be retained and reviewed periodically to account for changes in the AI's performance or its environment.
hazard: Risk classifications remain based on obsolete evidence.

statement: Record the specific evidence and rationale supporting each AI risk categorization decision.
quote: HDOs should keep record of the specific evidence and rationale (e.g., vendor model card information, vendor intake questionnaires, or other supplemental AI solution documentation to use as evidence for the team’s risk categorization decision).
hazard: Assigned risk levels lack traceable evidentiary support.

statement: Define documentation vendors must provide for AI features embedded in systems already in use.
quote: For AI features/capabilities increasingly embedded by vendors directly into systems already in use, HDOs should define what documentation they require vendors to provide (e.g., model/solution cards, transparency reports, among several other potential requirements) to support ongoing risk categorization and auditability.
hazard: Embedded vendor AI changes enter use without adequate risk documentation.

statement: Establish a vendor AI intake process as part of procurement.
quote: CHAI recommends establishing a vendor AI Intake process as part of procurement.
hazard: Vendor AI is purchased without structured governance intake.

statement: Classify administrative AI use cases without patient-data access as low risk by default.
quote: HDOs may classify all administrative AI use cases that do not access patient data as “Low Risk” by default.
hazard: Low-risk categorization is applied without an explicit data-access boundary.

statement: Formally designate the official or governance body responsible for reviewing and approving AI risk categorization.
quote: Who is the designated official or governance body responsible for reviewing and signing off on the risk categorization, and what is the defined scope of their authority and accountability for this decision? Organizations should elevate this designation formally, specifying decision-making rights and reporting obligations.
hazard: No accountable authority approves AI risk classifications.

statement: Specify the risk-categorization authority's decision-making rights, accountability, and reporting obligations.
quote: Who is the designated official or governance body responsible for reviewing and signing off on the risk categorization, and what is the defined scope of their authority and accountability for this decision? Organizations should elevate this designation formally, specifying decision-making rights and reporting obligations.
hazard: Risk decisions exceed delegated authority or escape required reporting.

statement: Document known AI limitations during risk categorization, including populations with lower accuracy.
quote: Are the known limitations of the AI system, such as specific populations where the model is less accurate, documented during the categorization process?
hazard: Known limitations are omitted from risk decisions.

statement: Document the methods and effort used to identify AI limitations so knowledge gaps remain visible.
quote: In addition, has the organization documented the methods and effort used to identify those limitations (e.g., vendor disclosures requested, internal testing performed, literature reviewed) so that gaps in knowledge are visible?
hazard: Absence of evidence is mistaken for evidence that limitations do not exist.

statement: Define a cadence for revisiting risk categorization against the current use-case scope.
quote: How often will the categorization be revisited to ensure it still reflects the current use case scope (e.g., review cadence)?
hazard: Expanded or changed use remains covered by an obsolete risk classification.

statement: Analyze the probability and magnitude of harm in detail for higher-risk AI use cases.
quote: For higher risk use cases, a detailed analysis of the probability and magnitude of harm is recommended.
hazard: Higher-risk deployments proceed without understanding likely harm and severity.

statement: Evaluate population sensitivity in higher-risk AI assessments.
quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.
hazard: Detailed assessments overlook increased susceptibility to harm in affected populations.

statement: Evaluate disparity risk in higher-risk AI assessments.
quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.
hazard: AI deployment creates or worsens disparities.

statement: Evaluate whether AI training-data provenance is verifiable.
quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.
hazard: Unknown data origins conceal quality, privacy, or representativeness problems.

statement: Assign higher default risk to models with unknown or unverifiable training-data provenance, regardless of intended use.
quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.
hazard: Low-risk use labels obscure uncertainty about model training data.

statement: Evaluate whether available information about an AI solution's training data is sufficient.
quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.
hazard: Deployment decisions rely on inadequate information about training-data suitability.

statement: Implement specific mitigation controls for identified AI hazards.
quote: Organizations should implement risk mitigation controls (i.e., specific actions taken to reduce identified hazards) and then re-evaluate the risk level to determine if the residual risk is acceptable.
hazard: Identified hazards remain unaddressed.

statement: Re-evaluate AI risk after mitigation to determine whether residual risk is acceptable.
quote: Organizations should implement risk mitigation controls (i.e., specific actions taken to reduce identified hazards) and then re-evaluate the risk level to determine if the residual risk is acceptable.
hazard: Mitigations are assumed adequate despite unacceptable remaining risk.

statement: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies specifying Safe Harbor or Expert Determination, considering applicable state privacy laws.
quote: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination) considering applicable state privacy laws
hazard: Patient data exposed through AI outputs or vendor pipelines due to inadequate de-identification

statement: Validate de-identification of any dataset before it is used in AI training, fine-tuning, or model development.
quote: validate de-identification before any dataset is used in AI training or model development
hazard: Re-identifiable patient data incorporated into models

statement: Conduct a formal reassessment of re-identification risk whenever de-identified datasets are combined or linked, and update HIPAA risk documentation.
quote: When de-identified datasets are combined or linked, conduct a formal reassessment of re-identification risk and update HIPAA risk documentation accordingly.
hazard: Linked datasets becoming re-identifiable in combination

statement: Treat text embeddings and LLM fine-tuning inputs derived from patient data as patient-level data and govern them accordingly.
quote: Any text embeddings or LLM fine-tuning inputs derived from patient data should be treated as patient-level data and governed accordingly.
hazard: Embeddings encoding patient-identifiable information escaping standard de-identification review

statement: Ensure de-identification policies account for privacy laws of all states where the organization operates or patients reside.
quote: De-identification policies should account for the privacy laws of all states in which the organization operates or in which patients reside.
hazard: Violation of state privacy laws stricter than HIPAA

statement: Use specialized NLP-based de-identification tools and additional validation steps for clinical notes and other free-text data.
quote: Develop specific procedures for clinical notes, imaging reports, and other free-text data, using NLP-based de-identification tools and additional validation steps.
hazard: Rule-based removal missing identifiers in unstructured text

statement: Apply more conservative de-identification, stricter access controls, or contractual downstream-use restrictions for data on sensitive populations used in AI or shared with vendors.
quote: Organizations using such data for AI training or sharing it with vendors should consider more conservative deidentification approaches, stricter access controls, and/or explicit contractual restrictions on downstream use.
hazard: Re-identification of behavioral health, SUD, HIV, reproductive health, or minors' data

statement: Define in policy who has authority to approve de-identification of data for AI training use.
quote: Document which method (Safe Harbor, Expert Determination, or synthetic data) will be used for which scenarios, and define who has authority to approve de-identification for AI training use.
hazard: Unaccountable approval of patient data use for AI

statement: For each new AI use case involving patient data, assess the dataset and intended use to select a de-identification method, and document the assessment.
quote: For each new AI use case involving patient data, evaluate the dataset and intended use to select the appropriate de-identification method. Document this assessment.
hazard: Inappropriate de-identification method for specific AI use

statement: Validate de-identification using automated tools supplemented by privacy officer or qualified expert review, and document results in the data acquisition register.
quote: Use automated tools for initial validation, supplemented by privacy officer or qualified expert review. Document the validation results and link them to the data acquisition register (Control 1).
hazard: Undetected residual identifiers in datasets

statement: Assign an owner and process for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation.
quote: Establish a process and owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation to help identify quality gaps and known sources of bias.
hazard: Unidentified bias worsening health disparities

statement: Define data quality thresholds for completeness, accuracy, and consistency and include them in procurement requirements for vendor AI tools.
quote: Establish acceptable thresholds for completeness, accuracy, and consistency for each dataset used in AI. Document these standards and include them in procurement requirements for vendor tools.
hazard: Unreliable AI outputs from poor-quality data

statement: Before piloting any vendor AI tool, compare dataset demographics to the served population and document significant gaps.
quote: Before using any dataset for AI training or validating/piloting any vendor tool, compare the demographic distribution of the dataset to the population the model will serve. Document any significant gaps--do not assume a mismatch disqualifies a tool, but ensure it is understood and disclosed.
hazard: Deploying tools that perform poorly for unrepresented local populations

statement: For each AI tool, map likely bias types (representation, label, temporal, selection, measurement) and how they may affect outputs.
quote: For each dataset or AI tool, explicitly map which types of bias (representation, label, temporal, selection, measurement) are likely present and how they may affect model outputs.
hazard: Unrecognized bias sources distorting outputs

statement: Evaluate and monitor AI tool performance across relevant subgroups rather than relying solely on aggregate metrics.
quote: Evaluate and monitor AI tool performance across relevant subgroups. Do not rely solely on aggregate performance metrics.
hazard: Aggregate metrics masking poor performance for subgroups

statement: Conduct bias assessments at deployment and at predefined post-deployment intervals, with frequency proportionate to tool risk and data sensitivity.
quote: Assessments should occur at data ingestion, during model training or validation (if applicable), at deployment, and at predefined post-deployment intervals.
hazard: Bias emerging or worsening from population change or data drift

statement: Scale post-deployment bias monitoring frequency and rigor to the AI tool's risk level and data sensitivity.
quote: The frequency and rigor of post-deployment bias monitoring should be proportionate to the risk level of the AI tool or the sensitivity of the data.
hazard: Insufficient monitoring of high-risk tools

statement: Evaluate ambient AI performance by language subgroup and capture language metadata when serving non-English-speaking populations.
quote: For example, a CHC that serves primarily non-English speakers, may want to look at how their Ambient AI solution performs by language subgroups, and may want to capture metadata associated with data language.
hazard: Ambient AI documentation errors for non-English speakers

statement: Maintain data preparation SOPs for data input into AI models, used for fine-tuning, or shared with third-party vendors.
quote: Note that not all organizations will be using data to develop or train models, but must still have data preparation SOPs for data that will be input into the model for use, used to fine-tune the model, or shared with third-party vendors.
hazard: Ad hoc, unauditable data handling for AI

statement: Define which categories of clinical data, including whether and when PHI, may be included in LLM prompts or context.
quote: Define what categories of clinical data may be included in prompts or context — including whether PHI is permitted and under what conditions.
hazard: Inappropriate PHI exposure through prompts

statement: Establish prompt templates for common clinical use cases and manage them as versioned, governed artifacts.
quote: Establish prompt templates for common clinical use cases; treat templates as versioned, governed artifacts rather than ad hoc text.
hazard: Uncontrolled ad hoc prompts producing inconsistent outputs

statement: Document rules for truncation and summarization when clinical records exceed LLM context window limits.
quote: Document rules for truncation and summarization when clinical records exceed context window limits — truncation decisions affect what information the model acts on.
hazard: Model acting on incomplete clinical information

statement: Specify logging requirements for prompt content, especially prompts containing PHI, to support audit and incident investigation.
quote: Specify logging requirements for prompt content, particularly for any prompts that include PHI, to support audit and incident investigation.
hazard: Inability to audit or investigate AI incidents

statement: Define eligibility criteria for documents included in a RAG retrieval corpus, such as only verified clinical guidelines.
quote: Define criteria for which documents or records are eligible/ineligible for inclusion in the retrieval corpus (e.g., only verified clinical guidelines, only records from defined date ranges).
hazard: Unreliable or biased grounding sources producing wrong outputs

statement: Document chunking and embedding strategies used to index RAG retrieval corpora.
quote: Document chunking and embedding strategies — how documents are divided and indexed affects what the model retrieves and ultimately generates.
hazard: Poor retrieval leading to inaccurate generated outputs

statement: Establish a freshness and update cadence for RAG retrieval corpora such as guidelines, formularies, and protocols.
quote: Establish a freshness and update cadence — clinical guidelines, formularies, and protocols change, and stale retrieval corpora produce outdated outputs.
hazard: Outdated guidance from stale retrieval content

statement: Define access controls for RAG retrieval corpora, including what patient data is indexed and who can query it.
quote: Define access controls for the retrieval corpus — what patient data, if any, is indexed, and who can query it through the AI system.
hazard: Unauthorized access to patient data through AI queries

statement: Document metadata tagging standards for retrieval corpora to support filtering, auditing, and corpus management.
quote: Document metadata tagging standards to support filtering, auditing, and corpus management over time.
hazard: Unmanageable, unauditable retrieval corpora

statement: Ask RAG tool vendors for source metadata and the minimum necessary organizational data the tool needs to access.
quote: For example, for a vendor providing a RAG-based clinical decision support tool, it may be important to know the metadata of the data sources it relies on and pulls from, and the minimum necessary data it needs to access from within your organizations, to successfully run.
hazard: Opaque vendor grounding sources and excess data access

statement: Have domain experts review clinical instruction-response pairs before inclusion in fine-tuning data.
quote: Clinical pairs should be reviewed by domain experts before inclusion.
hazard: Clinically incorrect fine-tuning data degrading outputs

statement: Document the ratio of domain-specific to general data in locally fine-tuned LLM datasets.
quote: Data mix ratios: Document the ratio of domain-specific to general data in the fine-tuning set. Overreliance on domain-specific data can cause the model to lose general reasoning capabilities.
hazard: Fine-tuned model losing general reasoning capabilities

statement: Apply heightened scrutiny to rare-condition cases in fine-tuning data to assess memorization and re-identification risk.
quote: Memorization risk assessment: Apply heightened scrutiny to rare-condition cases in fine-tuning data.
hazard: Model memorizing and revealing identifiable rare-case patient data

statement: Document the legal basis for using patient data in fine-tuning and ensure coverage by consents, BAAs, or DUAs.
quote: Document the legal basis for using patient data in fine-tuning. Finetuning constitutes a new use of data that should be explicitly covered by existing consents, BAAs, or DUAs.
hazard: Unauthorized secondary use of patient data

statement: Define and document which systems, APIs, and data sources an agentic AI system is authorized to query.
quote: Define and document which systems, APIs, and data sources an agentic AI system is authorized to query — this is the agentic equivalent of a training data inventory.
hazard: Agents accessing unauthorized systems or data

statement: Restrict agentic AI to least-privilege data access limited to systems relevant to its authorized task.
quote: Establish least-privilege data access: agents should only be able to query systems relevant to the specific task they are authorized to perform.
hazard: Excessive agent data access and privacy breaches

statement: Require explicit justification for cross-system data aggregation by agentic AI systems.
quote: Cross-system data aggregation should require explicit justification.
hazard: Unjustified aggregation increasing privacy risk

statement: Document how agent tool-call outputs are validated before being used in further reasoning.
quote: Document how tool-call outputs are validated before being used in further reasoning — unvalidated external outputs can introduce errors or adversarial content into the agent's reasoning chain.
hazard: Errors or adversarial content propagating through agent reasoning

statement: Log all tool calls and data queries made by agentic systems, not just final outputs.
quote: Specify logging requirements for all tool calls and data queries made by agentic systems — not just final outputs. This is essential for audit, incident investigation, and governance review.
hazard: Inability to audit or investigate agent actions

statement: Log agent access to data sources and human approvals or overrides for audit purposes.
quote: Access to different data sources, human approvals/override (where relevant), should be logged for audit purposes.
hazard: Untraceable human oversight decisions and data access

statement: Bring persistent agentic memory stores under formal data governance including access controls, retention policies, and BAA coverage.
quote: Govern agentic memory: if the agent maintains persistent memory across sessions, that memory store must be brought under formal data governance (access controls, retention policies, BAA coverage).
hazard: Ungoverned retention of PHI in agent memory

statement: For higher-risk agentic AI with PHI access or clinical workflow integration, define which actions require human review or confirmation before execution.
quote: For agentic AI systems operating on or with access sensitive data or that fall under higher-risk (e.g. access to patient data/PHI, payment data, or integrated into clinical workflows) define which types of actions/access require human review or confirmation before execution.
hazard: Unreviewed harmful autonomous agent actions

statement: Include meaningful human review in initial deployment phases of agentic systems before reducing oversight.
quote: Even where full automation is the operational goal, initial deployment phases should include meaningful review to validate that the system is behaving as expected before reducing oversight.
hazard: Undetected unexpected behavior after premature full automation

statement: Define conditions under which an agentic system must pause, escalate to a human, or decline action, such as irreversible clinical consequences.
quote: Establish escalation and halt procedures: Define conditions under which an agentic system should pause, escalate to a human reviewer, or decline to take action.
hazard: Irreversible or unsafe actions taken autonomously

statement: Document the escalation path and train frontline users and operators to initiate escalation or halt the agentic system.
quote: Document the escalation path clearly, and ensure that frontline users and operators know how to initiate escalation or halt the system.
hazard: Users unable to stop malfunctioning AI

statement: Review data preparation rules with clinical or other end-user experts to ensure they reflect clinical reality.
quote: Review with clinical or other end-user experts. For example, rules for handling missing lab values, encoding diagnosis codes, or selecting date windows should be reviewed with clinical staff to ensure they reflect clinical reality.
hazard: Data preparation choices misrepresenting clinical meaning

statement: Version-control all data preparation code and reference a specific version for each model submitted for review or deployment.
quote: Version-control all data preparation code. Each model version submitted for review or deployment should reference a specific, documented version of the preparation code.
hazard: Irreproducible, unauditable model behavior

statement: Record the data preparation SOP version and deviations in the model card.
quote: The data preparation SOP version and any deviations should be recorded in the model card (Domain 3: Organizational Resources Playbook, Control 3), enabling future audits and model updates.
hazard: Lost provenance hindering audits and updates

statement: Use a standard AI DUA addendum as a nonnegotiable baseline in vendor contracts.
quote: Use a standard AI DUA addendum as a nonnegotiable baseline rather than negotiating from a blank page.
hazard: Weak vendor data use protections

statement: Pursue coalition-level vendor negotiations through hospital associations, HCCNs, or GPOs to increase leverage.
quote: Pursue coalition-level negotiations through state hospital associations, HCCNs, or GPOs to increase leverage.
hazard: Insufficient leverage to secure protective contract terms

statement: Define 'modification' and 'derivative data' explicitly in AI vendor contracts.
quote: Define “modification” and “derivative data” explicitly in contracts to eliminate ambiguity.
hazard: Vendor redistribution of derived patient data

statement: Document all vendor deviations from standard contract terms in the AI Inventory Registry.
quote: Document all vendor deviations from standard terms in the AI Inventory Registry.
hazard: Untracked contractual risk exposure

statement: Require vendors to provide data lineage documentation as a procurement condition.
quote: Require vendors to provide data lineage documentation as a procurement condition.
hazard: Unknown provenance of vendor model data

statement: Require vendors to provide subgroup performance data before contract execution.
quote: Require vendors to provide subgroup performance data before contract execution rather than post-deployment.
hazard: Procuring tools that underperform for subgroups

statement: Document known bias limitations explicitly rather than skipping bias assessment.
quote: Accept and document known limitations explicitly rather than skipping assessment — transparency about bias is more defensible than an unsubstantiated claim of unbiased data.
hazard: Undisclosed bias and unsubstantiated fairness claims

statement: Work with vendors to accept de-identified data rather than PHI wherever technically feasible.
quote: Work with vendors to accept de-identified data rather than PHI wherever technically feasible, reducing the overall burden.
hazard: Unnecessary PHI exposure to vendors

statement: Implement a formal data request review requiring documented justification for every data element requested for AI.
quote: Implement a formal data request review process requiring documented justification for every data element requested.
hazard: Sharing more data than necessary

statement: Document in the data acquisition register why each data field is needed for the intended AI purpose.
quote: Embed minimum necessary assessments into the data acquisition register — each entry should document why each field is needed for the intended purpose.
hazard: Excess data collection creating compliance risk

statement: Contractually require vendors via the AI DUA addendum to document and justify requested data elements.
quote: Use the AI DUA addendum to contractually require vendors to document and justify the data elements they request.
hazard: Vendors over-requesting patient data

statement: Require completion of a security questionnaire by all new AI vendors before contracting.
quote: Security questionnaire completed by all new AI vendors prior to contracting.
hazard: Contracting with vendors having inadequate security

statement: Include model training restrictions, model weight controls, and right to audit in AI vendor DUAs.
quote: DUAs include model training restrictions, model weight controls (preventing vendors from retaining AI models trained on institutional data), and right to audit at any time.
hazard: Vendors retaining models trained on institutional patient data

statement: Require vendors to demonstrate HITRUST certification or SOC 2 Type II compliance before contracting.
quote: Vendors may be required to demonstrate HITRUST certification or SOC 2 Type II compliance before contracting.
hazard: Inadequate vendor security controls

statement: Prohibit export of text embeddings and LLM training or tuning ingredients from the secure data environment.
quote: Text embeddings or any ingredients used to train or tune language models are prohibited from export, as they can encode sensitive patient information.
hazard: Sensitive patient information leaking via embeddings

statement: Require manual data team review of every data export request.
quote: The organizations export review process requires manual review of every data export request by their data team.
hazard: Unauthorized patient data export

statement: Have the privacy officer review all AI data use cases before data is shared with a vendor or used for training.
quote: Privacy officer reviews all AI data use cases before any data is shared with a vendor or used for training.
hazard: Unreviewed patient data sharing with vendors

statement: Determine whether each AI system requires pre-implementation training for clinical users or operational staff.
quote: For each AI system, determine whether pre-implementation training is required for clinical users or operational staff.
hazard: Staff use AI without the knowledge needed for safe operation.

statement: Record each AI system's training requirements in the AI inventory during deployment review.
quote: Document the training requirement for each AI system in the AI inventory (see Control 6) at the time of deployment review.
hazard: Training requirements are overlooked before deployment.

statement: Assess training needs against clinical impact, over-reliance risk, workflow novelty, patient vulnerability, and evidence of misinterpretation.
quote: Factors that increase training necessity: direct clinical decision support, outputs that clinicians may over-rely on, novel interfaces or workflows, high-risk patient populations, or evidence of common misinterpretation in literature.
hazard: Training intensity does not match foreseeable risks.

statement: Include intended and out-of-scope uses in AI training requirements.
quote: For each AI solution requiring training, document what the training should cover: (1) What the AI does and does not do—intended use and out-of-scope uses,
hazard: Users apply AI outside its intended scope.

statement: Include instructions for interpreting AI outputs in training requirements.
quote: (2) How to interpret the tool's outputs, including confidence scores or probability estimates,
hazard: Users misinterpret AI outputs.

statement: Include known limitations, failure modes, and circumstances for distrusting outputs in AI training requirements.
quote: (3) Known limitations and failure modes—when to distrust the tool's output,
hazard: Users rely on AI despite recognizable failure conditions.

statement: Train clinicians on actions to take when AI outputs appear incorrect or unusual.
quote: (4) What action clinicians should take if the output appears incorrect or unusual,
hazard: Incorrect outputs are acted upon without appropriate intervention.

statement: Train users to report AI performance concerns and adverse events.
quote: (5) How to report performance concerns or adverse events related to the AI tool,
hazard: AI safety problems remain unreported.

statement: Include applicable regulatory requirements in AI training, including documentation requirements for AI-assisted decisions.
quote: (6) Applicable regulatory requirements (e.g., documentation requirements for AI-assisted decisions).
hazard: AI-assisted work violates applicable regulatory or documentation requirements.

statement: Evaluate vendor training materials against the organization's required training content.
quote: Where vendor training materials are available, evaluate them against these criteria and supplement where needed.
hazard: Vendor materials omit essential safety instruction.

statement: Supplement vendor training materials when required content is missing.
quote: Where vendor training materials are available, evaluate them against these criteria and supplement where needed.
hazard: Users receive incomplete preparation for safe AI use.

statement: Reassess retraining and competency needs after model updates, changes in performance evidence, or shifts in clinical use.
quote: Some AI solutions warrant periodic retraining or competency assessment—particularly when the AI model is updated, when clinical evidence about the tool's performance changes, or when the clinical context of use shifts.
hazard: User knowledge becomes outdated as the AI or its clinical context changes.

statement: Document whether each AI solution requires ongoing training.
quote: Document for each AI solution: whether ongoing training is required, at what cadence (annual, following model updates, following significant clinical events), whether formal competency assessment is warranted, and who is responsible for managing training completion.
hazard: Ongoing training needs are not addressed.

statement: Document the cadence and event triggers for ongoing AI training.
quote: Document for each AI solution: whether ongoing training is required, at what cadence (annual, following model updates, following significant clinical events), whether formal competency assessment is warranted, and who is responsible for managing training completion.
hazard: Retraining is delayed or inconsistently scheduled.

statement: Document whether each AI solution warrants formal user competency assessment.
quote: Document for each AI solution: whether ongoing training is required, at what cadence (annual, following model updates, following significant clinical events), whether formal competency assessment is warranted, and who is responsible for managing training completion.
hazard: High-risk AI is used without verifying user competence.

statement: Assign responsibility for managing AI training completion.
quote: Document for each AI solution: whether ongoing training is required, at what cadence (annual, following model updates, following significant clinical events), whether formal competency assessment is warranted, and who is responsible for managing training completion.
hazard: Required training remains incomplete because ownership is unclear.

statement: Consider scheduled continuing reviews of high-risk clinical AI covering clinical value, user feedback, and usage statistics.
quote: For high-risk clinical AI, consider mirroring the annual check-in model (similar to IRB continuing review) in which ongoing clinical value, user feedback, and usage statistics are reviewed at defined intervals.
hazard: High-risk AI remains deployed despite declining value or emerging use problems.

statement: Consider training boosters when monitoring reveals lack of AI use.
quote: Additionally training boosters may be required if monitoring reveals misuse or lack of use.
hazard: Knowledge gaps contribute to persistent nonuse.

statement: Assign a clinical champion to deliver structured orientation to all users of each new AI tool.
quote: A small FQHC uses a simple training checklist built into its AI deployment workflow: for each new AI tool, the clinical champion completes a brief structured orientation for all users covering what the tool does, how to read its output, and when to flag concerns.
hazard: Users begin using AI without basic orientation.

statement: Record users' completion of AI training.
quote: Training completion is noted in personnel records.
hazard: The organization cannot verify which users completed training.

statement: Provide annual refresher orientation for the highest-risk AI tools.
quote: For its highest-risk tool (a chronic disease risk score), the organization requires annual refresher orientation tied to its quality improvement review cycle.
hazard: Competence deteriorates during continued use of high-risk AI.

statement: Integrate AI training requirements into the standard clinical education workflow.
quote: A regional health system incorporates AI training requirements into its standard clinical education workflow.
hazard: Separate training processes are overlooked or burdensome.

statement: Require completion of AI training before granting tool access.
quote: For a new sepsis alert AI, a 30-minute online module is required before access is granted; completion is tracked in the LMS.
hazard: Untrained users gain access to clinical AI.

statement: Assess ongoing AI user competency annually with a case-based quiz.
quote: Ongoing competency is assessed annually via a brief case-based quiz.
hazard: Persistent misunderstandings remain undetected.

statement: Supplement vendor AI training with local clinical context.
quote: The system uses vendor training materials supplemented by local clinical context.
hazard: Generic training fails to prepare users for local workflows.

statement: Conduct a formal training needs assessment during pre-implementation validation.
quote: A large academic medical center conducts a formal training needs assessment for each AI system as part of the pre-implementation validation process.
hazard: Deployment proceeds without a systematic assessment of training needs.

statement: Tier AI training requirements by risk level and user role.
quote: Training requirements are tiered by risk level and user role.
hazard: Training is insufficient for high-risk roles or disproportionate for low-risk uses.

statement: Provide in-person or synchronous training for high-risk diagnostic AI.
quote: High-risk diagnostic AI (e.g., radiology AI) requires in-person or synchronous training with demonstration of competency before use.
hazard: High-risk users lack opportunities to resolve misunderstandings during training.

statement: Require demonstrated competency before users operate high-risk diagnostic AI.
quote: High-risk diagnostic AI (e.g., radiology AI) requires in-person or synchronous training with demonstration of competency before use.
hazard: Users operate high-risk AI without demonstrating safe use.

statement: Offer annual AI literacy workshops to all clinical staff.
quote: The institution runs annual AI literacy workshops for all clinical staff and tracks participation in its CME system.
hazard: Clinical staff lack foundational AI literacy.

statement: Have the AI Governance Committee review user-training records during annual AI system review.
quote: Training data is reviewed by the AI Governance Committee as part of annual AI system review.
hazard: Governance oversight misses training completion or competency gaps.

statement: Use EHR-native or vendor-managed cloud AI before investing in custom infrastructure.
quote: Start with EHR-native or vendor-managed cloud AI to leverage existing infrastructure before investing in custom infrastructure.
hazard: Infrastructure costs and complexity exceed organizational capacity.

statement: Require AI vendors to document their security architecture.
quote: Require vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports; apply output filtering for generative AI.
hazard: Vendor security weaknesses remain undisclosed.

statement: Require AI vendors to provide SOC 2 reports.
quote: Require vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports; apply output filtering for generative AI.
hazard: Vendor security controls lack independent assurance.

statement: Apply output filtering to generative AI.
quote: Require vendors to document their security architecture and provide SOC 2 reports; apply output filtering for generative AI.
hazard: Generated content unexpectedly exposes protected health information.

statement: Include penetration-testing and vulnerability-scanning rights in AI procurement contracts.
quote: Vendors frequently restrict or decline permission for penetration testing and vulnerability scans. Include testing rights in contract language at procurement stage—retrofitting contracts is significantly harder.
hazard: Contract restrictions prevent security assessment.

statement: Make the official AI governance process easy to find and understand through policy dissemination.
quote: Focus AI policy dissemination on making the governance process easy and visible; create a simple, low-friction intake pathway so staff want to use the official process.
hazard: Staff bypass governance because the official process is unclear.

statement: Create a simple, low-friction AI intake pathway for staff.
quote: Focus AI policy dissemination on making the governance process easy and visible; create a simple, low-friction intake pathway so staff want to use the official process.
hazard: Burdensome intake encourages unauthorized AI use.

statement: Use shared services, regional consortia, or health-center networks to address AI staffing and expertise gaps.
quote: Leverage shared services models, regional health system consortia, and primary care/health center controlled networks.
hazard: Insufficient expertise weakens AI security, bias evaluation, and governance.

statement: Collaborate with regional organizations pursuing similar AI solutions to share implementation burdens.
quote: Working together with regional organizations who are interested in similar solutions can help reduce or share burden.
hazard: Resource constraints prevent adequate implementation and oversight.

statement: Share AI implementation lessons through trade and membership organizations.
quote: Also sharing learnings across trade and other membership organizations can help.
hazard: Organizations repeat avoidable implementation and governance failures.

statement: Use existing frameworks to structure AI security evaluations when dedicated testing tools are unavailable.
quote: Use existing frameworks to structure evaluations even where dedicated tools don’t yet exist.
hazard: Immature security tooling leaves AI risks unevaluated.

statement: Add AI infrastructure documentation to existing IT asset-management processes.
quote: Start with a simple AI infrastructure addendum to existing IT asset management processes.
hazard: AI infrastructure is untracked or inadequately documented.

statement: Integrate AI documentation into existing workflows.
quote: Integrate documentation into existing workflows (e.g., auto-populate model as burdensome. card fields from MLOps platforms); start with minimum viable fields and expand over time
hazard: Documentation burden leads to incomplete governance records.

statement: Begin AI documentation with minimum viable fields and expand the requirements over time.
quote: Integrate documentation into existing workflows (e.g., auto-populate model as burdensome. card fields from MLOps platforms); start with minimum viable fields and expand over time
hazard: Excessive initial documentation demands undermine compliance.

statement: Include a time-bound vendor notification SLA for material AI changes and new versions in AI contracts and BAAs.
quote: Specifically, AI vendor contracts and BAAs should include a defined notification SLA, requiring the vendor to notify the organization within a specified timeframe whenever a material change occurs to the AI system or whenever a new version is deployed.
hazard: Unannounced changes leave model cards, inventories, and governance decisions outdated.

statement: Define material AI changes contractually, including use scope, features, performance, infrastructure, and subprocessors.
quote: Material changes should be explicitly defined in the contract to include changes, for example, to intended use, scope of use, or out-of-scope uses, added features, known performance changes or degradations, and changes to underlying infrastructure or subprocessors.
hazard: Ambiguous notification obligations allow important changes to go unreported.

statement: Prioritize applicable state and federal regulatory requirements, particularly for AI qualifying as Software as a Medical Device.
quote: Organizations should prioritize state and federal regulatory requirements, especially for AI solutions that meet the definition of a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), as defined by the FDA.
hazard: Voluntary governance practices displace binding regulatory obligations.

statement: Involve clinical, technical, compliance, ethics, patient, and community representatives in designing and stewarding AI programs.
quote: It is intended to support organizations in thinking through the design and stewardship of their AI programs and should be used in conjunction with from clinical leaders, technical experts, compliance officers, ethicists, patient and community representatives, and other advisors familiar with the specifics of your organization.
hazard: AI governance overlooks relevant expertise and affected communities' perspectives.

statement: Consult qualified legal counsel and relevant professional advisors before acting on the playbook.
quote: Readers should consult with qualified legal counsel, clinical experts, and other appropriate professional advisors before taking, or refraining from taking, any action based on the information in this playbook.
hazard: General guidance is applied without jurisdictional or organizational expertise.

statement: Identify how each AI solution enters the organization before selecting lifecycle governance processes.
quote: Before detailing the baseline operational controls for Subdomain 4.1: Responsible AI Lifecycle Management and Use of health AI solutions, organizations should first understand how AI solutions enter the organization, referred to as the ingestion modality.
hazard: Governance controls do not match the AI solution's origin or entry pathway.

statement: Include IRB representatives on the AI Governance Committee.
quote: Organizations where IRB representatives sit on the AI Governance Committee (AIGC) benefit from enhanced safety oversight and standardization.
hazard: Research and operational AI oversight remain disconnected.

statement: Obtain required IRB assessment and approval before deploying research AI.
quote: Research models/solutions typically require IRB assessment and approval prior to development or deployment.
hazard: Research AI is deployed without required ethical and safety review.

statement: Define an explicit pathway for transitioning successful research AI into operational use.
quote: HDOs should also define an explicit onramp path for transitioning a successful research model/solution into operational use.
hazard: Research AI enters clinical operations without appropriate deployment governance.

statement: Obtain IRB approval or a waiver for publication-oriented in-house AI when required.
quote: IRB approval or waiver may be required for in-house developed models/solutions if there is an intent to publish findings.
hazard: Publication-oriented AI work proceeds without applicable research oversight.

statement: Retain organizational accountability for safe implementation and oversight of vendor or co-developed AI.
quote: Development responsibilities are shared or externalized, while the HDO remains accountable for safe implementation and oversight within its environment.
hazard: External development creates an accountability gap for local deployment safety.

statement: Define academic partners' roles and responsibilities in AI codevelopment agreements.
quote: Partner universities serve as a key external collaborator for many healthcare organizations that are not university-operated Academic Medical Centers; the role and responsibilities of academic partners should be explicitly defined in codevelopment agreements.
hazard: Ambiguous partner responsibilities impede safe implementation and remediation.

statement: Consider periodic feature-inventory audits when vendors will not commit to advance AI-change notifications.
quote: Lastly, some vendors will not voluntarily commit to advance notification of model/solution updates or feature changes: in those cases, HDOs should consider adding periodic feature-inventory audits and/or contractual notification requirements as compensating controls.
hazard: Embedded AI features change without organizational awareness.

statement: Seek advance vendor notification of new AI functionality and upgrades.
quote: HDOs should strive for vendors to provide advance notification of new AI functionality or upgrades.
hazard: New capabilities become available before governance review can occur.

statement: Reassess newly introduced AI functionality through organizational intake and governance.
quote: HDOs should strive for vendors to provide advance notification of new AI functionality or upgrades. This allows new models/solutions to be re-assessed through the organizational intake and governance process.
hazard: New AI capabilities inherit approval without assessment of their distinct risks.

statement: Map AI product architecture, including third-party model API calls, to applicable contract terms.
quote: Vendors may also expose new functionality within existing terms and conditions, or rely on API calls to third-party models whose terms differ from the platform contract; understanding how product architecture maps to applicable contract terms is critical.
hazard: Third-party components introduce unrecognized contractual or data-handling obligations.

statement: Restrict AI use to a curated set of organization-approved LLM-backed solutions.
quote: Some organizations permit limited personal use under acceptable-use policies; others restrict use to a curated set of organizationapproved LLM-backed solutions.
hazard: Staff use unapproved LLM tools outside organizational safeguards.

statement: Explicitly state which AI solutions staff are permitted to use.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: Staff cannot distinguish authorized AI tools from prohibited tools.

statement: Define permitted AI-use conditions, including protected health information handling.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: Staff expose protected information through inappropriate AI use.

statement: Publish channels for staff to request new AI solutions.
quote: Either way, organizations should explicitly state which solutions are permitted, the conditions of use (including protected health information (PHI) handling), and the channels for requesting new solutions.
hazard: Unclear request pathways encourage shadow AI adoption.

statement: Address mobile and shadow AI in organizational policy.
quote: Mobile and shadow AI should be addressed in policy, training, and ongoing monitoring.
hazard: Personal-device and unauthorized AI use fall outside governance policy.

statement: Address mobile and shadow AI in workforce training.
quote: Mobile and shadow AI should be addressed in policy, training, and ongoing monitoring.
hazard: Staff misunderstand risks and rules for unofficial AI use.

statement: Include mobile and shadow AI in ongoing monitoring.
quote: Mobile and shadow AI should be addressed in policy, training, and ongoing monitoring.
hazard: Unauthorized AI use persists undetected.

statement: Check the organizational AI policy to determine which ingestion modalities are in scope and out of scope.
quote: HDOs should refer to their AI Policy document (see Domain 1: AI Policy Playbook) regarding which types of ingestion modalities are in-scope and out-of-scope.
hazard: AI entry pathways are handled inconsistently with organizational policy.

statement: Formally designate accountable owners for lifecycle compliance for each AI ingestion modality.
quote: It is recommended that each ingestion modality be paired with a formally designated accountable owner(s) (e.g., an executive sponsor and an operational owner) responsible for lifecycle compliance.
hazard: Ambiguous ownership leaves vendor and embedded AI unmanaged.

statement: Apply organizational lifecycle governance to every AI ingestion modality.
quote: The ingestion modalities in which AI solutions enter the organization need to be governed and managed across the organization’s defined AI lifecycle.
hazard: Some AI entry pathways bypass lifecycle controls.

statement: Adapt AI lifecycle step definitions to organizational context while maintaining alignment with emerging best practices.
quote: Organizations may adapt step definitions to reflect their unique context, while staying in alignment with emerging best practices.
hazard: A poorly fitted lifecycle process becomes impractical or ineffective.

statement: Apply risk-proportionate controls at each AI lifecycle step.
quote: Ensure a risk-proportionate approach across each lifecycle step (e.g., lightweight path for low-risk use cases).
hazard: High-risk uses receive inadequate controls while low-risk uses face unnecessary burden.

statement: Establish a strategy for prioritizing AI use cases before subsequent lifecycle activities.
quote: Before HDOs can work through subsequent lifecycle management steps, it is critical to establish a strategy to help drive use case prioritization, business case development, and governing body pre-approval.
hazard: AI adoption proceeds without clear organizational priorities.

statement: Define how AI business cases will be developed before subsequent lifecycle activities.
quote: Before HDOs can work through subsequent lifecycle management steps, it is critical to establish a strategy to help drive use case prioritization, business case development, and governing body pre-approval.
hazard: AI investments proceed without an articulated value case.

statement: Define a governing-body pre-approval process for AI use cases.
quote: Before HDOs can work through subsequent lifecycle management steps, it is critical to establish a strategy to help drive use case prioritization, business case development, and governing body pre-approval.
hazard: AI initiatives advance before governance leadership considers them.

statement: Define each AI use case by its problem, setting, and involved stakeholders.
quote: HDOs should identify a clear problem, its setting, and stakeholders involved (which together comprise a use case), thereby quantifying potential return on investment, return on health outcomes, and improvement of healthcare operations.
hazard: A solution is adopted without a clear problem or deployment context.

statement: Quantify the AI use case's potential financial, health-outcome, and operational benefits.
quote: HDOs should identify a clear problem, its setting, and stakeholders involved (which together comprise a use case), thereby quantifying potential return on investment, return on health outcomes, and improvement of healthcare operations.
hazard: Adoption decisions rely on unsubstantiated benefit claims.

statement: Use the AI solution's intended purpose to define verification and validation scope.
quote: The intended purpose a) defines the scope of verification & validation activities and b) allows reasonable delineation between user responsibility and vendor responsibility.
hazard: Evaluation does not address the actual intended deployment.

statement: Use the AI solution's intended purpose to delineate user and vendor responsibilities.
quote: The intended purpose a) defines the scope of verification & validation activities and b) allows reasonable delineation between user responsibility and vendor responsibility.
hazard: Users and vendors have unclear or conflicting responsibilities.

statement: Use the defined use case and projected benefits to decide whether to build, procure, or co-develop AI.
quote: Implementers use this information to decide whether to build an in-house AI solution, procure one from a third party, or partner with a third party to develop a solution.
hazard: The acquisition approach does not fit organizational needs.

statement: Route every AI solution through structured intake, regardless of whether formal procurement occurs.
quote: Not all AI solutions enter an organization through a formal procurement process; however, the initial step in managing any AI solution is a structured intake process.
hazard: Nonprocured AI bypasses governance review.

statement: Document essential solution and underlying-model information during intake to establish intended use, risk, and governance needs.
quote: Intake consists of gathering and documenting essential information about the AI solution and its underlying model(s) to establish a baseline understanding of intended use, risk, and governance needs.
hazard: Reviewers lack the baseline information needed to govern deployment.

statement: Explicitly capture intended AI users during intake.
quote: Intake should explicitly capture intended users in addition to the intended use.
hazard: Controls are designed without knowing who will use the AI.

statement: Collect AI intake information through a model card or comparable documentation.
quote: CHAI recommends collecting this information through a model card (see CHAI’s Applied Model Card, hereafter “Applied Model Card AMC)”) or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire (see CHAI’s AI Intake Questionnaire, under the “Tools & Resources” section in Subdomain 4.4: Third Party Management Playbook).
hazard: Inconsistent documentation impedes meaningful governance review.

statement: Use a standardized AI intake questionnaire where applicable.
quote: CHAI recommends collecting this information through a model card (see CHAI’s Applied Model Card, hereafter “Applied Model Card AMC)”) or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire (see CHAI’s AI Intake Questionnaire, under the “Tools & Resources” section in Subdomain 4.4: Third Party Management Playbook).
hazard: Important intake questions are omitted or handled inconsistently.

statement: Make model cards use-case-specific and inclusive of the model, technical infrastructure, and human workflows.
quote: A model card describes an AI solution in the context of a specific health use case and reflects the full operational system, including the model, technical infrastructure, and human workflows.
hazard: Model-only documentation obscures risks arising from the deployed system.

statement: Document intended use, workflow, primary users, target populations, and out-of-scope uses in model cards.
