hazard: Contractual oversight overlooking clinical, operational, or technical AI risks.

statement: Assign ownership of AI vendor contractual language and regulatory alignment to legal and compliance functions.
quote: (1) Legal and Compliance typically own contractual language and regulatory alignment;
hazard: Unclear responsibility for contractual protections and regulatory alignment.

statement: Assign clinical and IT operations accountability for how AI is integrated, monitored, and used.
quote: (2) Clinical and IT Operations typically own technical and clinical accountability for how AI is integrated, monitored, and used in practice;
hazard: Unowned clinical or technical responsibilities during AI operation.

statement: Ensure business units initiating or using AI understand their obligations.
quote: (3) Business Units, including the departments or teams that initiate or use AI solutions, should understand the obligations they carry and actively loop in legal and use case specific governance when issues such as scope creep, unexpected performance, or vendor-driven changes arise.
hazard: Business units failing to fulfill AI deployment obligations.

statement: Have business units involve legal and use-case governance when scope creep, unexpected performance, or vendor-driven changes arise.
quote: (3) Business Units, including the departments or teams that initiate or use AI solutions, should understand the obligations they carry and actively loop in legal and use case specific governance when issues such as scope creep, unexpected performance, or vendor-driven changes arise.
hazard: AI scope changes or performance problems proceeding without appropriate escalation.

statement: Define coordination among legal, compliance, clinical, IT, and business functions, including outside formal contract renewal cycles.
quote: Organizations should define how these functions coordinate, especially for situations that arise outside of formal contract renewal cycles.
hazard: Cross-functional gaps delaying responses to emerging vendor AI risks.

statement: Designate a single cross-functional liaison when limited resources constrain third-party AI governance.
quote: Smaller organizations without large legal departments should plan for this crossfunctional role even with limited resources, potentially by designating a single responsible liaison across functions.
hazard: Limited staffing leaving AI vendor coordination unowned.

statement: Align internal positions before approaching vendors about AI accountability and contract terms.
quote: Before approaching any vendor about accountability and contract terms, HDOs should achieve internal alignment.
hazard: Conflicting internal priorities weakening negotiations or delaying protective contract terms.

statement: Convene an AI negotiation team including legal or contracts, compliance or privacy, a clinical or area champion, and IT.
quote: Convene the internal negotiation team. At minimum, this should include a legal or contract representative, a compliance or privacy officer, a clinical or area expert champion who understands how the AI will be used in practice, and an IT representative.
hazard: Negotiations omitting essential legal, privacy, clinical, or technical expertise.

statement: Add negotiation-team staff when the AI use case requires additional expertise.
quote: Additional staff may be needed based on the use case.
hazard: Use-case-specific risks being missed during vendor negotiations.

statement: Establish a single decision-maker or owner for each AI vendor negotiation.
quote: Establish a single decision-maker or "owner" for the negotiation.
hazard: Unclear negotiation authority and inconsistent organizational commitments.

statement: Agree internally on non-negotiable contract requirements before vendor discussions.
quote: Before the vendor conversation, the internal team should agree on: a. The non-negotiable requirements: clauses you will not execute a contract without b. The preferred-but-flexible terms: positions you will advocate for but may accept alternatives on c. The walk-away criteria: conditions that would cause you to pause or terminate the engagement.
hazard: Execution of AI contracts without essential organizational protections.

statement: Agree internally on preferred but negotiable AI contract terms before vendor discussions.
quote: Before the vendor conversation, the internal team should agree on: a. The non-negotiable requirements: clauses you will not execute a contract without b. The preferred-but-flexible terms: positions you will advocate for but may accept alternatives on c. The walk-away criteria: conditions that would cause you to pause or terminate the engagement.
hazard: Inconsistent concessions or stalled negotiations over flexible contract terms.

statement: Define conditions for pausing or terminating an AI vendor engagement before negotiations begin.
quote: Before the vendor conversation, the internal team should agree on: a. The non-negotiable requirements: clauses you will not execute a contract without b. The preferred-but-flexible terms: positions you will advocate for but may accept alternatives on c. The walk-away criteria: conditions that would cause you to pause or terminate the engagement.
hazard: Continuing vendor engagements despite unacceptable terms or risks.

statement: Assess negotiating leverage using organizational size, vendor market position, solution uniqueness, and available alternatives.
quote: Assess the HDO’s leverage honestly. The negotiating position may depend on the organization's size, the vendor's market position, the uniqueness of the solution, and whether alternatives exist.
hazard: Negotiation strategies that fail to secure achievable AI protections.

statement: Prioritize achievable disclosure, monitoring, and documentation requests when negotiating leverage with dominant AI vendors is limited.
quote: Smaller organizations working with large, dominant AI vendors (e.g., major EHR platforms) may have limited leverage on standard contract terms and should plan accordingly by focusing on achievable asks (e.g. disclosure, monitoring obligations, model documentation).
hazard: Limited negotiating leverage resulting in no practical AI governance protections.

statement: Complete vendor AI intake to inform responsible AI review and needed contract terms.
quote: Complete the AI intake to inform Responsible AI (RAI) review. The information gathered during vendor AI intake (e.g., model card information, intake evidence gathering, training data disclosure, known limitations, regulatory status, etc.) directly informs which contract terms you need.
hazard: AI review and contracts being developed without evidence of solution-specific risks.

statement: Choose the sequence of AI intake, governance review, and contracting to match organizational maturity and vendor-management discipline.
quote: HDOs should pick the sequencing that fits their internal governance maturity and the strength of their vendor management discipline.
hazard: Procurement sequencing that leaves governance findings unable to influence contract protections.

statement: Consider structured multi-vendor evaluations or side-by-side proofs of concept where feasible.
quote: Optional: Consider a multi-vendor evaluation (RFP or "bake-off") where feasible.
hazard: Selecting AI vendors without comparative evidence or negotiating alternatives.

statement: Score vendor disclosure and monitoring commitments as procurement criteria in competitive AI evaluations.
quote: Competing vendors may be more willing to accept disclosure, monitoring, and other components when they know those terms are being used as scored procurement criteria, and comparative performance data gathered during the evaluation can be referenced in later negotiations to justify required SLAs or protections.
hazard: Vendor selection undervaluing disclosure and monitoring protections.

statement: Use comparative AI performance evidence to justify service-level agreements or protections during negotiations.
quote: Competing vendors may be more willing to accept disclosure, monitoring, and other components when they know those terms are being used as scored procurement criteria, and comparative performance data gathered during the evaluation can be referenced in later negotiations to justify required SLAs or protections.
hazard: Contractual performance protections lacking supporting comparative evidence.

statement: Evaluate the cost and expected return of parallel vendor proofs of concept before undertaking them.
quote: HDOs should weigh the cost considerations: standing up parallel proofs-of-concept across multiple vendors is resource-intensive, and the return on investment (ROI) of this approach depends on the use case and the number of credible vendors in the market.
hazard: Resource-intensive vendor evaluations consuming resources without sufficient benefit.

statement: Seek shared AI contract templates and negotiation support from hospital associations, FQHC networks, or regional HIEs when dedicated AI legal expertise is unavailable.
quote: Smaller organizations without dedicated AI legal expertise should reach out to their state hospital association, FQHC network, or regional health information exchange. Many are developing shared AI contract templates and peer networks specifically to help smaller organizations negotiate more effectively.
hazard: Weak AI contracts caused by limited specialized legal expertise.

statement: Specify vendor disclosure requirements for known AI model limitations and risks.
quote: Outline requirements for disclosure of known model limitations and risks; define roles and responsibilities pertinent to the AI solution and known risks; include contractual and operational risk mitigation provisions to de-risk the use of the solution.
hazard: Deployment decisions made without knowledge of model limitations or risks.

statement: Define organizational and vendor roles and responsibilities for each AI solution and its known risks.
quote: Outline requirements for disclosure of known model limitations and risks; define roles and responsibilities pertinent to the AI solution and known risks; include contractual and operational risk mitigation provisions to de-risk the use of the solution.
hazard: Accountability gaps for AI solution operation and known risks.

statement: Include contractual provisions mitigating risks from AI solution use.
quote: Outline requirements for disclosure of known model limitations and risks; define roles and responsibilities pertinent to the AI solution and known risks; include contractual and operational risk mitigation provisions to de-risk the use of the solution.
hazard: AI deployment risks lacking enforceable contractual protections.

statement: Establish operational provisions mitigating risks from AI solution use.
quote: Outline requirements for disclosure of known model limitations and risks; define roles and responsibilities pertinent to the AI solution and known risks; include contractual and operational risk mitigation provisions to de-risk the use of the solution.
hazard: AI risks remaining uncontrolled in day-to-day operation.

statement: Apply third-party AI disclosure, accountability, and risk-mitigation controls to every third-party relationship.
quote: Control 4.4.1 applies to all third party relationships.
hazard: Third-party AI arrangements escaping governance because of agreement type.

statement: Implement organization-owned workflow safeguards for risks that AI contracts do not fully resolve.
quote: Operational Controls handle the risks that the contract did not, or could not, fully resolve. These are workflow-level safeguards owned by the deploying organization.
hazard: Residual AI risks being mistaken for resolved contractual responsibilities.

statement: Reopen AI intake after material changes to the model, use case, or regulatory environment.
quote: After go-live, monitoring and re-review feed back into intake whenever there is a material change to the model, the use case, or the regulatory picture.
hazard: Material deployment changes invalidating prior risk assessments and protections.

statement: Create a working inventory of current AI vendor relationships before individual solution intake.
quote: Before beginning intake on any individual AI solution, it may be helpful to start with a working AI inventory of all current AI vendor relationships.
hazard: Existing AI vendors and contractual gaps being omitted from intake planning.

statement: Review existing contracts, licenses, subscriptions, BAAs, and DUAs to identify vendors providing or enabling AI functionality.
quote: Conduct a review of existing vendor contracts, software licenses, subscription agreements, BAAs, and data use agreements (DUAs) to identify vendors that provide or enable AI functionality.
hazard: AI functionality hidden within existing vendor agreements.

statement: Record each AI vendor relationship's solution name, ingestion modality, use-case type, governing contracts, and contract expiration or renewal date.
quote: For each AI vendor relationship, document: the name of the AI solution, the ingestion modality (standalone product vs. embedded feature), the type of use case (clinical, operational, administrative), the applicable contract(s), and the contract expiration or renewal date.
hazard: Incomplete AI vendor records impairing oversight and timely contract action.

statement: Start AI vendor discovery with the existing EHR vendor in smaller organizations.
quote: For smaller organizations, start with the existing EHR vendor.
hazard: Resource-constrained discovery overlooking AI in the organization's principal clinical platform.

statement: Review the existing EHR agreement for AI disclosure and governance rights in smaller organizations.
quote: Smaller organizations should review the current agreement to determine what disclosures or governance rights, if any, are already in place.
hazard: Organizations failing to use existing contractual AI oversight rights.

statement: Use two-stage vendor AI intake with initial triage followed by more detailed questions for higher-risk solutions.
quote: HDOs typically have a 2-part intake process with external vendors (e.g., Part 1: initial, light-touch set of intake questions to triage solutions; Part 2: additional, more robust set of intake questions for higher risk solutions).
hazard: Higher-risk AI receiving insufficient intake scrutiny.

statement: Document the AI solution's functionality, intended uses, and intended users during intake.
quote: Surface what the AI is, what it does, who it is for, and what is known and unknown about its performance, fairness, security, and lifecycle.
hazard: Reviewing or deploying AI without a clear intended scope.

statement: Document knowns and unknowns about AI performance, fairness, security, and lifecycle during intake.
quote: Surface what the AI is, what it does, who it is for, and what is known and unknown about its performance, fairness, security, and lifecycle.
hazard: Unrecognized evidence gaps about AI safety, fairness, security, or maintenance.

statement: Collect vendor attestations and supporting model cards, validation summaries, certifications, BAA templates, and monitoring plans.
quote: Collect the vendor's attestations and supporting evidence (model cards, validation summaries, certifications, BAA templates, monitoring plans).
hazard: AI procurement decisions based on unsupported vendor claims.

statement: Produce one evidence package for AI governance review without redundant questionnaires.
quote: HDOs should produce a single evidence package that the governance structure can reference, without redundant duplicate questionnaires.
hazard: Fragmented evidence and duplicate intake work undermining consistent AI review.

statement: Embed the AI intake questionnaire formally into the procurement workflow.
quote: Once an AI intake questionnaire is in place, HDOs should consider embedding it formally into the procurement workflow.
hazard: AI purchases bypassing standardized intake and evidence collection.

statement: Make a vendor model card or equivalent documentation a condition of AI contract execution.
quote: This might look like: Updating existing vendor intake questionnaires and procurement checklists to include AI-specific questions. Requiring AI vendors to provide a model card or equivalent documentation as a condition of contract execution for any AI solution.
hazard: Executing AI contracts without essential model documentation.

statement: Translate identified AI intake risks and vendor documentation gaps into specific contract requirements.
quote: Integrating AI intake findings into contract negotiations: use identified risks or gaps in vendor documentation to inform specific contract requirements.
hazard: Known AI risks or evidence gaps remaining unaddressed in contracts.

statement: Consult qualified legal counsel on AI vendor contracts, particularly indemnification, liability limits, and data ownership.
quote: Organizations should consult qualified legal counsel when reviewing AI vendor contracts, particularly provisions related to indemnification, limitation of liability, and data ownership.
hazard: Unfavorable or unclear allocation of AI liability and data rights.

statement: Assess each AI solution against organizational risk tolerance using intake responses and evidence.
quote: After intake, the organization should assess the solution against its own risk tolerance. The purpose of this phase is to apply the organization's own organizational positions to the intake responses and evidence and produce a risk assessment that drives the next two phases.
hazard: AI adoption inconsistent with organizational risk tolerance.

statement: Document whether each identified AI risk will be mitigated, transferred, or accepted.
quote: A risk assessment is most useful when it explicitly identifies which risks the organization plans to mitigate, which it plans to transfer, and which it plans to accept.
hazard: Identified AI risks lacking an explicit treatment decision.

statement: Decline AI adoption when risk assessment determines the solution is incompatible with organizational risk tolerance.
quote: In some cases, it will also determine when an organization chooses not to move forward with a solution, given its risk profile and the organization’s risk tolerance.
hazard: Proceeding with AI solutions whose risks the organization cannot accept.

statement: Make AI governance review a mandatory gate in the procurement approval workflow.
quote: Organizations may consider the following: Embedding your organization's AI governance review (which may consist of initial AI intake, risk assessment, evaluations) as a mandatory gate in the procurement approval workflow.
hazard: Procurement approval preceding necessary AI governance review.

statement: Link responsible AI governance review to negotiations so its findings can amend contract terms before execution.
quote: Linking the responsible AI governance review process to contract negotiation, so that any findings, such as model limitations, bias or subgroup performance gaps, or unacceptable risk profiles, can still be used to amend contract terms before execution.
hazard: Governance findings arriving too late to secure contractual protections.

statement: Have legal or compliance review the standard AI intake questionnaire before contract sign-off.
quote: For organizations using a standard AI intake questionnaire, ensuring the questionnaire is reviewed by legal and/or compliance before contract sign-off.
hazard: AI contracts signed without legal or compliance consideration of intake information.

statement: Document any AI contract executed before completion of full governance review.
quote: If a contract is executed before a full AI governance review can be completed, document this with a defined timeline for completing the review and a process for contract amendment if needed.
hazard: Unrecorded procurement exceptions concealing incomplete AI governance review.

statement: Set a defined deadline for completing AI governance review when a contract is signed before the review is complete.
quote: If a contract is executed before a full AI governance review can be completed, document this with a defined timeline for completing the review and a process for contract amendment if needed.
hazard: Deferred AI governance review remaining incomplete indefinitely.

statement: Establish a contract-amendment process for AI agreements signed before full governance review.
quote: If a contract is executed before a full AI governance review can be completed, document this with a defined timeline for completing the review and a process for contract amendment if needed.
hazard: Post-signature AI governance findings lacking a route to contractual correction.

statement: Reassess an AI solution's health equity impact when considering implementation in a new or different setting.
quote: An AI solution that is evaluated by one setting through HEAAL should be reassessed when a different setting considers implementation.
hazard: Unanticipated inequities caused by variations in patient population or workflow across settings.

statement: Apply the HEAAL framework every time the healthcare organization considers using a new AI solution.
quote: Thus, to ensure health equity, HEAAL should be applied every time a healthcare organization considers using an AI solution.
hazard: Deployment of biased AI solutions that worsen health inequities.

statement: Register AI product assessments and report evaluation progress to independent registries to ensure transparency.
quote: Similar to the registration of clinical trials, healthcare organizations can register AI product assessments and report progress in conducting HEAAL procedures.
hazard: Outward projection of equity commitment without genuine accountability or changes to practices.

statement: Implement the AI solution prospectively with proactive outreach to provide medical and social support for all high-risk patients.
quote: Prospective implementation of the AI solution with proactive outreach to provide medical and social support for all high-risk patients can improve health equity.
hazard: Worsening of health inequities due to systemic racism or inequitable diagnosis processes.

statement: Monitor generative AI outputs for confabulated content when integrating GAI into applications that inform consequential decisions, such as summarizing patient information.
quote: Risks of confabulated content may be especially important to monitor when integrating GAI into applications involving consequential decision making.
hazard: Confabulated patient summaries leading clinicians to incorrect diagnoses or wrong treatments

statement: Tailor how GAI risks are measured to the model's architecture, training data, access level, and use-case context.
quote: Organizations may choose to tailor how they measure GAI risks based on these characteristics.
hazard: Generic risk measurement missing risks specific to the model or use case

statement: Allocate risk management resources in proportion to the severity and likelihood of each GAI deployment's potential negative impacts.
quote: They may additionally wish to allocate risk management resources relative to the severity and likelihood of negative impacts, including where and how these risks manifest, and their direct and material impacts harms in the context of GAI use.
hazard: Under-resourcing oversight of high-severity, high-likelihood GAI harms

statement: Restrict model outputs for certain content or prompt types, and test whether less-explicit or novel prompts can still circumvent these controls.
quote: Many current systems restrict model outputs to limit certain content or in response to certain prompts, but this approach may still produce harmful recommendations in response to other less-explicit, novel prompts
hazard: Jailbreaks or novel prompts eliciting dangerous recommendations, including self-harm content

statement: Review all AI vendor contracts for legal and compliance requirements.
quote: legal and compliance review process for all AI vendor contracts.
hazard: Contractual gaps that expose the organization to legal or compliance violations.

statement: Maintain a master vendor registry recording data use agreement status and renewal dates.
quote: A master vendor registry tracks DUA status and renewal dates.
hazard: Untracked or expired agreements governing vendor data use.

statement: Update the standard AI contract addendum annually to reflect evolving regulatory guidance.
quote: Standard AI addendum developed internally, updated annually to reflect evolving regulatory guidance.
hazard: Outdated contractual protections and regulatory noncompliance.

statement: Have every new AI vendor complete a security questionnaire before contracting.
quote: Security questionnaire completed by all new AI vendors prior to contracting.
hazard: Contracting with vendors whose security weaknesses have not been assessed.

statement: Conduct annual compliance reviews of high-risk or high-data-volume AI vendors.
quote: Annual compliance reviews for high-risk or high-data-volume vendors.
hazard: Undetected vendor noncompliance affecting sensitive or large-volume data.

statement: Assign dedicated AI legal counsel to the AI procurement governance program.
quote: Comprehensive AI procurement governance program with dedicated AI legal counsel and privacy engineering team.
hazard: Insufficient legal expertise in AI procurement decisions.

statement: Assign a dedicated privacy engineering team to AI procurement governance.
quote: Comprehensive AI procurement governance program with dedicated AI legal counsel and privacy engineering team.
hazard: Privacy risks overlooked during procurement.

statement: Include restrictions on vendor model training in data use agreements.
quote: DUAs include model training restrictions, model weight controls (preventing vendors from retaining AI models trained on institutional data), and right to audit at any time.
hazard: Unauthorized vendor training on institutional or patient data.

statement: Include model weight controls preventing vendors from retaining models trained on institutional data.
quote: DUAs include model training restrictions, model weight controls (preventing vendors from retaining AI models trained on institutional data), and right to audit at any time.
hazard: Continued vendor possession of models containing institutional or patient information.

statement: Include the right to audit vendors at any time in data use agreements.
quote: DUAs include model training restrictions, model weight controls (preventing vendors from retaining AI models trained on institutional data), and right to audit at any time.
hazard: Inability to investigate vendor data handling or contractual compliance.

statement: Consider requiring HITRUST certification or SOC 2 Type II compliance before contracting with AI vendors.
quote: Vendors may be required to demonstrate HITRUST certification or SOC 2 Type II compliance before contracting.
hazard: Engaging vendors without demonstrated security assurance.

statement: Conduct joint security reviews for the highest-risk AI tools.
quote: Joint security reviews for highestrisk tools.
hazard: Unidentified security vulnerabilities in high-risk deployments.

statement: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies.
quote: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination) considering applicable state privacy laws; where relevant, evaluate each PHI-containing dataset to select the method that minimizes re-identification risk; validate de-identification before any dataset is used in AI training or model development; and maintain oversight of de-identified datasets, reassessing re-identification risk whenever datasets are linked or new identifiers emerge.
hazard: Inconsistent de-identification practices and unlawful exposure of patient information.

statement: Account for privacy laws in every state where the organization operates or patients reside.
quote: De-identification policies should account for the privacy laws of all states in which the organization operates or in which patients reside.
hazard: Violations of state privacy protections exceeding HIPAA requirements.

statement: De-identify data or obtain explicit patient authorization for uses or disclosures outside existing authorization, treatment, payment, operations, or BAA coverage.
quote: If no, de-identification or explicit patient authorization is the necessary condition for the activity to be permissible.
hazard: Unauthorized use or disclosure of protected health information.

statement: Consider de-identification for risk management even when existing authorization or BAA coverage permits identifiable data use.
quote: Does the recipient of this data (or the use of this data) fall within the covered entity's existing authorization framework, treatment, payment, operations, or a BAA? If yes, de-identification is generally not required but may still be advisable for risk management.
hazard: Avoidable exposure of identifiable patient data during otherwise authorized activities.

statement: Document which de-identification method will be used for each scenario.
quote: Document which method (Safe Harbor, Expert Determination, or synthetic data) will be used for which scenarios, and define who has authority to approve de-identification for AI training use.
hazard: Inappropriate or inconsistent selection of privacy protection methods.

statement: Define who can approve de-identification for AI training use.
quote: Document which method (Safe Harbor, Expert Determination, or synthetic data) will be used for which scenarios, and define who has authority to approve de-identification for AI training use.
hazard: Unaccountable approval of inadequately de-identified patient data.

statement: Assess the dataset and intended use for each new patient-data AI use case to select an appropriate de-identification method.
quote: For each new AI use case involving patient data, evaluate the dataset and intended use to select the appropriate de-identification method.
hazard: Selecting privacy protections unsuitable for the dataset or intended disclosure.

statement: Document each use-case assessment supporting selection of a de-identification method.
quote: For each new AI use case involving patient data, evaluate the dataset and intended use to select the appropriate de-identification method. Document this assessment.
hazard: Untraceable decisions about patient-data privacy protections.

statement: Remove all 18 HIPAA-specified identifiers when using Safe Harbor de-identification.
quote: Safe Harbor Method Remove all 18 HIPAA-specified identifiers, including:
hazard: Residual direct identifiers in data represented as de-identified.

statement: Use a qualified statistician or scientific expert to assess re-identification risk under Expert Determination.
quote: A qualified statistician or scientific expert analyzes the dataset and applies statistical or scientific principles to determine that the risk of identifying an individual is very small.
hazard: Unsupported conclusions that patient re-identification risk is sufficiently small.

statement: Document the methods and results supporting each Expert Determination.
quote: The expert documents the methods and results that justify this determination.
hazard: Unverifiable de-identification determinations.

statement: Govern patient-derived text embeddings and LLM fine-tuning inputs as patient-level data.
quote: Any text embeddings or LLM fine-tuning inputs derived from patient data should be treated as patient-level data and governed accordingly.
hazard: Exposure of patient-identifiable information encoded in embeddings or fine-tuning inputs.

statement: Maintain oversight of de-identified datasets, including reassessment when new identifiers emerge.
quote: Establish written HIPAA-compliant de-identification policies (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination) considering applicable state privacy laws; where relevant, evaluate each PHI-containing dataset to select the method that minimizes re-identification risk; validate de-identification before any dataset is used in AI training or model development; and maintain oversight of de-identified datasets, reassessing re-identification risk whenever datasets are linked or new identifiers emerge.
hazard: Previously de-identified data becoming identifiable as new information emerges.

statement: Formally reassess re-identification risk whenever de-identified datasets are combined or linked.
quote: When de-identified datasets are combined or linked, conduct a formal reassessment of re-identification risk and update HIPAA risk documentation accordingly.
hazard: Re-identification enabled by combining individually de-identified datasets.

statement: Update HIPAA risk documentation after reassessing linked or combined de-identified datasets.
quote: When de-identified datasets are combined or linked, conduct a formal reassessment of re-identification risk and update HIPAA risk documentation accordingly.
hazard: Privacy risk records failing to reflect increased linkage risk.

statement: Establish separate de-identification procedures for clinical notes, imaging reports, and other free-text data.
quote: Develop specific procedures for clinical notes, imaging reports, and other free-text data, using NLP-based de-identification tools and additional validation steps.
hazard: Identifying clinical details surviving procedures designed only for structured data.

statement: Use NLP-based de-identification tools for unstructured clinical text.
quote: Develop specific procedures for clinical notes, imaging reports, and other free-text data, using NLP-based de-identification tools and additional validation steps.
hazard: Patient identifiers and identifying combinations missed by rule-based removal.

statement: Apply additional de-identification validation steps to free-text clinical data.
quote: Develop specific procedures for clinical notes, imaging reports, and other free-text data, using NLP-based de-identification tools and additional validation steps.
hazard: Undetected residual patient-identifiable content in unstructured text.

statement: Review medical-image metadata for identifiers before sharing images or using them for AI training.
quote: Medical images (e.g., DICOM files) need particular care: metadata embedded in image headers often contains patient identifiers beyond the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor fields (such as institution name, acquisition date, equipment identifiers, and operator names) and must be reviewed and stripped before images are shared or used for AI training.
hazard: Patient identifiers overlooked in image headers.

statement: Strip identifying medical-image metadata before sharing images or using them for AI training.
quote: Medical images (e.g., DICOM files) need particular care: metadata embedded in image headers often contains patient identifiers beyond the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor fields (such as institution name, acquisition date, equipment identifiers, and operator names) and must be reviewed and stripped before images are shared or used for AI training.
hazard: Disclosure of patient information through embedded image metadata.

statement: Treat image pixels capable of identifying patients as patient-identifiable data.
quote: Pixel-level data in certain image types, including full-face photographs and some dermatology, ophthalmology, or plastic surgery images, may directly reidentify patients and should be treated accordingly.
hazard: Patient re-identification from images after metadata removal.

statement: Consider more conservative de-identification for sensitive-population data used for AI training or shared with vendors.
quote: Organizations using such data for AI training or sharing it with vendors should consider more conservative deidentification approaches, stricter access controls, and/or explicit contractual restrictions on downstream use.
hazard: Elevated re-identification risk for vulnerable or specially protected populations.

statement: Consider stricter access controls for sensitive-population data used for AI training or shared with vendors.
quote: Organizations using such data for AI training or sharing it with vendors should consider more conservative deidentification approaches, stricter access controls, and/or explicit contractual restrictions on downstream use.
hazard: Unauthorized access to data carrying heightened privacy protections.

statement: Consider explicit contractual restrictions on downstream use of sensitive-population data.
quote: Organizations using such data for AI training or sharing it with vendors should consider more conservative deidentification approaches, stricter access controls, and/or explicit contractual restrictions on downstream use.
hazard: Uncontrolled downstream reuse of sensitive patient information.

statement: Consult applicable federal, state, and local laws when handling sensitive-population data.
quote: This is an evolving area; consult applicable federal, state, and local laws and legal counsel.
hazard: Failure to honor heightened legal protections for sensitive patient data.

statement: Consult legal counsel about protections for sensitive-population data.
quote: This is an evolving area; consult applicable federal, state, and local laws and legal counsel.
hazard: Misinterpretation of evolving privacy obligations.

statement: Validate de-identification before using a dataset.
quote: Validate de-identification before use.
hazard: Use or disclosure of data incorrectly assumed to be de-identified.

statement: Use automated tools for initial de-identification validation.
quote: Use automated tools for initial validation, supplemented by privacy officer or qualified expert review.
hazard: Residual identifiers missed during initial dataset screening.

statement: Supplement automated de-identification validation with privacy officer or qualified expert review.
quote: Use automated tools for initial validation, supplemented by privacy officer or qualified expert review.
hazard: Overreliance on automated checks that miss contextual re-identification risks.

statement: Document de-identification validation results.
quote: Document the validation results and link them to the data acquisition register (Control 1).
hazard: Inability to verify that privacy validation occurred.

statement: Link de-identification validation results to the data acquisition register.
quote: Document the validation results and link them to the data acquisition register (Control 1).
hazard: Loss of traceability between datasets and their privacy validation.

statement: Use the EHR vendor's built-in de-identification tools where available.
quote: Uses the EHR vendor’s built-in de-identification tools where available.
hazard: Patient-data exposure where local de-identification capability is limited.

statement: Obtain Expert Determination services through a state HIE, regional HCCN, or contracted privacy consultant.
quote: For complex use cases requiring Expert Determination, leverages de-identification services available through the state HIE, regional HCCN, or contracted privacy consultant rather than building internal capability.
hazard: Inadequate de-identification assessments caused by unavailable internal expertise.

statement: Have the privacy officer review every AI data use case before vendor sharing or training use.
quote: Privacy officer reviews all AI data use cases before any data is shared with a vendor or used for training.
hazard: Patient data used or disclosed without privacy review.

statement: Log every validated dataset in the data acquisition register.
quote: All validated datasets are logged in the data acquisition register.
hazard: Untracked datasets and inability to establish validation status.

statement: Assign a dedicated privacy engineering team to manage de-identification for AI use cases.
quote: Dedicated privacy engineering team manages de-identification for AI use cases.
hazard: Insufficient expertise or ownership for technically demanding de-identification.

statement: Use Expert Determination for all AI training datasets.
quote: Expert Determination used for all AI training data, with independent statistical validation.
hazard: Re-identification risks not captured by simple identifier removal.

statement: Obtain independent statistical validation of Expert Determination for AI training data.
quote: Expert Determination used for all AI training data, with independent statistical validation.
hazard: Unchallenged errors in de-identification risk determinations.

statement: Explore synthetic data for the highest-risk use cases involving sensitive populations.
quote: Explores synthetic data generation (e.g., Syntegra, Synthea) for highest-risk use cases involving sensitive populations.
hazard: Re-identification of sensitive populations through use of real patient records.

statement: Keep text embeddings and LLM inputs within the secure data environment.
quote: Text embedding and LLM inputs treated as patient-level data and prohibited from leaving the secure data environment, consistent with Mayo Clinic Platform’s approach.
hazard: Export of sensitive patient information encoded in embeddings or LLM inputs.

statement: Prohibit export of patient-level or row-level data regardless of perceived re-identification risk.
quote: Patient-level or row-level data: No patient-level data of any kind may be exported, regardless of perceived re-identification risk.
hazard: Patient re-identification following export of granular records.

statement: Prohibit export of PII elements, including obfuscated or pseudonymized elements.
quote: PII data elements: All PII elements — including those previously obfuscated or pseudonymized — are prohibited from export (names, IDs, dates, locations, etc.).
hazard: Recovery or linkage of identities from exported identifiers.

statement: Allow export of aggregated metrics only when they represent at least 10 patients.
quote: Aggregated metrics: Only metrics representing 10 or more patients may be exported; no proportions that could derive a value less than 10.
hazard: Re-identification through small patient counts.

statement: Prohibit export of proportions from which a patient count below 10 could be derived.
quote: Aggregated metrics: Only metrics representing 10 or more patients may be exported; no proportions that could derive a value less than 10.
hazard: Inference of small patient groups from apparently aggregated statistics.

statement: Require manual data-team review of every data export request.
quote: The organizations export review process requires manual review of every data export request by their data team.
hazard: Unauthorized or identifying data leaving the secure environment.

statement: Temporarily block data access and export submissions when export denial rates consistently exceed 25%.
quote: A consistent export denial rate above 25% results in a temporary block from data access and export submission.
hazard: Repeated unsafe export attempts despite prior denials.

statement: Require exported files to include a READ ME documenting column names, source, description, and patient count per row.
quote: All exported files must include a READ ME file documenting column names, source, description, and patient count per row.
hazard: Uninterpretable exports and hidden patient-level disclosure risks.

statement: Establish a recurring process for evaluating AI data quality and bias.
quote: Establish a process and owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation to help identify quality gaps and known sources of bias.
hazard: Persistent or emerging data defects and biases going undetected.

statement: Assign an owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation.
quote: Establish a process and owner for recurring AI data quality and bias evaluation to help identify quality gaps and known sources of bias.
hazard: Data quality and bias monitoring neglected because responsibility is unclear.

statement: Set dataset-specific completeness, accuracy, and consistency thresholds before AI development or procurement.
quote: Define data quality standards before model development or procurement. Establish acceptable thresholds for completeness, accuracy, and consistency for each dataset used in AI.
hazard: Deployment using data inadequate for reliable AI performance.

statement: Document AI data quality standards.
quote: Document these standards and include them in procurement requirements for vendor tools.
hazard: Inconsistent or unverifiable acceptance of dataset quality.

statement: Include data quality standards in procurement requirements for vendor AI tools.
quote: Document these standards and include them in procurement requirements for vendor tools.
hazard: Purchasing tools whose data quality does not meet organizational requirements.

statement: Assess whether data are current enough for the intended AI use case.
quote: Timeliness: Is the data current enough for the intended use case?
hazard: AI outputs reflecting outdated clinical practices or patient populations.

statement: Compare dataset demographics with the intended patient population before validating or piloting a vendor AI tool.
quote: Before using any dataset for AI training or validating/piloting any vendor tool, compare the demographic distribution of the dataset to the population the model will serve.
hazard: Deploying tools whose underlying data poorly represent local patients.

statement: Document significant gaps between dataset demographics and the population the AI tool will serve.
quote: Document any significant gaps--do not assume a mismatch disqualifies a tool, but ensure it is understood and disclosed.
hazard: Unrecognized limitations affecting underrepresented patient groups.

statement: Disclose significant representativeness gaps without automatically treating a mismatch as disqualifying.
quote: Document any significant gaps--do not assume a mismatch disqualifies a tool, but ensure it is understood and disclosed.
hazard: Uninformed deployment decisions or unjustified rejection based solely on demographic mismatch.

statement: Map likely bias types and their potential effects on outputs for every dataset or AI tool.
quote: For each dataset or AI tool, explicitly map which types of bias (representation, label, temporal, selection, measurement) are likely present and how they may affect model outputs.
hazard: Unrecognized pathways through which data bias affects AI outputs.

statement: Evaluate AI performance across relevant subgroups rather than relying solely on aggregate metrics.
quote: Evaluate and monitor AI tool performance across relevant subgroups. Do not rely solely on aggregate performance metrics.
hazard: Poor subgroup performance hidden by acceptable overall performance.

statement: Monitor AI performance across relevant subgroups after deployment.
quote: Evaluate and monitor AI tool performance across relevant subgroups. Do not rely solely on aggregate performance metrics.
hazard: Emerging disparities in AI performance going unnoticed.

statement: Schedule bias assessments at data ingestion, applicable validation, deployment, and predefined post-deployment intervals.
quote: Assessments should occur at data ingestion, during model training or validation (if applicable), at deployment, and at predefined post-deployment intervals.
hazard: Bias introduced or worsened between isolated assessment events.

statement: Make post-deployment bias monitoring frequency and rigor proportionate to tool risk or data sensitivity.
quote: The frequency and rigor of post-deployment bias monitoring should be proportionate to the risk level of the AI tool or the sensitivity of the data.
hazard: Insufficient surveillance of high-consequence bias.

statement: Actively monitor all AI solutions for performance and intended outcomes.
quote: Their “Actively Monitored” principle ensures all AI solutions are actively monitored for performance and intended outcomes.
hazard: Performance degradation or failure to achieve intended clinical outcomes.

statement: Prioritize evaluation subgroups that matter most for the local population and use case.
quote: Consider which subgroups are particularly important for your population and use-case, and start there.
hazard: Limited evaluation resources overlooking locally important disparities.

statement: Consider evaluating ambient AI performance by language subgroup when serving primarily non-English-speaking patients.
quote: For example, a CHC that serves primarily non-English speakers, may want to look at how their Ambient AI solution performs by language subgroups, and may want to capture metadata associated with data language.
hazard: Inferior ambient AI performance for patients speaking particular languages.

statement: Consider capturing data-language metadata to support ambient AI evaluation.
quote: For example, a CHC that serves primarily non-English speakers, may want to look at how their Ambient AI solution performs by language subgroups, and may want to capture metadata associated with data language.
hazard: Inability to detect performance differences by language.

statement: Maintain data preparation SOPs for model inputs, fine-tuning data, and data shared with third-party vendors, even without developing models.
quote: Note that not all organizations will be using data to develop or train models, but must still have data preparation SOPs for data that will be input into the model for use, used to fine-tune the model, or shared with third-party vendors.
hazard: Ad hoc input preparation undermining reliability, reproducibility, and privacy.

statement: Clean AI data in ways that preserve integrity and match the intended deployment data environment.
quote: Data cleaning should be done to ensure data integrity while maintaining alignment with the intended model deployment data environment.
hazard: Data preparation choices reducing performance on live production inputs.

statement: Document rules for reconciling conflicting values across EHR modules, facilities, and encounter types.
quote: How to resolve inconsistencies across data sources: document rules for reconciling conflicting values from different EHR modules, facilities, or encounter types.

statement: Establish prompt templates for common clinical use cases.

statement: Manage prompt templates as version-controlled, governed artifacts.

statement: Document how clinical records exceeding context limits are truncated or summarized.

statement: Specify prompt-content logging requirements, particularly for prompts containing PHI.

statement: Consider obtaining source metadata for vendor RAG-based clinical decision support tools.

statement: Consider identifying the minimum institutional data a vendor RAG tool needs to operate.

statement: Define eligibility criteria for documents and records included in retrieval corpora.

statement: Document retrieval-corpus chunking strategies.

statement: Document retrieval-corpus embedding strategies.
quote: Document chunking and embedding strategies — how documents are divided and indexed affects what the model retrieves and ultimately generates.
hazard: Untraceable indexing choices affecting retrieved evidence and generated outputs.

statement: Establish a retrieval-corpus freshness and update cadence.

statement: Define which patient data may be indexed in retrieval corpora.

statement: Control who can query retrieval corpora through the AI system.
quote: Define access controls for the retrieval corpus — what patient data, if any, is indexed, and who can query it through the AI system.

statement: Document retrieval-corpus metadata tagging standards for filtering, auditing, and ongoing management.
quote: Document metadata tagging standards to support filtering, auditing, and corpus management over time.

statement: Document the legal basis for using patient data in fine-tuning.

statement: Limit agent data access to systems relevant to the specifically authorized task.

statement: Require explicit justification for cross-system data aggregation by agents.

statement: Specify logging requirements for every agent tool call and data query, not just final outputs.

statement: Log human approvals and overrides of agentic systems for audit purposes.

statement: Apply formal access controls to agent memory retained across sessions.

statement: Establish retention policies for agent memory maintained across sessions.

statement: Define conditions under which an agentic system must pause.

statement: Define conditions under which an agentic system must decline to act.

statement: Ensure frontline users and operators know how to halt agentic systems.

statement: Version-control all data preparation code.

statement: Make vendor data lineage documentation a procurement condition.

statement: Designate departmental AI Governance Champions to provide peer support and serve as first point of escalation for staff AI questions.
