statement: Assess AI explainability qualitatively with end users through user tests or questionnaires.
quote: Assess explainability qualitatively with end users
hazard: Explanations that do not support end-user understanding or decision making

statement: Evaluate whether AI explanations cause clinician overconfidence or overreliance by measuring confidence and performance with and without the tool.
quote: Evaluate if explanations cause end user overconfidence or overreliance
hazard: Automation bias and overreliance on AI outputs

statement: Stress-test whether AI explanations remain stable under input data perturbations.
quote: Evaluate if explanations are sensitive to input data variations
hazard: Unstable explanations that change with minor input variations

statement: Report AI evaluation results in peer-reviewed publications following AI reporting guidelines such as TRIPOD-AI.
quote: Report evaluation results in publication using AI reporting guidelines
hazard: Opaque or unverifiable evaluation evidence

statement: Create technical documentation for the AI tool, such as model cards covering training and testing data, evaluations, and limitations.
quote: Create technical documentation for AI tool
hazard: Lack of traceability about model characteristics and limitations

statement: Create clinical documentation and an AI information leaflet specifying intended use, target populations, instructions, benefits, and contraindications.
quote: Guidelines for clinical use, AI information leaflet (including intended use, conditions and diseases, targeted populations, instructions, potential benefits, contraindications)
hazard: Use outside intended populations or contraindicated settings

statement: Provide a risk management file listing identified risks, mitigation measures, and monitoring measures.
quote: Provide risk management file
hazard: Unmanaged or undocumented risks of the AI tool

statement: Create user and training documentation including user manuals, troubleshooting guides, and FAQs.
quote: Create user and training documentation
hazard: Incorrect use due to missing user guidance

statement: Identify and provide all locally required compliance documents and certifications for the AI tool.
quote: Identify and provide all locally required documentation

statement: Test the AI model using local data, such as a local clinical registry, before clinical use.

statement: Identify local factors such as operators, equipment, workflows, and acquisition protocols that could affect the AI tool's local validity.
quote: Identify factors that could affect AI tool’s local validity

statement: Assess the AI tool's integration with local clinical workflows and hospital IT systems.
quote: Assess AI tool’s integration within local clinical workflows

statement: Assess the AI tool's local practical utility, including time to operate, clinician satisfaction, and operational disruption.
quote: Assess AI tool's local practical utility and identify any operational challenges

statement: Implement local adjustments such as model calibration or fine-tuning to achieve local validity.
quote: Implement adjustments for local validity

statement: Compare the AI tool's performance with that of local clinicians via side-by-side comparison or in silico trial.
quote: Compare performance of AI tool with that of local clinicians
hazard: Deploying a tool that performs worse than local standard of care

statement: Implement mechanisms such as out-of-distribution detectors or automated image quality checks to identify erroneous input data.
quote: Implement mechanisms to identify erroneous input data
hazard: Erroneous or out-of-distribution inputs producing unreliable outputs

statement: Implement post-processing sanity checks or anomaly detection to detect implausible AI outputs.
quote: Implement mechanisms to detect implausible AI outputs
hazard: Implausible AI outputs reaching clinical decisions

statement: Provide calibrated per-patient uncertainty estimates indicating the AI tool's confidence.
quote: Provide calibrated uncertainty estimates to inform on AI tool’s confidence
hazard: Users unaware of low-confidence AI outputs

statement: Implement continuous quality monitoring, such as a real-time dashboard tracking data quality and performance metrics.
quote: Implement system for continuous quality monitoring
hazard: Undetected performance or data quality degradation in operation

statement: Implement a feedback portal enabling clinicians to report AI discrepancies or anomalies.
quote: Implement feedback mechanism for users to report issues
hazard: Unreported AI errors and anomalies

statement: Define a schedule for periodic audits of the AI tool, such as biannual or annual.
quote: Define schedule for periodic audits
hazard: Performance decay going unexamined over time

statement: Define audit criteria and metrics including accuracy, consistency, fairness, and data security.
quote: Define audit criteria and metrics
hazard: Audits that miss fairness, accuracy, or security failures

statement: Define datasets for periodic audits, such as newly acquired prospective data from the local hospital.
quote: Define datasets for periodic audits
hazard: Audits on stale data failing to reflect current performance

statement: Implement mechanisms to detect data or concept drift in input data distributions.
quote: Implement mechanisms to detect data or concept drifts
hazard: Silent performance degradation from data or concept drift

statement: Assign an internal auditing team or third-party auditor for the AI tool.
quote: Assign role of auditor(s) for AI tool
hazard: No accountable party conducting audits

statement: Update the AI tool or operational protocols based on audit results, including re-evaluation of the model.
quote: Update AI tool based on audit results
hazard: Known deficiencies persisting after audit

statement: Share detailed reports from audits and subsequent updates with healthcare managers and clinicians.
quote: Implement reporting system from audits and subsequent updates
hazard: Clinicians and managers unaware of audit findings and model changes

statement: Monitor the impact of AI updates on system performance and user satisfaction.
quote: Monitor impact of AI updates
hazard: Updates introducing regressions or user dissatisfaction

statement: Implement a logging framework capturing user actions, AI inputs, AI outputs, and clinical decisions.
quote: Implement logging framework capturing all interactions
hazard: Inability to trace AI-related decisions and errors

statement: Define logged data fields including timestamp, user ID, anonymised patient ID, action details, and results.
quote: Define data to be logged
hazard: Incomplete logs preventing auditing and troubleshooting

statement: Implement software that automatically records every data item and operation of the AI tool.
quote: Implement mechanisms for data capture
hazard: Gaps in usage records

statement: Secure AI usage logs using encryption and privacy-preserving techniques.
quote: Implement mechanisms for data security
hazard: Exposure of patient data through log files

statement: Restrict access to AI logs for auditing and troubleshooting to defined authorised personnel.
quote: Provide access to logs for auditing and troubleshooting
hazard: Unauthorised access to logs or inability to audit

statement: Provide a user interface for end users to log operational anomalies.
quote: Implement mechanism for end users to log any issues
hazard: Operational anomalies going unrecorded

statement: Analyze logs with time series statistics and visualisations to detect unusual activities and alert administrators.
quote: Time series statistics and visualisations to detect unusual activities and alert administrators
hazard: Unusual activity or misuse going undetected

statement: Create user manuals describing capabilities, limitations, troubleshooting steps, and examples.
quote: Create user manuals
hazard: Misuse from not understanding tool limitations

statement: Develop training materials and activities such as online courses, workshops, and hands-on sessions.
quote: Develop training materials and activities
hazard: Inadequately trained users misusing the AI tool

statement: Provide training in multiple formats and languages accessible to intended end users.
quote: Use formats and languages accessible to intended end users
hazard: Users excluded by inaccessible training formats or languages

statement: Customise training with role-specific modules for specialists, nurses, and patients.
quote: Customise training to all end user groups
hazard: Generic training failing to meet specific user group needs

statement: Include training that enhances AI and health literacy, including AI-driven clinical decision making.
quote: Include training to enhance AI and health literacy
hazard: Low AI literacy leading to misinterpretation of outputs

statement: Engage regulatory experts from intended local settings to investigate AI regulatory requirements.
quote: Engage regulatory experts to investigate regulatory requirements
hazard: Regulatory non-compliance

statement: Identify specific regulations applicable in the AI tool's intended markets, such as FDA SaMD or EU MDR and AI Act.
quote: Identify specific regulations based on AI tool’s intended markets
hazard: Deploying tools that violate jurisdictional regulations

statement: Define a list of milestones towards regulatory compliance, including clinical trials and postmarket follow-up.
quote: Define list of milestones towards regulatory compliance
hazard: Incomplete compliance pathway

statement: Assign roles for AI tool governance covering periodic auditing, maintenance, and supervision.
quote: Assign roles for AI tool’s governance
hazard: No one accountable for AI oversight and maintenance

statement: Define responsibilities of clinicians, healthcare centres, developers, and manufacturers for AI-related errors.
quote: Define responsibilities for AI related errors
hazard: Unclear liability when AI errors harm patients

statement: Define accountability mechanisms including liability, compensation, and support for patients harmed by AI.
quote: Define mechanisms for accountability
hazard: Harmed patients lacking compensation or support

statement: Conduct risk management as a continuous and transparent process throughout the AI tool's lifecycle.
quote: Therefore, in FUTURE-AI, risk management (as recommended in traceability 1) must be a continuous and transparent process throughout the AI tool’s lifecycle.
hazard: Emerging risks unaddressed after initial assessment

statement: Assess application-specific risks such as discrimination, drift, and patient harm early, then implement tailored mitigation measures.
quote: FUTURE-AI is a risk informed framework, proposing to assess application specific risks and challenges early in the process
hazard: Unidentified risks such as bias, drift, or security vulnerabilities

statement: Continuously engage multidisciplinary stakeholders to understand application-specific needs, risks, and solutions.
quote: FUTURE-AI is also an assumption-free, highly collaborative framework, recommending to continuously engage with multidisciplinary stakeholders to understand application specific needs, risks, and solutions (general 1).
hazard: Missed risks and factors reducing trust in the AI tool

statement: Engage healthcare professionals, domain experts, representative citizens, and ethicists early to investigate application-specific sources of bias.
quote: FUTURE-AI recommends that AI developers engage with healthcare professionals, domain experts, representative citizens, and/or ethicists early in the process to form interdisciplinary AI development teams and investigate in-depth the application specific sources of bias
hazard: Unrecognized domain-specific sources of bias and discrimination

statement: Continuously evaluate and fine-tune AI models over time after deployment.
quote: Furthermore, we recommend continuous evaluation and fine tuning of AI models over time.
hazard: Model performance decay over time

statement: Assess whether deployment conditions resemble testing conditions before relying on reported AI performance.
quote: Where these are similar, the reported performance metrics may be relied upon with some confidence; where they are not (e.g., an algorithm tested only on adults being considered for off-label use in a pediatric hospital) one should proceed with great caution, if at all.
hazard: Unreliable performance when deployment populations or equipment differ from those tested.

statement: Assess anticipated AI error frequency as part of deployment risk assessment.
quote: The consideration together of error frequency, detectability, correctability and impact provides a framework for assessing the direct risk of algorithmic errors.
hazard: Underestimation of risk from frequently occurring algorithmic errors.

statement: Assess whether workflow users will detect anticipated AI errors.
quote: One should consider the detectability of the errors that are anticipated.
hazard: AI errors passing unnoticed through clinical workflows.

statement: Assess the probability that detected AI errors will be corrected.
quote: For each detected error, what is the probability that the error will be corrected?
hazard: Recognized AI errors remaining uncorrected.

statement: Assess the expected patient and stakeholder impact of undetected or uncorrected AI errors.
quote: Finally, if an error is not detected or not corrected, what is the expected impact on patients or other stakeholders?
hazard: Underestimation of consequences from unresolved AI errors.

statement: Assess whether AI-related de-skilling could compromise radiologists' ability to perform tasks manually when the tool fails.
quote: Relying on an automated tool to perform a task may lead to de-skilling of radiologists for the task the tool has taken on. This risk is particularly problematic if the radiologist is expected to perform the task manually when the tool fails, but may no longer be skilled enough to do so adequately.
hazard: Loss of manual diagnostic capability during AI failure.

statement: Assess whether an AI tool could create or exacerbate healthcare disparities.
quote: A final aspect of risk that must be considered is the potential for AI to create or exacerbate healthcare disparities.
hazard: Creation or amplification of healthcare disparities.

statement: Search for biases that AI may inherit from historical healthcare inequities.
quote: There is no easy or straightforward process for comprehensively identifying these biases, but it is incumbent upon us as physicians and data scientists to think about, search for and mitigate these biases; if these questions are unasked, they will most certainly remain unanswered.
hazard: Unidentified biases perpetuating historical inequities.

statement: Mitigate identified AI biases that could perpetuate healthcare inequities.
quote: There is no easy or straightforward process for comprehensively identifying these biases, but it is incumbent upon us as physicians and data scientists to think about, search for and mitigate these biases; if these questions are unasked, they will most certainly remain unanswered.
hazard: Deployment of biased AI that worsens inequitable care.

statement: Define expected benefits and goals before planning AI integration.
quote: Once expected benefits and goals have been decided upon, cost–benefit analysis has been carried out and potential risks have been assessed, integration of the selected AI tools can be planned.
hazard: Deployment without defined clinical or operational objectives.

statement: Complete a cost–benefit analysis before planning AI integration.
quote: Once expected benefits and goals have been decided upon, cost–benefit analysis has been carried out and potential risks have been assessed, integration of the selected AI tools can be planned.
hazard: Deployment costs exceeding expected benefits.

statement: Assess potential risks before planning AI integration.
quote: Once expected benefits and goals have been decided upon, cost–benefit analysis has been carried out and potential risks have been assessed, integration of the selected AI tools can be planned.
hazard: Integration proceeding without understanding deployment risks.

statement: Consider local installation or cloud-based software according to local IT infrastructure and policies.
quote: Depending on the local IT infrastructure and policies, purchasers can consider different technical integrations—either as local installations with dedicated computational resources on site or as a cloud-based software as a service (SaaS) model.
hazard: Integration architecture incompatible with local infrastructure or policies.

statement: Orchestrate DICOM and HL7 routing so the correct patient studies, series, and slices reach the appropriate AI promptly.
quote: In both types of installation, data orchestration of DICOM and HL7 play a vital role ensuring the right slices from the correct series of the relevant study for the right patient in the right setting are sent to the appropriate AI in an optimized time.
hazard: Incorrect, incomplete, misrouted, or delayed imaging inputs.

statement: Structure local data contents to support robust AI orchestration.
quote: To achieve a robust orchestration, understanding and structuring the content of your data is essential.
hazard: Unreliable routing caused by poorly understood or unstructured data.

statement: Use imaging AI to identify study and series contents for data orchestration.
quote: A more robust option is to use imaging AI to determine the data contents at the studies and series level and use that output for orchestration.
hazard: Routing errors caused by incomplete or inconsistent DICOM metadata.

statement: Use computer vision to identify body parts on images for orchestration.
quote: Using computer vision AI to determine which body parts are on each image and if intravenous contrast has been administrated are two of the most useful additions.
hazard: Images being routed to AI intended for a different anatomical region.

statement: Use computer vision to identify intravenous contrast administration for orchestration.
quote: Using computer vision AI to determine which body parts are on each image and if intravenous contrast has been administrated are two of the most useful additions.
hazard: AI processing images with an inappropriate contrast status.

statement: Configure downstream orchestration to select workflows based on AI results.
quote: Downstream data orchestration from the AI system requires an intelligent system able to facilitate different workflows depending on an understanding of the AI results.
hazard: AI results failing to trigger appropriate downstream workflows.

statement: Enable radiologists to modify AI results within PACS.
quote: To optimize AI results management and integration, a PACS should enable the radiologist to interact with and modify the AI results and, if results are changed, empower the AI to immediately reprocess a new output.
hazard: Incorrect AI results remaining uncorrectable within clinical systems.

statement: Enable immediate AI reprocessing when radiologists change AI results in PACS.
quote: To optimize AI results management and integration, a PACS should enable the radiologist to interact with and modify the AI results and, if results are changed, empower the AI to immediately reprocess a new output.
hazard: Subsequent outputs remaining inconsistent with clinician corrections.

statement: Provide radiologist-updated AI results to the vendor for future model improvement.
quote: In addition, the updated AI result should be provided to the AI vendor so it can be used for future model improvement.
hazard: Recurring model errors remaining invisible to the vendor.

statement: Use a cloud-native environment to support sharing radiology data and AI results between PACS and AI models.
quote: This type of interaction is facilitated in a cloud-native environment where both the PACS and AI models can share radiology data and AI results.
hazard: Fragmented integration preventing interactive management of AI results.

statement: Store AI results together with radiologist feedback.
quote: Additionally, the ability to accept and store AI results along with radiologist feedback, optimize data security, and continuously monitor AI accuracy are crucial technical aspects that are facilitated in cloud-native systems.
hazard: Loss of clinician feedback needed to assess AI errors.

statement: Optimize data security in integrated AI systems.
quote: Additionally, the ability to accept and store AI results along with radiologist feedback, optimize data security, and continuously monitor AI accuracy are crucial technical aspects that are facilitated in cloud-native systems.
hazard: Compromise of clinical data exchanged or stored by AI systems.

statement: Integrate AI tools into usual clinical workflows and information systems to avoid requiring users to switch applications.
quote: Whatever the integration, ideally AI tools should be well integrated into the usual clinical workflow and information systems in order to avoid additional workload by requiring users to switch between applications.
hazard: Additional workload and workflow fragmentation.

statement: Test AI performance on local data using the systems and workflows intended for deployment.
quote: While FDA or other relevant authority approval/clearance data provides some insights, testing the AI model on local data, with the local systems and workflows used in practice, is essential to ensure accuracy and relevance when the model is deployed.
hazard: Regulatory performance claims failing to generalize to local practice.

statement: Adjust AI parameters when local validation indicates changes are needed before clinical implementation.
quote: Of course, vendors will have performed testing and quality assurance of the respective AI tools during regulatory approval, but purchasers should consider validation of the AI’s performance on a local dataset, and adjust parameters if needed prior to implementation in clinical practice.
hazard: Deployment with parameters unsuitable for local clinical conditions.

statement: Repeat local validation and necessary parameter adjustment after relevant changes to AI software or associated equipment.
quote: This process should be repeated whenever relevant changes are made to the AI software or the equipment used in combination with the AI.
hazard: Unrecognized performance changes following software or equipment modifications.

statement: Recalibrate decision thresholds when AI updates alter recall rates enough to compromise clinically acceptable diagnostic accuracy.
quote: In the example of a commercially available breast screening AI model an update of the AI tool resulted in a substantially different recall rate, requiring recalibration of the decision threshold to ensure continued usage with clinically acceptable diagnostic accuracy (61).
hazard: Unacceptable recall rates or diagnostic accuracy after model updates.

statement: Report software adverse events, including missed clinically relevant stroke findings and MRI degradation affecting anatomical or pathological structures.
quote: Guidance for manufacturers on reporting adverse incidents involving Software as a Medical Device under the vigilance system details various circumstances in which an adverse event should be reported—including “(failure) to identify clinically relevant brain image findings related to acute stroke” and “(degradation of MRI image) appearance of anatomical and pathological structures” (62).
hazard: Clinically important software failures remaining unreported.

statement: Maintain transparency when updating AI products.
quote: Similarly, the FDA’s Proposed Regulatory Framework for Modifications to Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device would expect manufacturers “to commit to the principles of transparency and real-world performance monitoring” when making updates to their products (63).
hazard: Product updates occurring without adequate visibility into changes.

statement: Familiarize implementation stakeholders with relevant clinical evaluation methods and metrics.
quote: Stakeholders in implementation of AI tools in clinical practice should therefore familiarize themselves with the relevant methods and metrics for clinical evaluation and devise strategies to verify performance claims prior to tool introduction, and should continuously monitor performance during routine usage (64).
hazard: Inadequate evaluation caused by unfamiliarity with appropriate methods or metrics.

statement: Continuously monitor AI performance during routine clinical use.
quote: Stakeholders in implementation of AI tools in clinical practice should therefore familiarize themselves with the relevant methods and metrics for clinical evaluation and devise strategies to verify performance claims prior to tool introduction, and should continuously monitor performance during routine usage (64).
hazard: Undetected deterioration in clinical AI performance.

statement: Educate users and stakeholders about human–AI interaction biases and interface-related effects on performance.
quote: These findings highlight the need for further education on those topics to increase awareness amongst users and stakeholders and allow for safe and successful implementation of AI into clinical routine (76).
hazard: Automation bias, algorithmic aversion, and interface effects degrading clinical decisions.

statement: Compare local AI performance against regulatory documentation, evaluating accuracy in relation to radiologist acceptance and engagement.
quote: The first step involves comparing the AI model’s performance on local data against regulatory authority documentation, specifically evaluating accuracy through the lens of radiologist acceptance and engagement with the AI tool.
hazard: Mismatch between documented performance, local accuracy, and clinical usability.

statement: Prioritize positive and negative predictive values at local disease prevalence when evaluating radiologist-facing AI accuracy.
quote: Hence, parameters that are radiologist-facing, including positive and negative predictive values for the disease prevalence are more relevant than overall accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), or sensitivity/specificity.
hazard: Misleading accuracy assessments that ignore disease prevalence and clinical experience.

statement: Calculate the enhanced detection rate from the combined true-positive findings of radiologists and AI.
quote: Secondly, calculate an “Enhanced Detection Rate,” the optimized detection that could be obtained through a combined detection of radiologist plus AI true positive results.
hazard: Failure to assess the potential incremental detection benefit of AI.

statement: Identify clinically impressive cases that demonstrate the AI model's value to users and stakeholders.
quote: Thirdly, impressive, or “WOW cases,” should be identified to demonstrate the AI model’s value to users and stakeholders.
hazard: Deployment decisions or user expectations disconnected from demonstrable clinical value.

statement: Categorize AI false positives and, when possible, false negatives to set radiologist expectations.
quote: Fourthly, categorizing AI false positives and, when possible, false negative cases can set radiologist expectations and improve their acceptance of an imperfect AI model (all AI models are imperfect).
hazard: Unrealistic expectations about model errors.

statement: Review evaluation findings, balancing positive predictive value against the number and value of clinically impressive cases, before deciding on deployment.
quote: Finally, all the findings should be reviewed to determine if the AI model is worthy of clinical deployment. Ultimately, the decision lies in the balance between positive predictive value (which is highly dependent on disease prevalence) and the value and number of “WOW” cases.
hazard: Deployment despite insufficient clinical value relative to false-positive burden.

statement: Consider limiting AI deployment to examination subsets with higher disease prevalence.
quote: Disease prevalence in a patient group presented to an AI model can be modified by properly selecting patient imaging locations, such as Emergency Department, inpatient, or outpatient. Hence, some AI models may be deployed on a subset of exams because disease prevalence in that exam subset is increased from baseline.
hazard: Excessive false positives and poor acceptance in low-prevalence populations.

statement: Use local clinical evaluation findings to educate radiologists before AI implementation.
quote: Utilizing information from the above 5-step clinical evaluation for radiologist education, coupled with change management, is vital to set user expectations before AI model implementation.
hazard: Users beginning clinical use with inaccurate expectations.

statement: Use change management to set user expectations before AI implementation.
quote: Utilizing information from the above 5-step clinical evaluation for radiologist education, coupled with change management, is vital to set user expectations before AI model implementation.
hazard: Poorly managed adoption and misaligned user expectations.

statement: Use a local AI champion to support radiologist adoption.
quote: A local AI champion plays a significant role in promoting AI adoption among radiologists.
hazard: Limited local support for effective AI adoption.

statement: Provide continuous user education throughout the AI lifecycle.
quote: Finally, continuous user education throughout the lifecycle of AI utilization and monitoring radiologist AI usage and the combined accuracy of radiologist plus AI are instrumental in ensuring optimal patient care.
hazard: User knowledge becoming inadequate as tools and workflows evolve.

statement: Monitor radiologists' use of AI tools.
quote: Finally, continuous user education throughout the lifecycle of AI utilization and monitoring radiologist AI usage and the combined accuracy of radiologist plus AI are instrumental in ensuring optimal patient care.
hazard: Unrecognized nonuse or ineffective use of deployed AI.

statement: Monitor the combined diagnostic accuracy of radiologists and AI.
quote: Finally, continuous user education throughout the lifecycle of AI utilization and monitoring radiologist AI usage and the combined accuracy of radiologist plus AI are instrumental in ensuring optimal patient care.
hazard: Acceptable standalone model accuracy masking poor human–AI performance.

statement: Plan for declining static-model performance as local data, equipment, protocols, software, and patient populations change.
quote: End users should expect the performance of static (also known as “locked algorithms”) AI model performance to decline over time, due to shifts in local input data, changes to imaging equipment or protocols, acquisition software updates influencing source image parameters such as noise levels, or naturally occurring changes in patient populations and demographics (77).
hazard: Assuming locked models retain their initial performance indefinitely.

statement: Make ongoing AI performance oversight a function of local AI governance.
quote: Therefore, as the use of AI becomes more prevalent and the AI tools being deployed become more diverse, institutions using AI should establish ongoing performance oversight as one function of a local AI governance process (78).
hazard: Performance degradation occurring without accountable institutional oversight.

statement: Provide baseline and longitudinal monitoring feedback to any continuously learning AI algorithms used for local refinement.
quote: In a potential future state where adaptive intelligence enables local model refinement, monitoring systems must be able to provide both baseline and longitudinal feedback information to continuously learning AI algorithms (77).
hazard: Adaptive model changes occurring without baseline or longitudinal performance feedback.

statement: Compare aggregated real-time AI performance against expected local, regional, or national benchmarks when feasible.
quote: An ideal monitoring solution collects real time data on model performance, aggregates and analyses results comparing against expected performance at the local, regional or national benchmark level when feasible.
hazard: Local performance deficits remaining undetected without benchmark comparisons.

statement: Confirm that ground truth and well-defined performance benchmarks are available before adopting real-time benchmark-based monitoring.
quote: However, this approach requires ready availability of ground truth and well defined performance benchmarks which is achievable today with some use cases and algorithms but not others.
hazard: Invalid performance assessments based on unavailable or poorly defined comparators.

statement: Compare triage AI outputs with radiologist reports to identify concordance and discordance when both address the same findings.
quote: One common approach with triage type AI models that are tuned to identify findings which are also reported by radiologists would be an analysis of concordance or discordance between radiologist reports and model inference output.
hazard: Triage model errors remaining undetected during routine use.

statement: Use longitudinal clinical data to validate AI risk scores.
quote: This approach may not work for quantitative outputs which cannot easily be reproduced by humans at scale or risk scores where validity can only be determined by analysis of longitudinal clinical data.
hazard: Risk scores being judged valid without observing relevant clinical outcomes.

statement: Have the local AI oversight group determine sufficient monitoring for each algorithm individually.
quote: It is incumbent on the local AI oversight group to determine on a case by case basis what sufficient monitoring looks like in a particular algorithm.
hazard: Generic monitoring failing to address algorithm-specific limitations.

statement: Check for imaging artifacts that could interfere with AI processing when assessing output validity.
quote: In all cases, but especially when using quantitative models, radiologists may be able to determine the general validity of the AI output by confirming the absence of relevant imaging artifacts that would interfere with AI processing.
hazard: Acceptance of invalid AI outputs caused by imaging artifacts.

statement: Tailor real-world monitoring strategies to model type and patient-safety risk from declining performance.
quote: Strategies for real-world monitoring of AI in clinical practice should take into account the type of AI model being used and the risk to patient safety if the model performance declines.
hazard: Monitoring intensity or methods mismatched to clinical risk.

statement: Combine AI outputs with longitudinal analysis using subsequent imaging or EHR data.
quote: It will be important for the imaging community to establish monitoring approaches which can combine model output with appropriate forms of longitudinal analysis (with future imaging or EHR derived data or combination),
hazard: Delayed or outcome-dependent model failures remaining undetected.

statement: Compare monitored AI outputs with other clinical biomarkers of the same disease process.
quote: through comparison to other clinical biomarkers of the same disease process, and with benchmark performance data from use of the same algorithm in a range of patients and a multitude of institutions.
hazard: Model outputs appearing plausible despite disagreement with other disease indicators.

statement: Review augmentative diagnostic or triage AI outputs for patient-specific failures before finalizing radiology reports.
quote: It should be noted that for almost all AI models with current regulatory approval, the model inference serves to augment, not replace, the radiologists’ interpretations, and therefore, patient-specific model failures of diagnostic or triage software are typically identified by the user before radiological reports are finalized and patient care initiated.
hazard: Patient-specific AI errors entering finalized reports and subsequent care.

statement: Establish robust continuous performance monitoring before deploying autonomously functioning AI.
quote: Robust continuous performance monitoring will be needed prior to deployment of any autonomously functioning AI algorithms and required for continuous-learning AI models.
hazard: Autonomous AI failures affecting patients without timely detection.

statement: Assess failure modes when planning autonomous AI implementation.
quote: In future autonomous AI implementation, thorough understanding of failure modes and associated safety net processes may become paramount.
hazard: Autonomous deployment without understanding potential failures.

statement: Establish safety-net processes for autonomous AI failure modes.
quote: In future autonomous AI implementation, thorough understanding of failure modes and associated safety net processes may become paramount.
hazard: Autonomous AI failures occurring without protective fallback processes.

statement: Define a notification plan for detected AI failures or performance drift.
quote: Institutions should develop a clearly defined escalation and resolution strategy when monitoring detects model failure or performance drift occurs that defines the notification and action plan, and the mode of operation while the model performance is being assessed and the cause of model failure determined.
hazard: Relevant personnel not being informed of detected model problems.

statement: Define actions for investigating and resolving detected AI failures or performance drift.
quote: Institutions should develop a clearly defined escalation and resolution strategy when monitoring detects model failure or performance drift occurs that defines the notification and action plan, and the mode of operation while the model performance is being assessed and the cause of model failure determined.
hazard: Detected model problems remaining unresolved.

statement: Define the operating mode to use while AI performance problems and their causes are investigated.
quote: Institutions should develop a clearly defined escalation and resolution strategy when monitoring detects model failure or performance drift occurs that defines the notification and action plan, and the mode of operation while the model performance is being assessed and the cause of model failure determined.
hazard: Unsafe or inconsistent clinical operations during AI failure investigations.

statement: Use periodic evaluation with updated local datasets when real-time performance data are limited or patient safety is not immediately affected.
quote: Re-evaluation of AI model performance using updated local data sets at specified intervals, but at least annually, may be an appropriate monitoring mechanism for models where gathering real-time data on model performance is limited (quantification, workflow enhancement, etc.) or in instances where patient safety will not be immediately impacted (80).
hazard: Models receiving no performance monitoring because real-time evaluation is impractical.

statement: Create an up-to-date evaluation dataset with an appropriate case count and parameters similar to the initial validation set for periodic reassessment.
quote: Such a system requires that a new up-to-date evaluation data set be created using an appropriate number of clinical cases and parameters similar to the initial validation set to re-evaluate the performance of the model under current conditions.
hazard: Reassessment using outdated, insufficient, or incomparable local data.

statement: Define baseline input-data characteristics for each AI model at acceptance.
quote: Since changes in equipment, protocols and naturally occurring changes in population demographics are known causes of input data (source image) drift and potentially reduced AI model performance, institutions could elect to define baseline input data characteristics at the time of model acceptance and then monitor for data drift against that baseline state specific to each AI model (82).
hazard: Lack of a model-specific reference for detecting input drift.

statement: Monitor input-data drift against each model's acceptance baseline.
quote: Since changes in equipment, protocols and naturally occurring changes in population demographics are known causes of input data (source image) drift and potentially reduced AI model performance, institutions could elect to define baseline input data characteristics at the time of model acceptance and then monitor for data drift against that baseline state specific to each AI model (82).
hazard: Unrecognized changes in the inputs on which model performance depends.

statement: Trigger model performance reassessment according to the timing and severity of detected input-data drift.
quote: By monitoring for individual components of data drift, institutions could trigger re-evaluation of model performance depending on timing and severity of changes and initiate appropriate steps to safeguard patient care.
hazard: Continued use of degraded models after clinically important input changes.

statement: Collect equipment manufacturer, protocol, radiation dose, and patient demographics as part of continuous AI monitoring.
quote: As explained above, harvesting of metadata about the examination should form part of this monitoring, and should include equipment manufacturer, protocol used, radiation dose and patient demographics.
hazard: Performance degradation without data needed to identify its source.

statement: Monitor equipment characteristics and examination parameters for deviations from manufacturer specifications.
quote: Other targets for monitoring include changes in input metadata (e.g. equipment manufacturer, magnetic field strength or number of CT detectors), other relevant examination parameters and relevant demographic data about individual patients, since deviation of any or several of these from manufacturer specifications can result in degraded performance.
hazard: AI receiving inputs outside manufacturer specifications.

statement: Use background natural language processing to support automated comparison with radiologist reports as an AI accuracy measure.
quote: Ideally this data collection could occur in the background, comparing information automatically extracted via suitable natural language processing methods against the radiologists’ reports as an AI accuracy measure, and data contained in the DICOM header to monitor the compliance of examination parameters with AI manufacturer specification of input data whenever feasible.
hazard: Manual monitoring burden limiting detection of model errors.

statement: Use DICOM headers to monitor examination-parameter compliance with AI manufacturer input specifications when feasible.
quote: Ideally this data collection could occur in the background, comparing information automatically extracted via suitable natural language processing methods against the radiologists’ reports as an AI accuracy measure, and data contained in the DICOM header to monitor the compliance of examination parameters with AI manufacturer specification of input data whenever feasible.
hazard: Unnoticed processing of examinations outside specified input conditions.

statement: Incorporate available patient demographic information from DICOM headers into monitoring data collection.
quote: Limited patient demographic information may also be found in the DICOM header and should be incorporated in the data collection.
hazard: Monitoring missing demographic changes associated with performance drift.

statement: Expand patient demographic data collection when needed for robust monitoring and bias detection.
quote: More robust monitoring and bias detection solutions may require expanded patient demographics.
hazard: Subgroup performance disparities remaining undetected with limited demographic data.

statement: Record AI performance information in a dedicated registry capable of reporting across sites and geographies.
quote: Relevant information about AI model performance should be recorded in a dedicated AI data registry that allows generation of reports across multiple sites and geographies.
hazard: Fragmented performance records preventing systematic and cross-site monitoring.

statement: Analyze local registry reports to identify performance degradation and potential sources of data drift.
quote: At the local level, registry reports would allow institutions to identify performance degradation within their own local environment and could enable a systematic evaluation of the sources of potential data drift on a near real-time basis.
hazard: Local causes of degraded performance remaining unidentified.

statement: Systematically analyze cases that the AI system does not process.
quote: Systematic analysis of cases that are not processed represent another important monitoring target. Such cases may point to systematic or anecdotal failure in the data acquisition or data transfer, impeding intended AI inference and preventing downstream clinical action to benefit from the same.
hazard: Silent acquisition or transfer failures preventing intended AI-supported clinical action.

statement: Aggregate monitoring data across institutions using the same AI model to help developers identify performance gaps.
quote: Aggregation of data from multiple institutions using the same AI models could provide information to developers to identify performance gaps that can be addressed in future versions of the algorithm, as well as meeting any future post-market surveillance regulatory requirements.
hazard: Performance gaps remaining hidden within isolated institutional datasets.

statement: Spot-monitor autonomous AI using intermittent random samples of a predetermined number of cases compared with ground truth.
quote: Therefore, one could imagine that performance monitoring could include intermittent random sampling of a pre-determined number of cases with ground truth comparison to spot-monitor performance over time.
hazard: Autonomous model performance deterioration remaining undetected between evaluations.

statement: Include robust real-time AI performance monitoring in change control plans for local tuning or continuous learning.
quote: Any change control plan must include robust real-time AI model performance and measures that mitigate patient risk.
hazard: Adaptive model changes causing undetected performance deterioration.

statement: Include patient-risk mitigation measures in AI change control plans.
quote: Any change control plan must include robust real-time AI model performance and measures that mitigate patient risk.
hazard: Model modifications introducing unmitigated patient-safety risks.

statement: Formalize local AI governance oversight and associated lifecycle processes.
quote: Given the complexity of managing all aspects of the AI lifecycle in clinical environments, provider entities engaging in the use of clinical AI are well served by formalizing local AI governance oversight and associated processes (78).
hazard: Uncoordinated management of procurement, deployment, monitoring, and replacement.

statement: Adjust local scanner protocols, orchestration, device configuration, and workflow integration as needed throughout the AI lifecycle.
quote: making adjustments to the local environment (e.g. scanner protocols, AI orchestration, device configuration, workflow integration including opportunistic capture of ground truth labels, etc.) over time as needed,
hazard: Local infrastructure and workflows becoming unsuitable for deployed AI.

statement: Integrate opportunistic capture of ground-truth labels into clinical workflows.
quote: workflow integration including opportunistic capture of ground truth labels
hazard: Insufficient reference data for evaluating deployed AI performance.

statement: Establish an orderly process for replacing deployed AI products with updates or alternatives.
quote: and an orderly process to replace currently deployed products with future updates or alternative products.
hazard: Disruptive or poorly controlled transitions between AI products.

statement: Train newly arriving clinical and technical staff on local AI tools and associated workflows.
quote: As new users arrive in a local practice, they need to be properly assimilated, oriented, and trained in the available AI tools and associated work processes, to become effective participants in this technology-assisted care delivery paradigm.
hazard: Staff turnover introducing users unfamiliar with AI tools and workflows.

statement: Assign shared responsibility for stakeholder AI competence to vendors and local governance leaders.
quote: Ensuring that all local stakeholders are up to date and competent in the use of AI technology is a shared responsibility between vendors and the leaders of local institutional governance and oversight.
hazard: Training and competency gaps caused by unclear responsibility.

statement: Re-evaluate the performance of every clinically deployed AI model at least annually.
quote: Monitoring strategies should include at minimum yearly re-valuation the performance of all AI models being used in clinical practice so that appropriate measures can be taken to ensure patient safety.
hazard: Long-term performance degradation escaping periodic reassessment.

statement: Consider more frequent reassessment according to patient risk from model failure and the clinical relevance of the AI output.
quote: The need for more frequent re-evaluations should also be considered based on patient risk in the event of model failure and clinical decision relevance of a specific AI output.
hazard: High-risk model failures persisting between infrequent evaluations.

statement: Require robust continuous performance monitoring for continuously learning AI models.
quote: Robust continuous performance monitoring will be needed prior to deployment of any autonomously functioning AI algorithms and required for continuous-learning AI models.
hazard: Continuous model changes introducing undetected safety or accuracy problems.

statement: Assess over-reliance and under-reliance biases in radiologist–AI interactions.
quote: These biases need to be both clarified and managed to ensure the AI’s output does not negatively influence the radiologist’s judgment. There are two general types of bias that can be introduced in a human–computer system, over-reliance, and under-reliance.
hazard: Inappropriate reliance on AI increasing false-positive and false-negative decisions.

statement: Manage over-reliance and under-reliance biases so AI output does not impair radiologists' judgment.
quote: These biases need to be both clarified and managed to ensure the AI’s output does not negatively influence the radiologist’s judgment. There are two general types of bias that can be introduced in a human–computer system, over-reliance, and under-reliance.
hazard: Acceptance of incorrect AI results or rejection of correct AI findings.

statement: Optimize the combined diagnostic output of radiologists and AI systems.
quote: Ultimately, the output of the combination of radiologist plus the AI system must be optimized.
hazard: Optimizing model performance while overlooking poorer combined clinical decisions.

statement: Implement continuous monitoring of AI inputs and outputs to detect missing or out-of-range inputs, inconsistent formats or units, and erroneous or implausible outputs.
quote: The AI tool should be developed and deployed with mechanisms for continuous monitoring and quality control of the AI inputs and outputs,47 such as to identify missing or out-of-range input variables, inconsistent data formats or units, incorrect annotations or data preprocessing, and erroneous or implausible AI outputs.
hazard: Bad input data or implausible AI outputs reaching clinical decisions undetected

statement: Provide calibrated uncertainty estimates with AI outputs so end users know the confidence level of results.
quote: For quality control of the AI decisions, uncertainty estimates should be provided (and calibrated53) to inform the end users about the degree of confidence in the results.54
hazard: Users over-trusting low-confidence AI outputs

statement: Establish a configurable periodic audit system specifying evaluation datasets and timelines, such as yearly evaluations.
quote: The AI tool should be developed and deployed with a configurable system for periodic auditing,47 which should define the datasets and timelines for periodic evaluations (eg, every year).
hazard: Undetected performance decline after deployment

statement: Design periodic audits to detect data or concept drift, new biases, performance degradation, and changes in end-user decision making.
quote: The periodic auditing should enable the identification of data or concept drifts, newly occurring biases, performance degradation or changes in the decision making of the end users.55
hazard: Drift, emerging bias, or altered clinician behaviour going unnoticed

statement: Apply necessary updates to AI models or tools based on periodic audit findings.
quote: Accordingly, necessary updates to the AI models or AI tools should be applied.56
hazard: Continued use of degraded or biased models

statement: Implement an AI logging system that traces users' main actions in a privacy-preserving manner and records which data are accessed and used.
quote: To increase traceability and accountability, an AI logging system should be implemented to trace the user’s main actions in a privacy preserving manner, specify the data that are accessed and used, record the AI predictions and clinical decisions, and log any encountered issues.
hazard: Lack of traceability and accountability for AI use

statement: Log AI predictions alongside the resulting clinical decisions and any issues encountered during use.
quote: To increase traceability and accountability, an AI logging system should be implemented to trace the user’s main actions in a privacy preserving manner, specify the data that are accessed and used, record the AI predictions and clinical decisions, and log any encountered issues.
hazard: Inability to investigate AI-related errors

statement: Use time series statistics and visualisations to inspect AI tool usage over time.
quote: Time series statistics and visualisations should be used to inspect the usage of the AI tool over time.
hazard: Unnoticed changes in usage patterns or misuse

statement: Assign post-deployment roles for risk management, periodic auditing, maintenance, and supervision, e.g., to IT teams or healthcare administrators.
quote: In particular, the roles of risk management, periodic auditing, maintenance, and supervision should be assigned, such as to IT teams or healthcare administrators.
hazard: No one accountable for ongoing oversight of deployed AI

statement: Clearly specify responsibilities for AI-related errors among clinicians, healthcare centres, AI developers, and manufacturers.
quote: Furthermore, responsibilities for AI related errors should be clearly specified among clinicians, healthcare centres, AI developers, and manufacturers.
hazard: Unclear liability for AI-related errors

statement: Establish accountability mechanisms with individual and collective liability plus compensation and support structures for patients harmed by AI errors.
quote: Accountability mechanisms should be established, incorporating both individual and collective liability, alongside compensation and support structures for patients affected by AI errors.
hazard: Patients harmed by AI errors lacking redress or support

statement: Engage clinical experts, patients, physicians, and other stakeholders early to define the AI tool's intended use and end-user requirements.
quote: The AI developers should engage clinical experts, end users (eg, patients, physicians), and other relevant stakeholders (eg, data managers, administrators) from an early stage to compile information on the AI tool’s intended use and end user requirements (eg, human-AI interfaces)
hazard: Tools misaligned with clinical needs and users

statement: Assess human factors affecting AI use, including digital literacy, age group, ergonomics, and automation bias, when defining user requirements.
quote: as well as on human factors that might affect the usage of the AI tool57 (eg, digital literacy level, age group, ergonomics, automation bias)
hazard: Unusable tools or automation bias among certain user groups

statement: Evaluate fit with current clinical workflow, including system-level implementation and interactions with other AI support tools.
quote: Special attention should be paid to the fit with the current clinical workflow, including system level implementation of AI and interactions with other (AI) support tools.
hazard: Workflow disruption and conflicting AI tool interactions

statement: Use majority voting among diverse stakeholders to identify the most relevant clinical issues for the AI tool to address.
quote: Using a majority voting strategy among diverse stakeholders to identify the most relevant clinical issues might help to ensure that solutions are broadly applicable rather than tailored to individual preferences.
hazard: Solutions tailored to individual preferences rather than broad needs

statement: Provide interfaces enabling end users to verify AI inputs and results and annotate input data in a standardised manner.
quote: Based on the user requirements, the AI developers should implement interfaces to enable end users to effectively use the AI model, annotate the input data in a standardised manner, and verify the AI inputs and results.
hazard: Users unable to check erroneous AI inputs or outputs

statement: Implement human-in-the-loop quality checks that let users flag biases, errors, or implausible explanations.
quote: Human-in-the-loop mechanisms should be designed and implemented to perform specific quality checks (eg, to flag biases, errors, or implausible explanations), and to overrule the AI predictions when necessary.
hazard: Biased or erroneous AI outputs going unchallenged

statement: Enable clinicians to overrule AI predictions when necessary.
quote: Human-in-the-loop mechanisms should be designed and implemented to perform specific quality checks (eg, to flag biases, errors, or implausible explanations), and to overrule the AI predictions when necessary.
hazard: Incorrect AI predictions dictating care

statement: Tailor human oversight mechanisms to each use case, accounting for regulations, automation benefits, and patient preferences on AI autonomy.
quote: Regulations, the benefits of automation, and patient preferences regarding AI autonomy might vary per use case and over time,58 therefore requiring use case specific human oversight mechanisms and periodic auditing and updates (see traceability 4).
hazard: Oversight inappropriate to use case risk or patient preferences

statement: Implement a user feedback interface for the AI tool.
quote: Implement mechanism for user feedback
hazard: User-identified problems not captured

statement: Provide training materials and activities in accessible formats and languages tailored to diverse end users, from specialists to citizens.
quote: the developers should provide training materials (eg, tutorials, manuals, examples) and/or training activities (eg, hands-on sessions) in an accessible format and language, taking into account the diversity of end users (eg, specialists, nurses, technicians, citizens, or administrators).
hazard: Misuse and errors from inadequate AI literacy

statement: Assess training of new end users, such as average time to reach competency and training difficulties.
quote: Assess training of new end users
hazard: Users insufficiently competent to use the tool safely

statement: Evaluate usability within local clinical workflows in real-world settings with representative, diverse end users by sex, age, role, digital proficiency, and disability.
quote: To facilitate adoption, the usability of the AI tool within the local clinical workflows should be evaluated in real world settings with representative and diverse end users (eg, with respect to sex, gender, age, clinical role, digital proficiency, and disability).
hazard: Tools unusable for some user groups in local settings

statement: Measure user satisfaction, performance, productivity, and human factors such as confidence, learnability, and automation bias in usability tests.
quote: The usability tests should gather evidence on the user’s satisfaction, performance and productivity, and assess human factors that might affect the usage of the AI tool57 (eg, confidence, learnability, automation bias).
hazard: Automation bias and poor usability undetected

statement: Evaluate clinical utility by demonstrating patient, clinician, or organisational benefits compared with current standard of care.
quote: The clinical evaluations of the AI tool should show benefits for the patient (eg, earlier diagnosis, better outcomes), for the clinician (eg, increased productivity, improved care), and/or for the healthcare organisation (eg, reduced costs, optimised workflows) compared with the current standard of care.
hazard: Deploying tools without proven benefit

statement: Demonstrate the AI tool is safe and does not harm individuals or specific groups, e.g., via randomised clinical trial.
quote: Additionally, it is important to show that the AI tool is safe and does not cause harm to individuals (or specific groups), such as through a randomised clinical trial.59
hazard: Patient harm from unsafe AI tools

statement: Inventory real-world sources of variation (equipment differences, machine faults, acquisition heterogeneity, adversarial attacks) that may affect robustness.
quote: At the design phase, the development team should first define robustness requirements for the AI tool in question by making an inventory of the sources of variation that might affect the AI tool’s robustness in the real world.
hazard: Performance failure under unanticipated real-world data variations

statement: Select and enrich training datasets to represent real-world variations identified at design.
quote: Therefore, the training datasets should be carefully selected, analysed, and enriched according to the sources of variation identified at the design phase (see robustness 1).
hazard: Poor generalisation to real-world populations and settings

statement: Evaluate robustness through stress and repeatability tests under conditions reflecting real-world data, equipment, clinician, patient, and centre variations.
quote: Evaluation studies should be implemented to evaluate the AI tool’s robustness (eg, stress tests, repeatability tests62) under conditions that reflect the variations of real world clinical practice.
hazard: Incorrect decisions from input variations

statement: Determine with end users and domain experts whether explainability is required for the AI tool.
quote: At the design phase, it should be established with end users and domain experts if explainability is required for the AI tool.
hazard: Opaque AI decisions where interpretation is needed

statement: Define anticipated explainability limitations to monitor, such as end-user over-reliance on AI decisions.
quote: (c) the potential limitations to anticipate and monitor (eg, over-reliance of the end users on the AI decision68)
hazard: Over-reliance on AI decisions

statement: Adapt the design of AI explanations for each end-user subgroup, e.g., heatmaps for clinicians, feature importance for patients.
quote: Adjust the design of the AI explanations for all end user subgroup
hazard: Explanations not meaningful to specific user groups

statement: Quantitatively assess the correctness of AI explanations using computational methods.
quote: The explainable AI methods should be evaluated, first quantitatively by using computational methods to assess the correctness of the explanations,70 71 then qualitatively with end users to assess their impact on user satisfaction, confidence, and clinical performance.72
hazard: Incorrect explanations misleading users

statement: Qualitatively evaluate AI explanations with end users for impact on satisfaction, confidence, and clinical performance.
quote: The explainable AI methods should be evaluated, first quantitatively by using computational methods to assess the correctness of the explanations,70 71 then qualitatively with end users to assess their impact on user satisfaction, confidence, and clinical performance.72
hazard: Explanations degrading clinical performance

statement: Identify whether AI explanations are clinically incoherent, sensitive to noise or attacks, or unreasonably increase confidence in AI results.
quote: The evaluations should also identify any limitations of the AI explanations (eg, they are clinically incoherent73 or sensitive to noise or adversarial attacks,74 they unreasonably increase the confidence in the AI generated results75).
hazard: Explanations causing overconfidence or misleading reasoning

statement: Continuously engage interdisciplinary stakeholders, including patient representatives, citizens, ethicists, and legal experts, throughout the AI lifecycle.
quote: Throughout the AI tool’s lifecycle, the AI developers should continuously engage with interdisciplinary stakeholders, such as healthcare professionals, citizens, patient representatives, expert ethicists, data managers, and legal experts.
hazard: Unanticipated needs and barriers to acceptance

statement: Put adequate data privacy and security measures in place throughout the AI lifecycle.
quote: Adequate measures to ensure data privacy and security should be put in place throughout the AI lifecycle.
hazard: Privacy breaches and data misuse

statement: Conduct a data protection impact assessment and establish post-deployment data governance such as data access logging.
quote: These might include privacy enhancing techniques (eg, differential privacy, encryption), data protection impact assessment, and appropriate data governance after deployment (eg, logging system for data access, see traceability 5).
hazard: Unassessed privacy risks and untracked data access

statement: When deidentifying data, assess the balance between health benefits and reidentification risks.
quote: If deidentification is implemented (eg, pseudonymisation, k-anonymity), the balance between the health benefits for citizens and the risks for reidentification should be carefully assessed and considered.
hazard: Patient reidentification

statement: Implement and regularly evaluate cybersecurity and attack-detection defences protecting the AI tool against malicious or adversarial attacks.
quote: Furthermore, the manufacturers and deployers should implement and regularly evaluate measures for protecting the AI tool against malicious or adversarial attacks, such as by using system level cybersecurity solutions or application specific defence mechanisms (eg, attack detection or mitigation).76
hazard: Adversarial or malicious attacks compromising AI outputs

statement: Define access control and logging data governance mechanisms.
quote: Define suitable data governance mechanisms
hazard: Unauthorised data access

statement: Adhere to applicable data protection regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA.
quote: Adhere to applicable data protection regulations
hazard: Regulatory non-compliance and privacy violations

statement: Define an evaluation plan specifying test data, metrics, and reference methods.
quote: To increase trust and adoption, an appropriate evaluation plan should be defined, including test data, metrics, and reference methods.
hazard: Inadequate or biased evaluation of AI tools

statement: Ensure test data are well separated from training data to prevent data leakage.
quote: In particular, the test data should be well separated from the training to prevent data leakage.77
hazard: Overestimated performance from data leakage

statement: Benchmark the AI tool against reference AI tools or standard practice.
quote: Finally, benchmarking with respect to reference AI tools or standard practice should be performed to enable comparative assessment of model performance.
hazard: Adopting tools no better than current practice

statement: Evaluate the AI tool at multiple sites using external datasets reflecting real-world variations in demographics, clinicians, and equipment.
quote: Select multiple evaluation sites
hazard: Poor generalisability to new sites

statement: Identify applicable AI regulations for the jurisdiction early in development.
quote: The development team should identify the applicable AI regulations, which vary by jurisdiction and over time.
hazard: Regulatory non-compliance

statement: Ensure healthcare AI tools in the EU comply with AI Act high-risk safety, transparency and quality obligations and conformity assessments.
quote: For example, in the EU, the recent AI Act classifies all AI tools in healthcare as high risk, hence they must comply with safety, transparency and quality obligations, and undergo conformity assessments.
hazard: Deploying non-compliant high-risk AI

statement: Have developers, domain specialists, and ethicists identify and address application-specific ethical and social issues during development and deployment.
quote: AI developers, domain specialists, and professional ethicists should identify, discuss, and address all application specific ethical, social, and societal issues as an integral part of the development and deployment of the AI tool.79
hazard: Unaddressed application-specific ethical harms

statement: Consult ethicists specialised in medical AI or the application domain on ethical considerations.
quote: Consult ethicists on ethical considerations
hazard: Overlooked ethical risks

statement: Assess the AI tool's impact on working conditions, power relations, and deskilling of healthcare professionals and citizens.
quote: Relevant issues might include the impact of the AI tool on the working conditions and power relations, on the new skills (or deskilling) of the healthcare professionals and citizens,80 and on future interactions between citizens, health professionals, and social careers.
hazard: Deskilling and worsened working conditions

statement: Consider strategies to reduce the AI tool's carbon footprint.
quote: Furthermore, for environmental sustainability, AI developers should consider strategies to reduce the carbon footprint of the AI tool.81
hazard: Environmental harm from AI energy use

statement: Regularly monitor and report the AI tool's energy usage, carbon emissions, and waste generation.
quote: Regularly monitor and report on the environmental impact of AI systems used in healthcare, including energy usage, carbon emissions, and waste generation
hazard: Unmeasured environmental impact

statement: Ensure local validity, training, monitoring mechanisms, and regulatory compliance during the deployment phase.
quote: Finally, the deployment phase is dedicated to ensuring local validity, providing training, implementing monitoring mechanisms, and ensuring regulatory compliance for adoption in real world healthcare practice.
hazard: Tool performing poorly in local setting

statement: Define the intended healthcare settings and the personnel, equipment, and IT resources needed at each setting.
quote: Define the resources needed at each setting
hazard: Deployment in settings lacking required resources

statement: Specify whether the AI tool is intended for high-end and/or low-resource settings.
quote: Specify if the AI tool is intended for high end and/or low resource settings
hazard: Failure in unintended resource settings

statement: Identify application-specific sources of bias beyond standard attributes, such as skin colour for skin cancer detection.
quote: Identify application specific sources of bias beyond standard attributes
hazard: Unrecognised bias against specific subgroups

statement: Use community-defined standards such as standard ontologies (DICOM, SNOMED) for AI inputs.
quote: Use a standard ontology for the AI inputs
hazard: Interoperability failures across settings

statement: Identify operational risks including misuse, application outside the target population, use by non-target users, and hardware failure.
quote: Identify all possible operational risks
hazard: Misuse or off-label application causing harm

statement: Assess and prioritise each risk by likelihood and consequences.
quote: Prioritise all the risks depending on their likelihood and consequences
hazard: Misallocated risk mitigation effort

statement: Define post-deployment mitigations such as user warnings, system shutdown, alternative procedures, or reverting to human judgment only.
quote: Warnings to the users, system shutdown, reprocessing of the input data, acquisition of new input data, use of an alternative procedure, or human judgment only
hazard: No fallback when AI fails in practice

statement: Conduct periodic risk assessments, e.g., every six months, to monitor and manage risks over time.
quote: Periodic risk assessment every six months
hazard: Emerging risks unmanaged over time

statement: Maintain a comprehensive risk management file listing risks, likelihoods, consequences, mitigations, and monitoring strategy.
quote: Including all risks, their likelihood and consequences, risk mitigation measures, risk monitoring strategy
hazard: Undocumented risks and mitigations

statement: Request approval before collecting data on personal attributes used for fairness analysis.
quote: Request approval for collecting data on personal attributes
hazard: Unauthorised collection of sensitive personal data

statement: Define fairness metrics and criteria, then evaluate fairness across attributes such as sex, age, skin colour, and comorbidity.
quote: Define fairness metrics and criteria
hazard: Undetected performance disparities across subgroups

statement: Report identified and uncorrected biases in the AI information leaflet and technical documentation.
quote: Report identified and uncorrected biases
hazard: Users unaware of known biases

statement: Evaluate whether AI explanations cause end-user overconfidence or overreliance, comparing performance with and without the AI tool.
quote: Evaluate if explanations cause end user overconfidence or overreliance
hazard: Overreliance on AI

statement: Evaluate AI tool safety by tracking side effects or major adverse events.
quote: Side effects or major adverse events in randomised control trials173 174
hazard: Unrecognised adverse events from AI use

statement: Identify application-specific sources of AI bias during the design phase.
quote: At the design phase, the interdisciplinary AI development team (see glossary) should identify possible types and sources of bias for their AI tool.33
hazard: Unrecognised biases causing unequal performance and patient harm.

statement: Collect relevant individual attributes to support bias identification and fairness assessment.
quote: To identify biases and apply measures for increased fairness, relevant attributes of the individuals, such as sex, gender, age, ethnicity, risk factors, comorbidities, or disabilities, should be collected.
hazard: Inability to detect unequal performance across patient groups.

statement: Obtain informed consent for collecting individual attributes used in fairness assessment.
quote: This should be subject to informed consent and approval by ethics committees to ensure an appropriate balance between the benefits of non-discrimination and the risks of reidentification.
hazard: Collection of sensitive attributes without informed agreement.

statement: Obtain ethics committee approval for collecting individual attributes used in fairness assessment.
quote: This should be subject to informed consent and approval by ethics committees to ensure an appropriate balance between the benefits of non-discrimination and the risks of reidentification.
hazard: Reidentification risks outweighing the benefits of fairness assessment.

statement: Measure similarity of medical profiles when verifying equal treatment.
quote: Measuring similarity of medical profiles should also be included to verify equal treatment (eg, risk factors, comorbidities, biomarkers, anatomical properties34).
hazard: Unequal treatment of patients with comparable medical profiles.

statement: Systematically collect dataset provenance, acquisition equipment, preprocessing, and annotation information to assess technical and human biases.
quote: Furthermore, relevant information about the datasets, such as the centres where they were acquired, the machine used, the preprocessing and annotation processes, should be systematically collected to address technical and human biases.
hazard: Undetected bias attributable to acquisition sites, equipment, preprocessing, or annotation.

statement: Consider imputing missing attributes when complete data collection for fairness assessment is logistically challenging.
quote: When complete data collection is logistically challenging, two alternative approaches can be considered: imputing missing attributes or removing samples with incomplete data.
hazard: Incomplete attributes preventing meaningful fairness assessment.

statement: Consider removing samples with incomplete attributes when complete data collection for fairness assessment is logistically challenging.
quote: When complete data collection is logistically challenging, two alternative approaches can be considered: imputing missing attributes or removing samples with incomplete data.
hazard: Incomplete attributes undermining fairness assessment.

statement: Evaluate missing-attribute handling methods case by case against the AI system’s context and requirements.
quote: The choice between these methods should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, considering the specific context and requirements of the AI system.
hazard: Inappropriate missing-data handling distorting fairness assessments.

statement: Apply bias detection methods using fairness metrics when individual and data attributes are available.
quote: When possible—that is, the individuals’ and data attributes are available—bias detection methods should be applied by using fairness metrics such as true positive rates, statistical parity, group fairness, and equalised odds.31 35
hazard: Undetected disparities in AI performance across groups.

statement: Test proposed bias mitigation measures for their effects on both fairness and accuracy.
quote: To correct for any identified biases, mitigation measures should be tested, such as data resampling, bias free representations, and equalised odds postprocessing,36 37 38 39 40 to verify their impact on both the tool’s fairness and the model’s accuracy.
hazard: Ineffective bias mitigation or reduced clinical accuracy.

statement: Minimise identified AI biases to achieve highly similar performance across patient subgroups.
quote: As, in practice, perfect fairness might be impossible to achieve, fair AI tools should be developed such that potential AI biases are identified, reported, and minimised as much as possible to achieve ideally the same but at least highly similar performance across subgroups to be considered fair.31
hazard: Persisting performance disparities and unequal patient outcomes.

statement: Document any bias remaining after mitigation.
quote: Importantly, any remaining bias should be documented and reported to inform the end users and citizens (see traceability 2).
